## Notes for whoever picks this up

- **Re-check against `main` first.** The review ran at `0cf74cb9c` (2026-11-04); the code links below are pinned to that commit. If the problem is already gone, comment with the evidence and close as fixed.
- **Read [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/main/AGENTS.md)**: the trait-method promotion (`extend`) policy, deprecated blocks go in `deprecated.mbt`, `moon info && moon fmt` at the end.
- **This is an API change, so the `.mbti` diff is the deliverable.** Prefer deprecate-then-remove: keep the old name as `#deprecated("use X")` pointing at the replacement. Put the before/after `.mbti` diff in the PR description.
- **Settled contracts — don't re-litigate:** Strings are valid UTF-16; `raise?` for eager non-mutating higher-order functions; `Json(x)` instead of `x.to_json()`.
- **If the right answer needs a maintainer decision** (naming, which semantics to keep), post the options with a recommendation as a comment here before writing a large patch.
- **Verify:** `moon check`, `moon test` on every target the package builds for (`--target native` for `async/*`), plus a test that pins the new behaviour.
- **PR text:** `Closes #<this issue>` and `Part of #4613 (P1-1)`. Don't write `Fixes #4613`; that would close the parent.

## Done when

- [ ] Decision recorded here (or the report's proposal accepted as-is)
- [ ] Change merged, or closed as won't fix with a one-line reason
- [ ] `.mbti` diff reviewed; every deprecation names its replacement
- [ ] Tests pin the new behaviour on all relevant targets

title: Pre-1.0 API decisions: 39 freeze calls + 44 API findings (split from #4612)
body:
# Pre-1.0 API decisions (split from #4612)

The API half of the round-2 pre-1.0 review, moonbitlang/core#4612 (HEAD 0cf74cb9c, 2026-11-04). #4612 keeps the security, bug and performance items. Everything here is a naming, signature, error-type or visibility decision that becomes a breaking change once 1.0 ships, so each one needs a call — fix it, or mark it won't fix — before the freeze.

- **Part 1 — 39 decisions** (`P1-1` … `P1-39`, IDs unchanged from #4612), grouped by theme. Each has a concrete proposal in its batch report.
- **Part 2 — 44 smaller API findings** (23 Low, 21 Medium) that appear only in a batch report, grouped by report.

P0 security fixes that also change an API stay in #4612 because they must ship regardless: P0-4 (TLS: require `host`), P0-12 (#4596, non-raising in-place Array callbacks), P0-14 (deprecate `UInt::trunc_double`).

### How to track

| State | Markdown |
|---|---|
| **TODO** | `- [ ] **P1-12** …` (append `— PR #NNNN` once one is open) |
| **Resolved** | `- [x] **P1-12** … — ✅ #NNNN` |
| **Won't fix** | `- [x] ~~**P1-12** …~~ — 🚫 Won't fix: <one-line reason>` |

Every item has its own **sub-issue** (linked at the end of each line, and listed under *Sub-issues*) with the full report context, pinned code links and notes for whoever picks it up — hand that issue to a person or agent. Close the sub-issue when it's done (or won't fix) and tick the box here.

In PR descriptions write `Part of #4613 (P1-12)`, **not** `Fixes #…` — that keyword would close the whole issue.

Evidence, reproductions and proposed signatures are in the batch reports, posted as comments on #4612 (links below). `[batch:N]` points at line N of that report; finding IDs like `builtin-10` match the headings there.

---

## Part 1 — decisions to settle before 1.0

### A. Errors
- [ ] **P1-1** **Every `*ErrorKind` / `LimitKind` / json `ParseError` / path `ResolveError` / protocol enum is exhaustive `pub(all)`** — adding a variant after 1.0 breaks user `match`. Only 4 enums in core use `#non_exhaustive`. Proposal: `#non_exhaustive` on all of them now. [cross-package:27] — #4618
- [ ] **P1-2** **Codec errors (`InflateError`, `GzipError`, `ZlibError`, `ZipError`) have no `Show`/`Debug`/`Eq`**; kind names differ per package. [cross-package:20], [net-compress:204] — #4619 — PR #4709
- [ ] **P1-3** **Untyped/private errors**: argparse (`Failed(Error)` wrapping private `Message(String)`; `ParseOutcome` is `pub(all)`), regex constructors raise internal `ParserError`, `@shell` error type private, `async/gzip` raises private `gzip_internal` errors. [tooling:14], [text:97], [async-io:221] — #4620
- [ ] **P1-4** **Task groups report the last error, not the first** (cleanup errors from cancelled siblings overwrite the root cause). Go errgroup / Kotlin keep first, Trio aggregates. Semantic is hard to change later. [async-runtime:33] — #4621
- [x] **P1-5** **Integer `/ 0`, `% 0`, `MIN / -1` have no contract** — native returns 0, js throws bare `Error`, wasm-gc traps. Pick and document one. [numerics:37] — #4622 — ✅ #4776 (documented as no portable result; panic-on-zero deferred post-1.0)

### B. One concept, one shape (sync/async and sibling packages)
- [ ] **P1-6** **Two gzip implementations**: delete `async/internal/gzip_internal` (2.4k lines, weaker ratio by 46–75%, rejects FNAME, single member, no level, P0-1) and build `async/gzip` + HTTP on `@gzip.Encoder/Decoder::step`. [net-compress:51], [cross-package:33] — #4623
- [ ] **P1-7** **compress family has three naming schemes**: flate `deflate_all`/`inflate_exact`/`Incremental*` vs gzip/zlib `compress`/`decompress`/`Encoder`/`Decoder`; trailing-garbage handling differs; no `consumed` count; `strategy?` vs `level?`. [net-compress:175], [cross-package:109] — #4624
- [ ] **P1-8** **`async/shell` vs `async/process` vocabulary** (`env?`/`extra_env?`, `String`/`StringView` cwd, `Capture`/`Collect`, `stdout_bytes`/`stdout_binary`, exit code field vs method). [cross-package:41] — #4625
- [ ] **P1-9** **Label spellings** across async/compress: `allow_exist?`/`allow_existing?`, `max_concurrent?`/`max_concurrency?`, `max_output?`/`max_output_bytes?` (Int32 vs UInt64), `size?`/`capacity?`/`size_hint?`, `end`/`finish`. **Durations** are bare `Int32` ms under five names. [cross-package:72,92] — #4626
- [ ] **P1-10** **Byte-buffer parameters in three shapes** (`MutArrayView[Byte]` / `FixedArray`+`offset?`+`max_len?` / `Bytes`+`offset?`+`len?`); file offsets `Int64` in fs vs `UInt64` in zip. [cross-package:103,155] — #4627
- [x] **P1-11** **AGENTS.md promotion policy not applied anywhere in async/*** (9 types; `Timestamp`'s `sub` deprecated). [cross-package:98], [async-io:282] — #4628 — ✅ #4706

### C. path
- [ ] **P1-12** **`pub(all) struct Path(String)` freezes the representation** (can't become abstract or OS-string-backed; literal sugar `let p : Path = "a"` breaks if made read-only — needs a compiler literal hook). No `Hash`/`Compare`/`ToStringView`; nothing in core consumes `@path` (`@fs` takes `StringView`). Decide: text-only-and-fail-loudly vs abstract + literal trait. [path:16], [cross-package:66] — #4629
- [ ] **P1-13** **`/` and `join` collapse `..` lexically every call and never replace on an absolute RHS** (`"/a" / "/b"` = `/a/b`; `"C:\a" / "D:\b"` = `C:\a\D:\b`) — opposite of pathlib/Rust; undocumented; symlink-unsafe. Plus Win32 namespace-root mangling (`\\?\C:\` → `\\?\C:`). [path:31,44] — #4630

### D. Collections
- [x] **P1-14** **Mutation-during-callback contract**: no container documents traversal invalidation; tree `each` silently skips. (The Array `retain` half is P0-12 / #4596; its audit text about map `update` callbacks is stale, they became `raise?` on Nov 3.) [builtin:72], [mutable-collections:118] — #4631 — ✅ #4786
- [x] **P1-15** **JS views over a mutated Array are type-unsound** (`undefined` as `T`); `MutArrayView` writes after growth reach the array only on JS. [builtin:59] — #4632
- [ ] **P1-16** **Sorted collections**: four types (mutable/immutable × map/set), four different APIs. SortedSet lacks `first`/`last`/`pop_*`/nearest-key/`rev_iter`/`range_bounds`/`retain`; immut SortedMap/Set lack the ordered-query API; `range` is positional + `Iter2`-only and #4333 copied it into more methods. Settle once. [mutable-collections:53,70], [immutable-collections:49] — #4633
- [x] **P1-17** **Duplicate semantics**: `@immut/hashmap.HashMap([(k,a),(k,b)])` keeps first, everything else keeps last; sets differ similarly; `SortedSet::add` replaces an equal element while every other set keeps it. [immutable-collections:40], [mutable-collections:169] — #4634 — ✅ #4728, #4729, #4730, #4731
- [ ] **P1-18** **Map insert verb went opposite ways**: mutable `set`, immutable `add`; `update` only on VectorMap; live `merge` alias next to `union`. [cross-package:145], [immutable-collections:90] — #4635
- [x] **P1-19** **`capacity` units**: builtin `Map(capacity=)` counts entries but `Map::capacity()` counts buckets; HashMap/HashSet/Set count buckets at different load factors. [builtin:108], [mutable-collections:88] — #4636 — ✅ #4759, #4760, #4761
- [x] ~~**P1-20** **`List::compare` is lexicographic**, every other sequence compares length first. [mutable-collections:125]~~ — #4637 — 🚫 Won't fix: List length isn't O(1), so shortlex would lose the early exit at the first differing element; List stays the deliberate exception.
- [ ] **P1-21** **Constructors**: 14 types still have live `T::new`; three spellings of empty (`new()`, `empty()`, `T([])`). Evidence across batches points to `T(...)` as the convention (88 types already). [cross-package:122] — #4638

### E. Text / regex / json
- [ ] **P1-22** **`BytesRegex` is half a twin of `Regex`** (missing 7 methods) and neither `MatchResult` exposes offsets. Settle the string-side names (`find` = first + `find_all`?) before copying. [text:62], [cross-package:150] — #4639
- [x] **P1-23** **`StringScanner` is `pub(all)` with public `mut cursor`** — checked constructor bypassable. [text:116] — #4640
- [ ] **P1-24** **`ToJson for Bytes` uses a bespoke `\xNN` string format** — freezes at 1.0. [text:142] — #4641
- [ ] **P1-25** **Safe-named APIs build invalid Strings**: `Bytes::to_unchecked_string` (odd length → different result per backend) and `Buffer::to_string` / `Show for Buffer` (reads bytes as unchecked UTF-16LE, so `write_string_utf8("hé")` round-trips as garbage). Violates the valid-UTF-16 contract via the ordinary `Show` path. [builtin:81], [text:49] — #4642
- [x] **P1-26** **`Json::number(repr?)` / `Number(_, repr~)` accept arbitrary text that `stringify` writes verbatim** (`json/json.mbt:335`) — output injection; decide validated number vs explicit raw. [text:194] (raised to P1 by Codex) — #4643 — ⏭️ Deferred post-1.0 (fix is non-breaking: `stringify` can validate `repr` and fall back to the `Double`)

### F. Numerics
- [x] **P1-27** **Conversion spelling now frozen by layering**: E4059 forbids methods on foreign types, so conversions into `Float`/`Int16` can only be `T::from_*`, while everything else is `x.to_T()`. Proposal: move `Int16`/`Float` into builtin; deprecate the Wasm-named duplicates (`convert_uint`, `extend_uint`, `trunc_double`, `Double::from_int`, `Int64::from_int`). Parity matrix in the report. [numerics:53] — #4644
- [ ] **P1-28** **Option/Result asymmetry still open** (`Option::flatten` deprecated / `Result::flatten` live, no `Result::map_or`, `Result::unwrap_or_else(() -> T)`). [numerics:150] — #4645
- [x] **P1-29** **`BigInt::to_octets(length?)` treats `length` as a minimum** (`bigint/bigint_wide.mbt:966`) — rename `min_length` or add exact-width checked serialisation. (new, from Codex; verified by reading) — #4646
- [ ] **P1-30** **Parser grammars differ**: `+5`, `0x10`, `1_000` parse with `parse_int` but not `parse_bigint`. (HTTP's use of literal syntax is P0-2 — numeric parsing for wire formats needs a strict mode.) [numerics:131] — #4647

### G. async API shape
- [ ] **P1-31** **Process stdio fields and `ProcessResult` getters are placeholders that abort** when not redirected; `DuplicateStdout` hits bare `panic()`. [async-io:84] — #4648
- [ ] **P1-32** **Reader/Writer**: no `flush`/`shutdown`, no TCP half-close; three `pipe()` functions and two `PipeRead`/`PipeWrite` pairs; platform-varying fd alias leaks; `raw_fd` mbti stale. [async-io:116,150,161,170] — #4649
- [ ] **P1-33** **`@socket.Addr`**: port silently truncated (70000 → 4464), `ip()` returns 0 for IPv6, ordering compares port before IP. [async-io:180] — #4650
- [ ] **P1-34** **TLS truncation policy**: a transport close without TLS `close_notify` is reported as clean EOF (`async/tls/openssl.mbt:527`, deliberate) — EOF-delimited protocols can't detect truncation. Expose a strict mode / distinguishable error. (new, from Codex; verified by reading) — #4652
- [ ] **P1-35** **Process exit status is an overloaded `Int32`** (signals as `-signal_number`, `async/process/process.mbt:179`); TCP `accept` reports the listener's wildcard address as the local address (`async/socket/tcp.mbt:199`). [async-io:197,247] — #4653
- [ ] **P1-36** **Exhaustive public enums + `os_error` exposes runtime helpers; `runtime_internal` is a public non-experimental package**; sync primitives split across three single-type packages. [async-runtime:124,133,154] — #4654

### H. Tooling / prelude
- [ ] **P1-37** **`Debug` is `pub(open)` but every `Repr` builder is `#doc(hidden)`** — ~20 core packages call them; they freeze under unreviewed names. Pick, rename, unhide. [tooling:28] — #4655
- [ ] **P1-38** **Prelude re-exports** now include `FuncRef`, `V128` (side effect of cac7e0647), test-harness types, `UninitializedArray`; live duplicate names (`every`/`exists`, `code_unit_at`, `Iter::head`/`collect`/`combine`). [tooling:112], [builtin:94] — #4656
- [ ] **P1-39** **`Rand::int(limit=0)` means full range**; `@env.args()` shape differs per target; `Rand()` fixed seed on wasm-gc; stream stability unpromised (it is ChaCha8Rand — document it). [tooling:70,76,88] — #4657

## Part 2 — smaller API findings from the batch reports

#### `builtin` — [report](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/issues/4612#issuecomment-6620746235)

- [ ] **builtin-10** The new `range_equal` family (since 2026-10-27) is incomplete, next to more ad-hoc allocation-avoidance helpers (Medium · breaking: no) — #4658
- [ ] **builtin-11** `MutArrayView::blit_from_array` (added 2026-10-23) adds a fourth blit shape (Medium · breaking: no) — #4659
- [ ] **builtin-12** Small gaps (Low · breaking: no) — #4660 — PR #4707
- [x] **builtin-15** `pad_start`/`pad_end` mix units (Low · breaking: yes) — #4661 — ✅ #4785 (pad counted in UTF-16 units, finishing the JS alignment of 1634bf48c; no `.mbti` change)

#### `text` — [report](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/issues/4612#issuecomment-6620746724)

- [ ] **text-12** `internal_search` is unmarked public API, and the READMEs teach it (Low · breaking: no) — #4662
- [ ] **text-14** `Lexbuf::from_fn` source cannot raise (Low · breaking: no) — #4663

#### `numerics` — [report](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/issues/4612#issuecomment-6620747252)

- [ ] **numerics-9** Tuple `Default` is invisible unless `@tuple` is imported, and tuple `Hash` stops at arity 7 (Medium · breaking: no) — #4665 — PR #4707
- [ ] **numerics-10** Integer primitives that are missing on every width, and `next_power_of_two`'s contract (Medium · breaking: partly) — #4666
- [ ] **numerics-11** BigInt signatures to settle (beyond #4272's `abs`/`signum`/`to_octets` items) (Medium · breaking: yes) — #4667
- [ ] **numerics-15** Floating-point nits (Low · breaking: no) — #4668 — PR #4710

#### `mutable-collections` — [report](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/issues/4612#issuecomment-6620747729)

- [ ] **mutable-collections-10** SortedMap still lacks most of the Map/HashMap mutation API; its `get_or_init`/`update_or_default` contract is stricter than its siblings' (Medium · breaking: no) — #4671
- [ ] **mutable-collections-11** Queue keeps references to removed elements and offers no way to release them (Medium · breaking: no) — #4672 — PR #4705

title: Pre-1.0 review, round 2: security, bugs and performance (API decisions split to #4613)
body:
# Pre-1.0 API review, round 2 — consolidated findings (HEAD 0cf74cb9c, 2026-11-04)

11 reviewers (10 per-package batches + 1 cross-package), each with an independent Codex pass whose claims
were re-verified by the reviewer. Follows up moonbitlang/core#4272 (2026-09-24), which did not cover anything
added since: `async/*`, `compress/*`, `archive/zip`, `path`, the bytes regex.

Raw totals (overlaps not merged): **48 High, 95 Medium, 58 Low.** Per-batch reports hold the evidence,
file:line references, reproductions and proposed signatures. They are posted as comments on this
issue (index at the bottom); `[batch:line]` points at a line of that batch's report.

Severity here is re-ranked across batches:
- **P0** — security / memory safety / data loss. Fix regardless of 1.0, non-breaking.
- **P1** — API decisions that are breaking (or deprecate-then-remove) and must be settled before 1.0 — **moved to #4613**.
- **P2** — non-breaking correctness bugs.
- **P3** — performance.

### How to track

Every item has a stable ID (`P0-3`, `P1-12`, `P2-27`, …). Mark its state by editing this issue:

| State | Markdown |
|---|---|
| **TODO** | `- [ ] **P2-5** …` (append `— PR #NNNN` once one is open) |
| **Resolved** | `- [x] **P2-5** … — ✅ #NNNN` |
| **Won't fix** | `- [x] ~~**P2-5** …~~ — 🚫 Won't fix: <one-line reason>` |

In PR descriptions write `Part of #4612 (P0-5)`, **not** `Fixes #4612` — that keyword would close the whole issue.

API decisions (P1) and every API finding from the batch reports are tracked in #4613. The 26 non-API findings that appear only in a batch report are tracked by a checklist at the top of that report's comment (IDs like `builtin-13`, `path-11`); everything else is cross-referenced there without a checkbox, so each finding is tracked exactly once. GitHub's task-progress counter only counts this body.

---

## P0 — security, memory safety, data loss

Reproduced by test in the batch review; code paths re-confirmed by a final Codex pass.

- [ ] **P0-1** **Remote-triggerable abort in the async gzip decoder**: a 32767-byte stored block followed by a 65535-byte one overruns the 32 KiB history ring (`append_history_bytes`, `async/internal/gzip_internal/decoder.mbt:428`) → SIGABRT in debug and release native. Triggers whenever the caller's output buffer is > 32 KiB; reachable via `async/gzip` and HTTP auto-decompress (on by default). `compress/gzip` decodes the same bytes fine. [net-compress:35]
- [ ] **P0-2** **HTTP framing / request smuggling**: `Content-Length: 0_3` accepted; chunk sizes `0x3` and `0_3` accepted (wire numbers parsed with MoonBit literal syntax); CL + Transfer-Encoding both present → read as chunked, connection kept alive; bare LF in header values; no header size/count limits. Legit `Content-Length: 3 ` (trailing OWS) is rejected. [net-compress:85,105]
- [ ] **P0-3** **CRLF injection**: outgoing request target written verbatim (`async/http/send.mbt:364`); header CR/LF silently stripped instead of rejected (`:56`). [net-compress:127]
- [ ] **P0-4** **TLS without `host` checks the chain but not the hostname** (`async/tls/openssl.mbt:423`) — MITM with any valid cert. Require `host`, or make "no hostname check" an explicit opt-out. [async-io:78]
- [ ] **P0-5** **Unchecked offset/len in `RawFd::read/write`** and UDP send/sendto (`async/raw_fd/raw_fd.mbt:88`): `write(b"abcd", offset=2, len=64)` sends 62 bytes of heap; read side segfaults. Not covered by open PR #4483. [async-io:53]
- [ ] **P0-6** **Use after close**: `Directory::close` twice = double free (`async/fs/dir.mbt:137`); `Tls` read/write after close segfaults (`openssl.mbt:517,589`). [async-io:68]
- [x] **P0-7** **Checked `FixedArray` blits are OOB** (`builtin/fixedarray_block.mbt:162`): no `len >= 0` check, `offset + len` overflows; `len=-1` SIGSEGV, `src_offset=Int::max` reads OOB on native. [builtin:25]
- [x] **P0-8** **`HashMap::map` + callback that clears the source → `to_array` SIGSEGV** (stale size, `hashmap/hashmap.mbt:874`, `utils.mbt:159`). Builtin `Map::map` aborts. Same class: Deque `map` gives `length > capacity`, `extract_if` leaves `length == -1`, `Set::filter` returns duplicates. [mutable-collections:38,98,110] — ✅ #4712, #4713, #4751; `filter` duplicate keys (and duplicates from `HashMap::map` when the callback moves entries in the live table) 🚫 Won't fix: memory-safe, and mutating callbacks give unspecified results by policy (see #4714)
- [x] **P0-9** **Deque/Queue iterators** read live `buf/head` with a snapshotted `len` (`deque/deque.mbt:1583`): wasm-gc null deref, native phantom elements, js early stop; `clear()+shrink_to_fit()` → modulo by zero. Fix: snapshot `(buf, head, len)` like Array. [mutable-collections:20]
- [ ] **P0-10** **`@fs.write_text/write_binary(append=true)` truncates first** (`async/fs/file.mbt:594`). [async-io:37]
- [ ] **P0-11** **`@fs.rmdir(symlink, recursive=true)` deletes the target directory's contents** (`dir.mbt:86`). Windows: `rmdir("C:", recursive=true)` deletes under `C:/`. [async-io:46], [path]
- [ ] **P0-12** **Array `retain`/`retain_map`/`extract_if` lose elements when the `raise?` callback raises** (`builtin/array.mbt:1249`; `[1,2,3]` → `[2,2,3]` on all backends). Land #4596 before 1.0. [builtin:72] — PR #4596
- [ ] **P0-13** **WebSocket**: masking direction not enforced (`conn.mbt:369`), close handshake can't complete after `send_close`, close code 1006 sendable, UTF-8 check accepts overlong `0xC0/0xC1` (`utils.mbt:52`), truncated payload looks like clean EOF. [net-compress:141]
- [x] **P0-14** **`UInt::trunc_double`** is the raw `%f64.to_u32` primitive (`builtin/intrinsics.mbt:941`) under a doc that promises saturation: js wraps, wasm-gc traps, native release is C UB (one run produced an 11 MB NUL string). `UInt64::trunc_double` is documented as raw but has the same divergence. Deprecate both → `Double::to_uint/to_uint64`. [builtin:43], [numerics:20]

Demoted from P0 after the Codex cross-check (tracked as P2-11, P2-12, P2-13 and P1-25):
process aborts with no security boundary; zip duplicated-central-record amplification (configured limits do hold, defaults allow Int32-sized output); `Bytes::to_unchecked_string` / `Buffer::to_string` invalid UTF-16 (API shape).

## P1 — API decisions → #4613

The 39 API decisions (`P1-1` … `P1-39`, IDs unchanged) and the 44 API findings that were only in batch reports now live in #4613, so API work can be tracked on its own. P1 references below and in the batch reports point there.

title: native: an object leaks after a closure capturing it is removed from its own Array field by clear/pop
[BUG] wasm-gc: invalid module (global.set type mismatch in __moonbit_init) with moonbitlang/async >= 0.22.6
body:
## Summary

On the wasm-gc backend, a test that calls `@async.with_timeout_opt` (or `@async.with_timeout`) from `moonbitlang/async` 0.22.6 or later compiles to an invalid Wasm module. The module fails validation in `__moonbit_init`:

```
Uncaught CompileError: WebAssembly.Module(): Compiling function #256:"_M0FP017____moonbit__init" failed: global.set[0] expected type (ref null 115), found call of type (ref 111) @+28463
```

With `--release` the same validation error appears, this time on `ref.as_non_null`:

```
CompileError: WebAssembly.Module(): Compiling function #212 failed: global.set[0] expected type (ref null 117), found ref.as_non_null of type (ref 112) @+24896
```

The same code passes on wasm, js and native.

## Reproduction

`moon.mod`:

```
name = "repro/wasmgc_init"

version = "0.1.0"

import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.7",
}
```

`lib/moon.pkg`:

```
import {
  "moonbitlang/async",
}
```

`lib/lib_test.mbt`, the only source file:

```moonbit
///|
async test "x" {
  let r = @async.with_timeout_opt(10, () => 1)
  ignore(r)
}
```

```
moon update
moon test --target wasm-gc            # CompileError above
moon test --target wasm-gc --release  # CompileError above
moon test --target wasm               # Total tests: 1, passed: 1
moon test --target js                 # Total tests: 1, passed: 1
moon test --target native             # Total tests: 1, passed: 1
```

## What triggers it

| variant | wasm-gc |
|---|---|
| async 0.22.7 or 0.22.6, `with_timeout_opt` / `with_timeout` | invalid module |
| async 0.22.7, empty `async test` or only `@async.sleep(1)` | no crash; `Total tests: 0` |
| async 0.22.5, same test | no crash; `Total tests: 0` |
| whitebox test, or the call wrapped in a generic `async fn` in the library | still an invalid module |

Version 0.22.6 is the first `moonbitlang/async` release whose `internal/coroutine` imports `moonbitlang/core/async/runtime_internal`. The global whose initializer fails may come from that runtime.

In both the 0.22.5 rows and the empty-test row, wasm-gc reports `Total tests: 0`. It seems `async test` blocks are not executed on wasm-gc, but the test binary is still compiled and instantiated. That is where validation fails.

We first hit this in a real project, [Luna-Flow/mare_mark](https://github.com/Luna-Flow/mare_mark) (`src/runner` whitebox tests). For now we pin `moonbitlang/async@0.22.5`.

## Environment

```
moon 0.1.20261028 (e1e1f15 2026-10-28)
moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62 (2026-10-28)
moonrun 0.1.20261028 (e1e1f15 2026-10-28)
macOS, Darwin arm64
```

The generated code looks like a wasm-gc codegen problem: a global is declared with a nullable reference type, but its initializer stores a value of a different, unrelated reference type. Filing here because the compiler repo does not accept issues.

cc @Yu-zh (wasm-gc) @Guest0x0 (async runtime)

title: BigInt::from_octets makes misaligned 64-bit loads on native (UBSan abort)
body:
`BigInt::from_octets` reads each full limb with the bytes pattern
`input[byte_len - 8 - i * 8:] is [u64be(word), ..]` (`bigint/bigint_wide.mbt`,
line 948 in 0.10.17+d971670cd, line 945 on `main` today). On the native backend
this compiles to one 64-bit load. When the `BytesView` does not start on an
8-byte boundary, the load is misaligned. That is undefined behavior in C, and a
build with UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer stops:

```
thread 11032 panic: load of misaligned address 0x7c99a9b for type 'const uint64_t' (aka 'const unsigned long'), which requires 8 byte alignment
.../lib/core/bigint/bigint_wide.mbt:948:29: in BigInt::from_octets.inner
    guard! input[byte_len - 8 - i * 8:] is [u64be(word), ..]
```

**Reproduction** (Linux x86-64, zig 0.17.0 as the C compiler, debug build, which
enables UBSan; moon 0.10.17+d971670cd):

```moonbit
test "from_octets on a view that starts at an odd offset" {
  let bytes = Bytes::make(33, b'\x01')
  // 32 bytes from offset 1: each 8-byte word is misaligned.
  let n = @bigint.BigInt::from_octets(bytes[1:])
  assert_eq(n.to_octets(length=32), bytes[1:].to_owned())
}
```

A common caller is an ECDSA public key: the coordinates of an uncompressed SEC 1
point start at offset 1 (`point[1:1 + size]`). We saw this in moonrockz/moon-lander
CI (the "Test native (zig)" job of PR #142,
https://github.com/moonrockz/moon-lander/pull/142), through moonbitstack/mooncrypt's
`ecdsa.PublicKey::new`. gcc and clang builds without UBSan, and macOS arm64, do
not show it, because those CPUs allow unaligned loads.

**Suggested fix:** read the word byte by byte (or with a memcpy-based unaligned
load in the C runtime) instead of a direct 64-bit load, or have the `u64be`
pattern compile to an unaligned-safe load on native.

title: Make StringScanner read-only: #visibility(change_to="readonly"), then pub
body:
## Summary

Make `@lexbuf.StringScanner` read-only, so a scanner can only be created with the checked constructor `StringScanner(data, cursor=...)` (#4511) and its cursor can only be moved by `lexscan`. Then a scanner's cursor is always in range and on a character boundary. Generated `lexscan` code relies on that when it builds captures with `StringView::exact_view`, and could later use the unchecked `unsafe_view`.

Today `StringScanner` is `pub(all)`, so `StringScanner::{ data: "😀", cursor: 1 }` and `scanner.cursor = n` are accepted. A cursor inside a surrogate pair makes a zero-width capture at the scan origin abort.

## Steps

1. **Migration warning (core).** Mark the struct:
   ```moonbit
   #visibility(change_to="readonly", "Create a scanner with `StringScanner(data, cursor=...)`; its fields will be read-only.")
   pub(all) struct StringScanner { ... }
   ```
   Outside core, `StringScanner::{ ... }` and `scanner.cursor = ...` then warn (`alert_visibility`), while reading `data` and `cursor` stays allowed. Two things were checked with `moonc v0.10.17`:
   - **Generated code:** `lexscan`'s own write to `cursor` does not trigger the warning.
   - **Constructor calls:** they did trigger it, because a call to a custom constructor (`StringScanner(...)`, which runs `StringScanner::StringScanner`) was checked as creating the value. The compiler fixed that on 2026-10-27 (compiler commit `ee4ac6bebc3`).

   **Timing:** only after the toolchain release whose compiler includes `ee4ac6bebc3`. Otherwise every call to the recommended constructor warns. Core's own tests that build the struct literally need `#warnings("-alert")` or a switch to the constructor.
2. **Compiler.** Generated `lexscan` code commits the cursor with `scanner.__unsafe_set_cursor(n)` (#4511) instead of assigning `scanner.cursor`, both after a match and when the catch-all resets the cursor to the scan origin. It still reads `scanner.data` and `scanner.cursor`, which stays allowed under `pub`. This is tracked in the compiler repository and has to ship before step 3.
3. **Read-only (core).** Change `pub(all) struct StringScanner` to `pub struct StringScanner` and drop the `#visibility` attribute. Do this in or after the release whose compiler includes step 2, because generated code from older compilers assigns `cursor` and would no longer compile.
4. **Specification.** In moonbitlang/lexscan_spec, migrate the 23 fixtures that build `@lexbuf.StringScanner::{ ... }` to `StringScanner(...)`. moonbitlang/lexscan_spec#19 already makes the cursor-boundary rule normative and leaves direct cursor assignment unspecified (LS-016A retired).

## Out of scope

There is no public `seek` or `set_cursor`: user code no longer moves a scanner's cursor. Code that needs to backtrack creates a new scanner with `StringScanner(scanner.data, cursor=saved)`.

title: Deprecate String::view and StringView::view now that the compiler no longer emits them
body:
## Summary

Deprecate `String::view(start_offset~, end_offset?)` and `StringView::view(start_offset~, end_offset?)`.

`view` checks bounds but not surrogate pairs, so it can build a `StringView` that splits a pair. Its doc comment keeps it undeprecated only because the compiler emitted it for `lexmatch`/`lexscan`:

> The compiler generates calls to `view` for lexmatch/lexscan. Keep this method without deprecation until compiler lowering changes.

The compiler no longer emits `view`. Since compiler commit `8ac62e34cdc` (in the release after `moonc v0.10.17`), generated code uses:
- `exact_view(start=, end=)` for captures, `before` and `after` of `lexmatch`, `=~` and `lexscan` over a `StringScanner`;
- `exact_view(start=).has_prefix(literal)` for the block backend's literal comparison.

## Plan

1. **Stack on #4507**, which adds `unsafe_view(start~, end~)` and already migrates core's raw slicing (string operations, percent encoding, JSON numbers, lexer buffers) to it.
2. **Add `#deprecated`** to `String::view` and `StringView::view`, pointing to the three replacements:
   - `exact_view(start~, end?)`: checked, aborts on a split surrogate pair;
   - `unsafe_view(start~, end~)`: unchecked, for callers that guarantee the bounds;
   - `s[a:b]` / `clamped_view`: total, clamps and snaps to character boundaries.

   Remove the "keep this method without deprecation" comment.
3. **Migrate the remaining callers** inside core. Run `moon check --deny-warn --target all` to find them. Tests that cover `view` itself keep it, under `#warnings("-deprecated")`.
4. **Run** `moon info`, `moon fmt` and `moon test --target all`.

## Timing

Merge this together with, or after, the toolchain release whose compiler includes `8ac62e34cdc`. With the `v0.10.17` compiler, generated code still calls `view`. Deprecating it before that release would put deprecation warnings on users' `lexmatch` and `lexscan` code, which they didn't write, and break `--deny-warn` builds.

## Related

- Once `unsafe_view` (#4507) is in the core the compiler pins, the compiler can switch its generated `exact_view` calls to `unsafe_view`. Their offsets are always in range and on character boundaries, so the checks are redundant there.
- #4515 exposes `String::unsafe_range_equal`. The compiler will use it for the block backend's literal comparison, to compare without building a view at all.

title: argparse: a parse entry point that returns help and version requests without exit
body:
## Problem

`Command::parse` prints help or version text and then exits the process with code 0. This occurs for `--help`, `-h`, `help <subcommand>`, `<subcommand> --help`, `--version`, `arg_required_else_help` with no arguments, and flags with `FlagAction::Help` or `FlagAction::Version`.

A program that must keep control cannot use `parse` for these requests:

- A WebAssembly module that an embedder runs. On wasm, the exit is the WASI import `proc_exit`. On wasm-gc, it is `__moonbit_sys_unstable.exit`. An embedder (for example a browser host) may not supply the import, and an exit stops the embedder's call.
- A host framework that must return a result after help (for example, skip configuration and return exit code 0 to its caller).
- Tests that check help output through the parser.

`DisplayHelp` and `DisplayVersion` are private, and `parse` catches them internally, so a caller cannot get the text. The only public alternatives are to disable the built-in flags (which loses `help <subcommand>`, `arg_required_else_help` and custom `Help` actions) or to inspect argv before the parse (a second, partial parser).

## Proposal

Add a parse entry point that returns the request in place of the exit:

```moonbit
pub(all) enum ParseOutcome {
  Parsed(Matches)
  Help(String)     // the text that parse prints, without its final newline
  Version(String)
}

#as_free_fn
pub fn Command::try_parse(self : Command, argv? : ArrayView[String], env? : Map[String, String]) -> ParseOutcome raise
```

`Command::parse` keeps its behavior and calls `try_parse`. Parse errors still raise as they do now. The name and shape are a proposal; another name (for example `parse_outcome`) is fine.

We use `moonbitlang/core/argparse` in a host framework (moonrockz/moon-lander) that runs on native, js, wasm and wasm-gc. Its embedded driver must return control to the embedder for `--help` and `--version`. I can open a pull request with this change and tests.

title: API follow-up for the flate / gzip / zlib / ZIP PR series
body:
Track API design follow-ups for the complete series in one place: #4459 (`compress/flate`), #4460 (`compress/gzip`), #4461 (`compress/zlib`), and #4455 (`archive/zip`). These are decisions and consistency improvements to handle separately after the current correctness review, not requests to redesign each layer in its implementation PR.

Reviewed interfaces: [flate at 200a5ecd](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/200a5ecd084682baf1fe1034e11f0750f3eb71d1/compress/flate/pkg.generated.mbti), [gzip at 796cef1c](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/796cef1c6c50693d75204d3b4601c8a0ddf224c4/compress/gzip/pkg.generated.mbti), [zlib at 5a1f15f3](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/5a1f15f310ef81d2c3883cd1352c10aa396253c2/compress/zlib/pkg.generated.mbti), and [ZIP at 59decff4](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/59decff4f44ee671f16ad0c3da8947ec72390254/archive/zip/pkg.generated.mbti).

- [ ] **Naming and effort selection.** Raw whole-buffer functions use `deflate_all` / `inflate_all`, reusable workspaces use `Compressor` / `Decompressor`, streaming raw codecs use `Deflater` / `Inflater`, and wrappers use `compress` / `decompress` plus `Encoder` / `Decoder`. Decide a coherent vocabulary while keeping the whole-buffer/streaming distinction clear. Also decide whether split/optimal algorithms belong in separate public function names or a common effort/strategy API.

- [ ] **End-of-input and trailing-data contracts.** Raw `Inflater::step` leaves truncation detection to callers; gzip/zlib decoders additionally expose `finish(input, output)`. Raw one-shot decoding offers both prefix and exact variants, gzip one-shot decoding concatenates members and ignores non-member trailing data, and zlib one-shot decoding requires exact framing. Streaming wrappers accept read-ahead and expose `unused_input()`. Document a common driving contract and choose explicit framing controls where useful; preserve the real distinction between a final DEFLATE block and physical EOF for concatenated gzip members.

- [ ] **Return counts with the operation.** `StepResult` and `DecompressResult` are values, but `Decompressor::decompress` requires a subsequent `last_consumed()` call, and ZIP `EntryReader::step` requires `last_produced()`. Consider returning the useful counts alongside bytes/status so callers can retain a result without consulting mutable state from a later call. Include the meaning of `consumed` when input is buffered or read ahead.

- [ ] **Caller-owned output buffers and exhaustion.** Codec `step` methods accept `MutArrayView[Byte]`, while flate one-shot `*_into` methods and ZIP `EntryReader::step` require `FixedArray[Byte]`. Consider consistent slice support for reusable buffers. Compression `compress_into` returns `None` on insufficient capacity, whereas decompression raises `OutputLimitExceeded`; decide and document the intended distinction, including partial-output handling.

- [ ] **Limits, cancellation, and dictionary parity.** `inflate_all` / `inflate_exact` accept `max_output` and cancellation; `Decompressor::decompress` and gzip/zlib `decompress` do not. ZIP has several limit types with Int32 versus UInt64 ceilings and different label names. Consider a consistent bounded convenience API, so callers do not have to implement a streaming driver merely to impose a limit. Zlib dictionaries are available only through the streaming constructors; decide whether whole-buffer calls should expose them too. Specify whether cancellation responsiveness is measured by decoded output only or also by input/work.

- [ ] **Reusable codec lifecycle.** Raw `Deflater` and `Inflater` both have `reset`, zlib `Encoder` has `reset`, but gzip `Encoder` and both wrapper decoders do not. Decide which codecs promise workspace reuse, what reset retains, how dictionaries/options apply to the next stream, and whether callback reentrancy is supported or explicitly rejected.

- [ ] **ZIP editing identity and metadata policy.** Directory APIs distinguish duplicate names by index; `Archive::get` / `replace` / `remove` operate on the first matching name and offer no equivalent index-based mutation. Decide how an editor targets a specific duplicate entry. Also make the metadata policy explicit: `DirectoryEntry` exposes timestamps/attributes, while editable `Entry` does not; fresh writes and replaced entries regenerate headers, while `preserve=true` reuses unchanged source records. Consider metadata access/editing and a preservation policy suitable for editing existing archives.

Keep further API findings from this series in this issue. Resolve the decisions together, then implement them in focused follow-up changes with migration notes and examples. Related broader API consistency tracking: #4272.

title: async_io/http: discard buffered body bytes before reading the next message
body:
Found while reviewing #4431 at commit `b8f106888fe25a7fa95153fe0ec19d7c49b77a05`. Tracking separately for a later fix.

`Reader::skip_body` returns immediately when `self.body is Empty`, but this describes how much body data remains in the underlying transport, not how much remains unread in the reader controller. Operations such as `peek` and `read_until` can fetch the entire body into `ctrl` while leaving some of it unconsumed.

The early return preserves those bytes across the next HTTP message. They are then returned as the beginning of the next message's body. This affects connection reuse, including `Client::end_request`, which calls `skip_body` before parsing the next response.

Source: [parser.mbt, lines 459–465](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/b8f106888fe25a7fa95153fe0ec19d7c49b77a05/async_io/http/parser.mbt#L459-L465).

### Reproduction

Add this white-box test under `async_io/http` and run it with `moon test async_io/http/review_probe_wbtest.mbt --target native` (also reproduces with `--target wasm`).

```moonbit
///|
async test "discard buffered response tail before next message" {
  let source = @io.MemoryReader(w => w.write(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 3\r\n\r\na|bHTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\n\r\nc"))
  defer source.close()
  let reader = Reader::new(source)
  ignore(reader.read_response(auto_decompress=false, request_method=None))
  inspect(@io.BinaryReader::read_until(reader, b"|").unwrap(), content="b\"a\"")
  reader.skip_body()
  ignore(reader.read_response(auto_decompress=false, request_method=None))
  inspect(@io.BinaryReader::read_all(reader), content="b\"c\"")
}
```

Expected second body: `b"c"`.

Actual second body: `b"bc"` — the unconsumed `b` from the first response survives `skip_body`.

### Expected behavior

Discard buffered body bytes as well as any body data still in the transport before proceeding to the next message. In particular, an `Empty` body must not bypass clearing/draining `ctrl`.

Add regression coverage for a partial buffered read followed by skipping and reusing the connection, including a next response with an empty body.

Reproduced on native and Wasm with Moon 0.1.20261021 and moonc v0.10.17+093cb8f9c.

title: Proposal: move `derive` to a leading `#derive(...)` attribute
body:
## Proposal

Move `derive` from a trailing clause after the type body to a leading attribute:

```moonbit
///|
/// Behavior for flag args.
#derive(Eq, Compare, @debug.Debug)
pub(all) enum FlagAction {
  SetTrue
  SetFalse
  Count
  Help
  Version
}
```

instead of today's

```moonbit
///|
/// Behavior for flag args.
pub(all) enum FlagAction {
  SetTrue
  SetFalse
  Count
  Help
  Version
} derive(Eq, Compare, @debug.Debug)
```

This repository has 840 types that close with `} derive(...)`, plus 331 one-line derives such as `struct P(Int) derive(Eq)`.

## Why: tools and readers want declaration metadata before the body

- **The declaration reads top to bottom.** Doc, attributes, name, generics, then body. Today part of a type's meaning (which traits it implements) comes after the body, so a long enum puts it hundreds of lines below the name.
- **The item ends at its `}`.** A line-based tool (folding, outline, hover card, signature preview, diff hunk header) can treat attributes plus header as the item's summary. Today a tool has to look past the closing brace.

  Concrete case: an editor outline that folds every type to `enum X { … }` has to special-case `} derive(...)`, because folding the closing line would hide the derive list. Those types end up as two rows: `enum X {⋯` and `} derive(...)`. With a leading attribute that case disappears.
- **One mechanism for metadata.** Item-level metadata already uses leading attributes: `#deprecated`, `#alias`, `#doc(hidden)`, `#internal`, `#cfg`. `derive` is the same kind of declaration-level information, so parsers, formatters and code actions get one rule: attributes precede the item.
- **Edits land next to the name.** Adding a derive changes a line beside the header, so diff context shows which type changed. An "add derive" code action has one fixed insertion point instead of searching for the matching `}`.

## Alternative: a bare leading `derive(...)`

```moonbit
derive(Eq, Compare)
enum X { ... }
```

This keeps the keyword but reads like a top-level function call, and it adds a second prefix form alongside `#` attributes. `#` already marks "metadata about the next item", so `#derive(...)` fits the existing reading and grammar better.

## Costs and open points

- **One more line per type.** `} derive(Eq)` reuses the closing line; `#derive(Eq)` adds one. Folded, both take two lines, but the leading form puts them in reading order.
- **Migration.** This is mechanical, and `moon fmt` could rewrite existing code. Both forms would need to be accepted for a transition period, perhaps with a warning for the trailing one.
- **Argument grammar.** Derive options such as `#derive(ToJson(style="flat"))` need the attribute argument grammar to support nested calls and labelled arguments. `#alias(new, deprecated="...")` suggests it mostly does.
- **Ordering convention.** `///|` doc comment, then attributes (`#derive`, `#deprecated`, …), then the declaration, so the `///|` marker still starts the item.
- **Precedent.** Rust uses a leading `#[derive(...)]`; Haskell uses a trailing `deriving` clause.

title: regex parser: report errors at the start of the offending construct
body:
`ParserError(at=…)` from the runtime regex parser (`string/internal/regex_parser`) reports some errors at the start of the offending construct and others after it. That makes positions hard to rely on, and they differ from the compiler's regex literal diagnostics.

For the 45,868 patterns that both the compiler's literal parser and `@string.Regex` reject (corpus of the 2026-10-19 consistency audit), the runtime position equals the start of the compiler's error span in 39,235 cases. The systematic differences:

| Construct | Example | Runtime `at` | Compiler span |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| escape errors that are checked after the escape is read | `\x41` (byte escape in a string regex) | 4 | 0–4 |
| | `[\x41]` | 5 | 1–5 |
| | `\u{110000}` (above U+10FFFF) | 10 | 0–10 |
| | `\ud800` (surrogate) | 6 | 0–6 |
| repetition count too large | `a{257}` | 2 | 1–6 |
| unclosed class | `[` | 1 (end of input) | 0–1 (the `[`) |
| incomplete escape at the end | `a\` | 1 (the `\`) | 2–2 (end of input) |

**Cause:** in the first group, a `lexmatch` arm binds `after=rest` and then reports `ctx.error_at(rest, …)` with the shadowed `rest`, which is the position after the escape. For example: `(re"^\\x" + (re"[0-9A-Fa-f]{2}" as hex), after=rest) => { … raise ctx.error_at(rest, HINT_BYTE_ESCAPE_NOT_ALLOWED) }`. The same happens for `\xHH` and `\u{…}` in both `term` and `class_atom`, and for `\uHHHH` in `term` (`class_atom` already binds `rest2` there).

**Proposal:** report every error at the start of the construct it is about: the backslash of an escape, the `{` of a quantifier, the `[` of an unclosed class. For escapes this means binding the suffix under a different name (`after=rest2`) and passing the original view to `error_at`. Keep `at` as one offset, but choose it the same way everywhere.

title: Proposal: IEEE float operators and Hash; total_compare with NaNs first and equal signed zeros
body:
For `Double` and `Float`, preserve fast IEEE equality and relational operators, keep Hash consistent with that equality, and provide an explicit `total_compare` with numerical ordering, equal signed zeros, and all NaNs equivalent and ordered first.

The design priority is performance and predictable behavior for correct numerical code: every non-NaN input, including signed zeros, infinities, and subnormals, must behave consistently across the comparison interfaces. NaN represents an erroneous or invalid numerical result for this design's ordinary use case. We accept disagreement between IEEE operators and total comparison on NaNs rather than making every ordinary comparison pay for stronger NaN equality semantics.

This follows the sorting failure in #4350 and the alternative implementation explored in draft PR #4407.

## Proposed contract

| API | Semantics |
| --- | --- |
| `Eq` / `==` | IEEE equality: signed zeros equal; a NaN is unequal to every value, including itself |
| `!=` | Negation of IEEE equality; true whenever either operand is NaN |
| `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | IEEE numerical comparisons; false whenever either operand is NaN |
| `Hash` | Consistent with IEEE equality; both signed zeros hash identically |
| Existing `Compare::compare` | Ordinary comparison path; must agree with numerical order and `Eq` on non-NaN inputs; not redirected through `total_compare` |
| `total_compare` | Numerical order, signed zeros equivalent, and all NaNs in one equivalence class before every number |

`total_compare` is a separate, opt-in function. It does not replace `Double::compare`, `Float::compare`, ordinary relational operators, or the comparison path used by everyday generic algorithms. Default operations should not pay for total NaN handling.

When neither operand is NaN, ordinary `compare` must agree with equality and numerical ordering, including signed zeros. Require:

```text
a == b  iff a.compare(b) == 0
sign(a.compare(b)) == sign(total_compare(a, b))
```

For neither operand NaN, also require:

```text
a == b  iff total_compare(a, b) == 0
a != b  iff total_compare(a, b) != 0
a <  b  iff total_compare(a, b) <  0
a <= b  iff total_compare(a, b) <= 0
a >  b  iff total_compare(a, b) >  0
a >= b  iff total_compare(a, b) >= 0
```

In particular:

```text
-0.0 == +0.0                        true
-0.0 < +0.0                         false
+0.0 < -0.0                         false
total_compare(-0.0, +0.0)            0
hash(-0.0) == hash(+0.0)             true
```

Always require `a == b implies hash(a) == hash(b)`. Hashing does not execute a floating comparison as its definition; it respects the equality contract. Normalizing the zero encodings and hashing the remaining bits is one implementation. There is no requirement to canonicalize NaNs for Hash.

Equality and ordering of zeros do not erase their stored signs or change arithmetic. For example, reciprocals of the two zeros can still have opposite signs.

## NaNs and total comparison

Use **MoonBit total ordering: numerical order, equal signed zeros, and all NaNs equivalent and first**. This is the selected policy for both floating widths.

In ascending order:

```text
{all NaNs}
negative infinity
negative finite numbers (including subnormals)
{-0.0, +0.0}
positive finite numbers (including subnormals)
positive infinity
```

For `total_compare`, ignore NaN sign, signaling/quiet status, and payload. Any two NaNs compare as zero; any NaN precedes every non-NaN value. This defines equivalence for total comparison only: ordinary `nan == nan` remains false.

This is deliberately different from IEEE `totalOrder` in two ways: signed zeros are merged, and all NaNs are merged into one class at the beginning. IEEE `totalOrder` distinguishes the zeros and NaN encodings, placing negative NaNs before numbers and positive NaNs after numbers; see [the IEEE-based ordering documented by Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f64.html#method.total_cmp). Document this API as MoonBit's total ordering, not as an exact implementation of IEEE `totalOrder`.

The selected policy agrees with ordinary comparisons on every non-NaN input, gives NaNs a predictable place in sorting, and admits an implementation using ordinary floating comparisons without extracting NaN payloads. It does not rewrite floating values or canonicalize their stored bits.

A C reference implementation for `Double` is:

```c
#include <math.h>

int total_compare(double a, double b) {
    return (a > b) - (a < b)
         + (!!isnan(b) - !!isnan(a));
}
```

It returns `-1`, `0`, or `+1`. The same algorithm applies to `Float` using `float` parameters.

- When neither operand is NaN, the second term is zero and the first term gives the numerical comparison. Both signed zeros naturally compare as zero.
- When either operand is NaN, both numerical comparisons are false, so the first term is zero.
- The second term returns `-1` when only `a` is NaN, `+1` when only `b` is NaN, and zero when both are NaN. The `!!` converts `isnan`'s result to exactly zero or one.

This is a reference implementation, not a required lowering. Use ordinary IEEE comparison settings; optimizations that assume NaNs cannot occur would invalidate it. Benchmark equivalent implementations under this fixed policy.

IEEE operator results on NaNs remain specified. Treating NaN as an error case does not introduce undefined behavior or authorize the compiler to assume NaNs cannot occur.

The deliberate exception is agreement between the interfaces:

```text
nan == nan                          false
total_compare(nan, nan)              0
```

Do not require unconditional `Eq` reflexivity for floats. Do require the total comparator to remain lawful for every input, including NaNs:

```text
total_compare(a, a) == 0
sign(total_compare(a, b)) == -sign(total_compare(b, a))
total_compare(a, b) <= 0 && total_compare(b, c) <= 0
    implies total_compare(a, c) <= 0
```

Its zero result defines its own equivalence relation. That relation agrees with IEEE equality on non-NaN values. Returning zero whenever either operand is NaN is invalid because it would make NaN equivalent to distinct ordinary numbers.

## Ordinary generic algorithms and collections

**NaN is an invalid input for ordinary comparison-based generic algorithms and collection operations that rely on equality/ordering laws.** Their supported domain is non-NaN values, including both signed zeros, infinities, and subnormals. For composite or derived keys, this precondition applies to the floating components participating in comparison.

Within that domain, ordinary `Eq`, `compare`, and relational operators agree. Generic sorting, sortedness checks, binary search, ordered maps/sets, and their derived/composite comparison paths can continue using the ordinary traits. This proposal does not require a new generic total-order trait or automatic use of `total_compare`.

For example, a sorted map may use ordinary `compare` for lookup and ordinary `==` / `<` for insertion when these relations agree on its supported inputs. It does not need a migration solely to make NaN keys work. NaN keys or elements violate the ordinary algorithm's comparison precondition, so correct sorting, searching, or key lookup is not guaranteed for those inputs. Primitive float operators still retain their specified IEEE results.

This is a documented precondition, not a requirement to insert NaN validation into every comparison or collection operation. Preserve performance for valid inputs and test consistency, especially for signed zeros.

Callers that intentionally need to sort data containing NaNs can explicitly supply `total_compare` to a comparator-taking API. Such an opt-in path must consistently use the supplied comparison relation for all related ordering and key-equivalence decisions, including subsequent searching. A comparator-driven ordered collection would need that same relation for insertion, lookup, deletion, and bounds. This consistency requirement applies to the opt-in total-order path; it does not impose NaN support on ordinary collections.

Ordinary Hash remains tied to IEEE `Eq`. Different NaN encodings need not hash identically even though `total_compare` equates them. If a caller separately defines a key type whose equality uses total-comparison equivalence, its Hash must also merge NaNs; that wrapper is not required for everyday generic code or by this proposal.

## Performance rationale

Ordinary `==` and relational comparisons can retain direct hardware floating-point comparisons (such as ARM `fcmp` and SIMD comparisons) and the corresponding native operations on other backends. Signed-zero equality and unordered NaN handling are already implemented by these operations. Do not lower these operators through `total_compare`.

Hash only needs to respect ordinary equality, including equal signed zeros; additional NaN canonicalization is unnecessary. The extra work needed for total ordering belongs in the explicit operation used by sorting or other callers that request it.

A preliminary C benchmark on Apple M4 Max with Homebrew Clang 20.1.8, `-O3 -mcpu=native`, and no fast-math compared full three-way comparators. The table reports median throughput on finite doubles in loops that store each comparison result:

| Implementation | Scalar, ns/element | Auto-vectorized, ns/element |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| IEEE NaN ordering with equal zeros, integer keys | 0.634 | 0.381 |
| All NaNs first and equivalent, normalized integer keys | 0.979 | 0.606 |
| All NaNs first and equivalent, floating-comparison expression above | 0.384 | 0.271 |

Both policies merge signed zeros. The bit-key comparator is an alternative policy used as a baseline; it is not the selected policy. The NaNs-first expression used floating-point comparisons without data-dependent conditional branches in the inspected scalar assembly. In this result-storage workload it was faster than the tested IEEE bit-key implementation; adding NaN normalization to the integer-key implementation was slower. Thus NaNs-first does not inherently impose a penalty relative to bit-derived IEEE ordering.

With 515 NaN operands out of 2,048 (approximately 25%), the same expression measured 0.386 ns/element scalar and 0.271 vectorized; the IEEE bit-key comparator measured 0.635 and 0.383 respectively. The input sets also included random bit patterns and zeros/infinities.

**Loop shape matters.** In a separate loop accumulating comparison results, the same expression measured 1.259 ns/element scalar versus 0.646 for the IEEE bit-key comparator. An equivalent NaNs-first conditional formulation measured 0.533 scalar in that loop. The inspected expression lowering introduced a longer dependency chain through the running sum. In the vectorized accumulation loop, the expression measured 0.347 versus 0.441 for the bit-key comparator. These results favor investigating the simple NaNs-first policy, but do not establish a universal implementation winner or an application-level speedup.

The measurements used cached 1,024-element array pairs, one quarter of pairs made bit-identical, 20.48 million comparisons per run, nine runs with rotating kernel order, and consumed results. Three-way results were encoded uniformly as `compare + 1` in both loop shapes. Scalar builds disabled loop and SLP vectorization. Correctness checks passed for 22 edge encodings, including signed zeros, infinities, quiet/signaling NaNs, and 100,000 random pairs, plus agreement among equivalent kernels on benchmark inputs.

These are preliminary C loop-throughput measurements for binary64, not instruction latency, MoonBit backend measurements, full sorting or Hash benchmarks, or a complete proof of comparator laws. Measure binary32 and full compiler/core implementations separately, and retain generated-code and workload-dependent effects when choosing lowerings.

The [earlier PR #4407 measurements](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/5ad03888/docs/float-semantics-benchmarks.md) concern a different policy that changes ordinary NaN equality and comparison. They are background evidence about that implementation, not measurements of this proposal.

## Implementation and validation

1. Add and document separate `total_compare` functions for both floating widths using numerical order, equal signed zeros, and all NaNs equivalent and first. Show explicit use with comparator-taking sorting/searching APIs. Do not replace existing float `compare`, ordinary operators, or default generic comparison paths with these functions.
2. Document the non-NaN precondition for ordinary generic operations that rely on equality/ordering laws, including derived/composite comparisons and collection keys. Verify ordinary `Eq`, `compare`, relational operators, and Hash agree on their supported domain. No automatic NaN checking or collection-wide migration to total comparison is required.
3. Preserve IEEE behavior for direct, generic, first-class, derived, and compiler-specialized primitive float operators, including constant evaluation and patterns where applicable. Explicit total-comparison calls must not be optimized back into ordinary float comparisons on NaN inputs. Preserve floating representations and arithmetic; normalize signed zeros for Hash.
4. Test both widths over signed zeros, infinities, subnormals, finite extremes, NaN signs/payloads, quiet/signaling NaNs, and random bit patterns. Check ordinary comparison laws and operator/comparator agreement on non-NaN inputs; check `total_compare` laws for all inputs. Verify every NaN compares as zero against every other NaN and precedes every non-NaN. Test ordinary collections on supported inputs, and explicitly comparator-driven sorting/searching on inputs that include NaNs.
5. Measure ordinary operations and explicit total comparison separately across native, Wasm, Wasm GC, and JS. Include direct/generic calls, hashing, sorting/searching, and collections; retain absolute timings, raw runs, versions, and dispersion. Confirm everyday non-NaN operations incur no new total-comparison overhead. Verify the opt-in policy across backends, including runtimes that canonicalize NaNs; its result must not depend on a particular NaN sign or payload.

This proposal retains IEEE operators and supplies total ordering explicitly. It replaces the earlier requirement that ordinary `Eq` and all comparisons agree on NaNs; the earlier reference implementations/tests that imposed reflexive NaN equality are not the contract for this revision.

- [x] I do think that this should be part of the core library and should be delivered to all MoonBit developers.

title: [BUG] moon fmt rewrites a long `x => x` lambda into `x => { x }`, which the compiler reads as a record literal
body:
## Summary

`moon fmt` rewrites an identity lambda `x => x` on an over-long line into

```moonbit
x => {
  x
}
```

The current parser reads a lambda body of the form `{ ident }` as a **record literal** (single-field shorthand), so the formatted file no longer compiles (`There is no record definition with the fields: x`). Running `moon fmt` a second time makes the intent explicit by turning the body into `{ x, }`. When a record type with a matching field exists, the program would silently change meaning instead of failing to compile.

## Reproduction

`moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12)`, `moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa`. Package with an empty `moon.pkg` and this single file `src/a.mbt` (it compiles before formatting):

```moonbit
///|
fn apply(a : Int, b : Int, f : (Int) -> Int) -> Int {
  f(a) + b
}

///|
test "t" {
  let result_value_of_the_apply_call : Int = apply(1000000000, 1000000000, x => x)
  ignore(result_value_of_the_apply_call)
}
```

```
$ moon check        # ok
$ moon fmt
$ moon check
Error: [4033]
  8 │ ╭─▶   let result_value_of_the_apply_call : Int32 = apply(1000000000, 1000000000, x => {
 10 │ ├─▶   })
    │ ╰────────── There is no record definition with the fields: x.
Error: [4028] ...
```

After the first `moon fmt` the file contains

```moonbit
  let result_value_of_the_apply_call : Int32 = apply(1000000000, 1000000000, x => {
    x
  })
```

and after a second `moon fmt`

```moonbit
  let result_value_of_the_apply_call : Int32 = apply(1000000000, 1000000000, x => {
    x,
  })
```

## Notes

- The lambda is only rewritten like this when the line is longer than 80 columns (here 82 before formatting). With a shorter line, or when the formatter breaks the argument list over several lines, `x => x` is left alone. I did not pin down the exact width rule.
- `apply(x => { x }, 1)` written by hand is also rejected by the compiler for the same reason, and `fn(x) { x }` is still a block. So either the formatter must not emit a block containing only an identifier after `=>`, or the parser rule needs to differ from the formatter's output.
- We hit this while migrating a library to the new toolchain (`Hom::postulate(source, target, x => x)` in tests). Our workaround is a named function (`fn identity(x : Int32) -> Int32 { x }`).
- Related: the `moon fmt --check` CI step passes on the broken output until the code is compiled, so the formatter's output is not covered by the format check alone.

cc @Yoorkin (formatter)

title: Audit callback iteration order in HashMap::map and other map transformations
body:
PR #4355 makes builtin `Map::map` invoke callbacks in insertion order. Track an audit of the other map transformations so callback order is deliberate and documented, especially when callbacks have side effects or raise errors.

This is about callback evaluation order, which can differ from the iteration order of the returned map. It does not propose insertion-order guarantees for unordered hash maps.

## Scope and current observations

- [`@hashmap.HashMap::map`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/e96ede8b5d909fdfc7a36952ddb14068f04b7414/hashmap/hashmap.mbt#L849-L877): scans occupied table slots in ascending slot order; callback order is not documented. Check consistency with `each`/`iter` for the same unchanged map.
- [`@immut/hashmap.HashMap::map`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/e96ede8b5d909fdfc7a36952ddb14068f04b7414/immut/hashmap/HAMT.mbt#L415-L439): recursively maps HAMT nodes and collision buckets. The package explicitly leaves iteration order unspecified; decide whether callback traversal should nevertheless match `each`/`iter` for a given map, without promising stability across insertions, hash seeds, or implementations.
- [`@immut/sorted_map.SortedMap::map`](https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/e96ede8b5d909fdfc7a36952ddb14068f04b7414/immut/sorted_map/utils.mbt#L169-L182): evaluate callback traversal relative to ascending-key `each`/`iter`. Its implementation places the current node's callback before the recursive subtree mappings, so preserving the returned tree's key order alone is not sufficient evidence of callback order.

## Tasks

- [ ] Audit `map` against `each`, `iter`, and `fold` where available; distinguish output ordering from callback ordering.
- [ ] Decide and document each collection's callback-order contract. For unordered hash maps, explicitly distinguish unspecified key order from consistency between traversal APIs.
- [ ] Add tests that record visited keys and use order-sensitive mapped values. Cover empty/singleton maps, collisions, growth, deletion/reinsertion, and immutable collision buckets as applicable.
- [ ] For raising callbacks, test which error is observed and that no later callbacks run after it. Compare against the map's own traversal rather than hard-coding hash order unless that order is promised.
- [ ] Benchmark any implementation changes and note observable behavior changes for effectful callbacks.

Related: #4355 (builtin `Map::map`), #4272 (API consistency). Structural mutation of the source from inside its callback is a separate policy discussion tracked in #4326.

title: [BUG] Float::to_json emits NaN/Infinity as numbers, producing invalid JSON that @json.parse rejects
body:
**Describe the bug**
`Float::to_json` encodes NaN and ±Infinity as JSON numbers, so `stringify` produces `NaN`, `Infinity` or `-Infinity`. These are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 §6), and `@json.parse` rejects its own output. `Double::to_json` handles the same values by encoding them as the strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`, so Float and Double are inconsistent.

**To Reproduce**

```moonbit
test {
  let nan : Float = [@float.not_a_number][0]
  let s = nan.to_json().stringify()
  println(s)                           // NaN
  println((try? @json.parse(s)) is Ok(_)) // false
  println(@float.infinity.to_json().stringify())     // Infinity
  println(@double.not_a_number.to_json().stringify()) // "NaN"
}
```

The output is the same on wasm-gc, js and native.

**Cause**
`float/methods.mbt` has `impl ToJson for Float` as `Json::number(self.to_double())`, without the non-finite checks that `impl ToJson for Double` has in `builtin/json.mbt`. `Json::stringify` then writes the non-finite number as it is.

**Expected behavior**
`Float::to_json` should behave like `Double::to_json`, for example by delegating to it: `self.to_double().to_json()`. `FromJson for Float` then reads the value back the same way as for Double. Separately, `stringify` could refuse or encode non-finite numbers when the input is `Json::number(NaN)`, so that it never produces invalid JSON.

**Additional context**
Still present on `main` (e96ede8b).

title: [BUG] quickcheck splitmix: mix_gamma can return an even gamma, and mix64 deviates from the reference
body:
**Describe the bug**
`quickcheck/splitmix/random.mbt` follows the Haskell `splitmix` package (same function names: `mix64variant13`, `mix_gamma`, `shift_xor_mul`), but three details differ from the reference. The most important one is that `mix_gamma` no longer guarantees an odd gamma.

| | reference (Haskell `splitmix`; Java `SplittableRandom.mixGamma` is equivalent) | core |
|---|---|---|
| odd gamma | `z1 = mix64variant13 z0 .\|. 1` | `let z1 = mix64variant13(z0 \| 1)`: the `\| 1` is applied to the input, not the result |
| bit-transition count | `popCount (z1 `xor` (z1 `shiftR` 1))` | `(z1 \| (z1 >> 1)).popcnt()`: OR instead of XOR |
| `mix64` | `shiftXorMultiply 33 0xff51afd7ed558ccd`, then 33, then `shiftXor 33` (MurmurHash3 `fmix64`) | the first shift is `30` |

**To Reproduce**
Replicating core's `mix_gamma` gives an even gamma for 50,035 of 100,000 seeds; the reference never does. The "too few bit transitions" fix-up branch fires 0 times with core's formula versus 2,161 times with the reference, because the OR-based count is almost always ≥ 24. The replica matched MoonBit's output on all four backends for 64 seeds.

**Expected behavior**
Gamma must be odd. With an even gamma, `seed += gamma` has period 2^(64 − v₂(gamma)) instead of 2^64, and streams produced by `split` are less independent, which is exactly what `mixGamma` in the SplitMix paper (Steele, Lea, Flood, OOPSLA 2014) is meant to prevent. The fix:

```moonbit
fn mix_gamma(z0 : UInt64) -> UInt64 {
  let z1 = mix64variant13(z0) | 1
  let n = (z1 ^ (z1 >> 1)).popcnt()
  if n >= 24 { z1 } else { z1 ^ 0xaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa }
}
```

and `mix64` with shifts 33/33/33.

**Additional context**
This only affects the statistical quality of quickcheck's generated data. The output is bit-identical across backends, so reproducibility is not affected. Still present on `main` (e96ede8b). Changing it would change the sequences generated for existing seeds.

title: [BUG] atan2 and acos ports drop two fdlibm lines (m &= 1, SET_LOW_WORD), losing accuracy and diverging from js
body:
**Describe the bug**
Two lines of fdlibm were lost when `atan2` and `acos` were ported to `math/trig_double_nonjs.mbt` (used on wasm, wasm-gc and native). Both functions stay within 1 ulp, but they are less accurate than the original fdlibm, and they are the main source of bitwise differences from the js backend, which uses V8's fdlibm.

**1. `atan2(y, x)` with `x < 0` and `|y / x| > 2^60`**

```moonbit
test {
  let x = [-5.0e-324][0]
  let y = [1.0][0]
  println(@math.atan2(y, x).reinterpret_as_uint64().to_string(radix=16))  // 3ff921fb54442d19
  println(@math.atan2(y, -x).reinterpret_as_uint64().to_string(radix=16)) // 3ff921fb54442d18
}
```

The result should be π/2 rounded, `0x3ff921fb54442d18`. That is what x > 0 gives and what js gives; wasm, wasm-gc and native return `…d19`.

fdlibm `e_atan2.c` reads `if(k > 60) { z=pi_o_2+0.5*pi_lo; m&=1; }`. Clearing bit 1 of `m` makes the final `switch` return `±z` instead of computing `pi - (z - pi_lo)`. The port keeps `z = pi_o_2 + 0.5 * pi_lo` but drops `m &= 1`, so for `x < 0` it evaluates `pi - (z - pi_lo)`, which rounds differently. In a randomized comparison, 2,336 of the 2,737 inputs where `atan2` differed between js and wasm came from this branch.

**2. `acos(x)` for `x > 0.5`**

fdlibm `e_acos.c` uses

```c
df = s;
SET_LOW_WORD(df,0);
c  = (z-df*df)/(s+df);
```

Clearing the low word makes `df*df` exact, so that `c` is the true correction term. The port has `let df = s` followed by `let c = (z - df * df) / (s + df)`, without the truncation. Against MPFR on the same inputs with x > 0.5, core gave 675 results that are not correctly rounded (max 0.829 ulp). V8's fdlibm gave 98 (max 0.591 ulp). This branch accounts for most of the 794 inputs where `acos` differs between js and wasm.

**Expected behavior**
Port both lines from fdlibm (`m = m & 1` in the `k > 60` branch; zero the low 32 bits of `df` before computing `c`), so that the results match fdlibm and the js backend.

**Additional context**
Measured against MPFR 4.2.2, correctly rounded to binary64. Both are still present on `main` (e96ede8b), in `math/trig_double_nonjs.mbt`.

title: [BUG] @math.hypot / hypotf exceed 1 ulp and miss exact results (hypot(99, 20) != 101)
body:
**Describe the bug**
`@math.hypot` and `@math.hypotf` have errors of up to 1.74 and 1.85 ulp, and they get exact cases wrong. For example `hypot(99, 20)` is not `101`. In 4,740 Pythagorean-triple inputs (the triples as given, and scaled by 2^900 and by 2^-1000), 1,053 (22%) were off by 1 ulp. A constant in the implementation also has the wrong value.

**To Reproduce**

```moonbit
test {
  let a = [99.0][0]
  println(@math.hypot(a, 20.0) == 101.0) // false
  println(@math.hypot(a, 20.0))          // not 101
}
```

The worst case found is `hypot(0xc127d00ce80451e2, 0xc13dac6a5bf9e60e)` (given as bit patterns), which returns `0x413ff91b885e098e`, 1.74 ulp from the correctly rounded result.

**Cause**
- `math/algebraic_double_nonjs.mbt`: the result is computed as `x * sqrt(1 + r*r)` with `r = y / x`. The quotient and the square each add a rounding, and the total error is not bounded below 1 ulp. fdlibm `e_hypot.c` and musl `hypot.c` keep the error below 1 ulp, and CORE-MATH's `hypot` is correctly rounded.
- `double_epsilon` is `0x0.0000000000001P-1022`, the smallest subnormal (4.9e-324), not the machine epsilon 2^-52 (the Boost original uses `tools::epsilon<T>()`). As a result the early-return branch that depends on it never fires. I saw no wrong result from this, but the constant does not mean what its name says.
- `hypotf` (`math/algebraic.mbt`) computes in binary32. musl computes `hypotf` in double, which is almost always correctly rounded.

**Expected behavior**
Error below 1 ulp, with exact results whenever the true result is representable, as in fdlibm and musl. Correct rounding (IEEE 754-2019 §9.2) is the ideal.

**Additional context**
- #3913 (NaN/inf handling) is a different issue.
- Measured against MPFR 4.2.2. Still present on `main` (e96ede8b). On js, V8's `Math.hypot` gave the same results as wasm for these inputs.

title: [BUG] Double::compare / Float::compare return 0 for NaN, so sort does not sort
body:
**Describe the bug**
`Double::compare` and `Float::compare` return `0` whenever either operand is NaN. The documentation says "If either value is NaN, returns an implementation-defined value that is consistent with total ordering", but returning `0` makes NaN equal to every value, so the relation is not transitive. As a result `Array::sort` does not sort the non-NaN elements correctly either.

**To Reproduce**

```moonbit
test {
  let nan = 0.0 / [0.0][0]
  let a : Array[Double] = [3.0, 1.0, nan, 2.0, 0.0, -1.0]
  a.sort()
  println(a)               // [1, 3, NaN, -1, 0, 2] on every target
  println(nan.compare(1.0)) // 0
  println((1.0).compare(nan)) // 0
}
```

**Cause**
`%f64_compare` (`builtin/intrinsics.mbt`) and `%f32.compare` (`float/methods.mbt`); on js it is `(a >= b) - (a <= b)`, and the other targets have the same semantics.

**Expected behavior**
Either `compare` implements a total order, for example IEEE 754-2019 §5.10 `totalOrder`, or "NaN sorts after every number" with `-0 < +0` optional, so that `sort`, `binary_search`, `sorted_map` and `sorted_set` behave; or the documentation states that `compare` is a partial order and that sorting arrays containing NaN is unspecified.

**Additional context**
- Commit 9e35c77c (sorted_map) already notes that relational operators disagree with `Compare::compare` for NaN, but `compare` itself was not changed.
- Still present on `main` (e96ede8b).

title: [BUG] Float::from_int64 / from_uint64 round twice on the js backend
body:
**Describe the bug**
On the js backend, `Float::from_int64`, `Float::from_uint64` and the deprecated `Int64::to_float` / `UInt64::to_float` round twice: first to Double, then to Float. The result is not correctly rounded and differs from wasm, wasm-gc and native.

**To Reproduce**

```moonbit
test {
  let x = [9007199791611905L][0] // 2^53 + 2^29 + 1
  println(Float::from_int64(x).reinterpret_as_uint().to_string(radix=16))
}
```

| input | wasm / wasm-gc / native | js | correctly rounded |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Float::from_int64(2^53 + 2^29 + 1)` | `5a000001` | `5a000000` | `5a000001` |
| `Float::from_int64(2^62 + 2^38 + 1)` | `5e800001` | `5e800000` | `5e800001` |
| `Float::from_uint64(2^53 + 2^29 + 1)` | `5a000001` | `5a000000` | `5a000001` |

`Int → Float` and `UInt → Float` are correct on js, because a 32-bit value converts to Double exactly.

**Cause**
- `float/methods.mbt`: under `#cfg(target="js")`, `Float::from_uint64` and `Float::from_int64` are `Float::from_double(self.to_double())`.
- The intrinsics `%i64.to_f32` / `%u64.to_f32` are lowered on js to `Math.fround(<convert to f64>)`.

The first conversion rounds 2^53 + 2^29 + 1 to 2^53 + 2^29, which is a binary32 tie; ties-to-even then rounds down.

**Expected behavior**
IEEE 754-2019 §5.4.1 `convertFromInt` rounds once, here to nearest with ties to even, giving the same bits on every target.

A possible fix on js is to round to odd before `Math.fround`. Let `n = bit_length(|x|)`. If `n > 53`, take `k = n - 53` and `y = (|x| >> k) | (low k bits != 0)`, then compute `Number(y) * 2^k`, which is exact, and apply `Math.fround`. Because 53 ≥ 2·24 + 2, rounding to odd first and then to binary32 is a single correct rounding.

**Additional context**
Still present on `main` (e96ede8b).

title: [BUG] Integer division and remainder by zero do not panic on native and on js --release
body:
**Describe the bug**
Integer division and remainder by zero are documented to panic, for example `Int::op_div` "Throws a panic if `divisor` is zero" (`builtin/intrinsics.mbt`), and likewise for `Int64` and the `UInt`/`UInt64` remainders. On wasm and wasm-gc they trap, and on js in debug they panic. On native (debug and release) and on js `--release`, they silently return a value, and that value changes with the optimization level.

**To Reproduce**

```moonbit
test {
  let z = [0][0] // runtime zero, so the division is not constant-folded
  println("7/0=\{7 / z} 7%0=\{7 % z}")
}
```

| target | `7 / 0` | `7 % 0` |
|---|---|---|
| wasm, wasm-gc (debug and release) | trap: divide by zero | trap: remainder by zero |
| js (debug) | panic | panic |
| js `--release` | `0` | `0` |
| native debug (arm64) | `0` | `7` |
| native `--release` (arm64, clang -O2) | `0` / SIGTRAP | `0` / SIGTRAP |

Observed with moon 0.1.20260920 / moonc v0.10.14 on macOS arm64. Under native `--release` the outcome depends on the surrounding code. As a standalone test it printed `0`; placed in core's own `builtin` test package on `main`, it instead killed the process with SIGTRAP; and another build measured `7 / 0 = 7`. `Int64` behaves the same on native. `UInt`, `Int16`, `UInt16` and `Byte` behave the same on native and js `--release`. On x86-64 native, the division by zero is expected to raise SIGFPE instead.

**Cause**
This is in code generation, not in core's MoonBit source:
- js debug emits `if (z === 0) { $panic(); }` before the division, but js release drops it and emits `7 / z | 0`. Because `Infinity | 0` and `NaN | 0` are both `0`, the result is `0`.
