title: js backend: lower %bytes.unsafe_{read,write}_uint64_{le,be} to DataView get/setBigUint64 (12-18x)
body:
## Summary

On the js backend, `%bytes.unsafe_read_uint64_{le,be}` and `%bytes.unsafe_write_uint64_{le,be}` are not lowered — the MoonBit fallback bodies in `builtin/bytes_unsafe.mbt` are emitted as real functions and called. Since `UInt64` compiles to `BigInt` on js, those fallbacks are 12–18× slower than what the backend could emit with `DataView.getBigUint64` / `setBigUint64`.

**This needs no core change.** The four intrinsic names are already declared, native already lowers them, and the fallback bodies must stay anyway for backends that don't. The ask is purely that the js backend start lowering these four existing intrinsics.

## Measurements

Prototyped with `extern "js"` and measured with `moon bench --release`, 4096-byte buffer swept at every valid offset (~4090 ops), 2 runs in agreement:

| operation | current (fallback) | `DataView`, cached | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Bytes::unsafe_read_uint64_be` | 451.2 µs | 35.8 µs | **12.6× faster** |
| `FixedArray::unsafe_write_uint64_le` | 556.8 µs | 30.7 µs | **18.2× faster** |

Even the naive lowering — `new DataView(...)` constructed per call, no caching — measures 182.4 µs on the read, still 2.5× faster than today. So caching is an optimization, not a precondition for the win.

## Why 64-bit only

The same experiment on the narrower widths goes the other way, and it should **not** be done there:

| operation | current | `DataView`, cached | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Bytes::unsafe_read_uint32_le` | 3.77 µs | 29.7 µs | 7.9× slower |
| `Bytes::unsafe_read_uint16_le` | 2.36 µs | 30.1 µs | 12.8× slower |

A `DataView` accessor call costs roughly **7.3 ns regardless of width** — every `DataView` row above lands at ~30 µs. That is a bargain against the 64-bit path's ~110 ns/read and ~136 ns/write of BigInt churn, and a disaster against the 16/32-bit paths, which are plain `Uint8Array` indexing and constant shifts at 0.58–0.92 ns/op after moonbitlang/core#4097.

Control: the `extern "js"` boundary itself is free. A minimal extern doing one index read measures 2.38 µs against 2.41 µs for the identical read written in MoonBit — V8 inlines the extern closure completely — so the numbers above are real `DataView` costs and would persist as compiler-emitted code.

## Why the current output is so expensive

Read, per 8-byte value — 7 intermediate BigInt allocations, 14 `BigInt.asUintN(64, …)` masks, and a BigInt allocated for each *constant* shift amount:

```js
BigInt.asUintN(64, BigInt.asUintN(64, /* … 7 deep … */
  to__uint64(bytes[index]) | BigInt.asUintN(64, to__uint64(bytes[index + 1 | 0]) << BigInt(8 & 63))) | …)
```

Write is worse — a BigInt→Number conversion per byte, eight per call:

```js
bytes[index] = (Number(BigInt.asIntN(32, value)) | 0) & 255;
```

`getBigUint64` allocates exactly one BigInt (the result) and does the byte assembly in C++.

## Implementation notes

- Both receiver types are typed arrays at runtime, so one emission covers them: `Bytes` is a `Uint8Array` (`$makebytes` returns `new Uint8Array(a)`), and I confirmed `FixedArray[Byte]` also exposes `.buffer`. Note the read intrinsic is declared on `Bytes` **and** reused by the private `fixedarray_read_uint64_{le,be}` helpers on `FixedArray[Byte]` (`builtin/bytes_unsafe.mbt:641,655`), so both need to lower.
- Index with `bytes.byteOffset + index`, not bare `index` — subarray-derived views have a non-zero `byteOffset`.
- Cache the `DataView`. A last-buffer guard (`if (bytes.buffer !== lastBuf) { … }`) is what I measured and is enough for monomorphic loops; a `WeakMap` keyed on the buffer would be more general.
- `DataView` handles unaligned offsets natively, which matters — these reads are unaligned by nature.
- **Semantic difference worth a deliberate decision:** `DataView` throws `RangeError` past the end of the buffer, whereas the current fallback silently reads `undefined`. Arguably an improvement, but it is a behaviour change to an explicitly-unsafe API, so it should be chosen rather than inherited.

## Context

Found while investigating why `Hasher::combine_bytes` regressed on wasm-gc in moonbitlang/core#3278, which led to moonbitlang/core#4097 (unrolling all 18 intrinsic fallback bodies). #4097 took the 64-bit js helpers from 386.8 µs to 342.5 µs on the read — real, but ~11%, because the loop was never the bottleneck there. `DataView` is what actually closes that gap.

title: immut/vector: `concat` builds a 33-child node and returns wrong elements
body:
## Summary

`Vector::concat` can build a node with 33 children — one more than
`BRANCHING_FACTOR`. When that node is also classified radix, indexing masks
child index 32 back to 0 and reads return the wrong element. Silent corruption:
correct length, and `to_array()`/`iter()` are correct too, but `at`/`get`/`set`
are wrong for a range of indices.

## Reproducer

```moonbit
test {
  let mut left : @vector.Vector[Int] = @vector.new()
  for i in 0..<1056 {
    left = left.push(i)
  }
  let joined = left.concat(@vector.makei(1024, i => 1056 + i))
  println(joined.length())                                     // 2080, correct
  println(joined.iter().to_array() == Array::makei(2080, i => i))  // true
  println(joined[2048])                                        // 1024, expected 2048
}
```

32 indices come back wrong.

## Cause

`rebalance` (`immut/vector/tree.mbt`) assumes that any redistribution result
wider than `BRANCHING_FACTOR` fits into exactly **two** nodes:

```moonbit
let new_child_1 = FixedArray::makei(BRANCHING_FACTOR, i => new_t[i])
let new_child_2 = FixedArray::makei(new_t.length() - BRANCHING_FACTOR, i => {
  new_t[i + BRANCHING_FACTOR]
})
```

That holds for `Tree::concat`, whose leaf case hands `rebalance` a center with
at most 2 children, giving `tri_merge` at most `31 + 2 + 31 = 64` entries.

It does **not** hold for `Tree::concat_with_suffix`, which threads the left
vector's tail through the splice. Its leaf case builds a center of up to three
leaves (`[left, Leaf(suffix), right]`), so `tri_merge` can return
`31 + 3 + 31 = 65` entries. `redis_plan` correctly keeps all 65 when they are
already full, and the split then produces nodes of 32 and **33** children.

## When it misreads

The over-wide node is always malformed, but it only returns wrong elements once
it is *also* radix — that is what makes `radix_indexing` mask with `BITMASK`
and wrap child 32 to 0. A node that keeps its sizes array indexes through the
search path and stays correct despite being 33 wide.

Being radix needs all 65 leaves full, which needs the left vector's tail to be
a full chunk — so the left operand has to be push-built at a length whose tree
is exactly 32 full leaves and whose tail is exactly full (1024 + 32 = 1056).

Sweeping left lengths 1024..1200 against right lengths {1024, 1056}, for both
`makei`-built and push-built left operands: **126** results are structurally
malformed (33-child node), of which **2** actually misread — both push-built at
length 1056.

So the blast radius for wrong answers is narrow, but the malformed shape is
broad, and it is one classification change away from misreading everywhere.

## Impact

Reachable from a single `concat` of two ordinary vectors. Wrong elements rather
than a crash, and `iter()`/`to_array()` still look right because they walk the
tree in order rather than by index, which makes it easy to miss.

## Suggested fix

Partition `new_t` into `ceil(new_t.length() / BRANCHING_FACTOR)` nodes instead
of always two. The maximum merge width is 65, so that is at most three nodes.

Found while reviewing `immut/vector` (see also #4083, #4084, #4085).

title: immut/vector: `concat` overflows `size` silently (structural sharing makes it cheap to reach)
body:
## Summary

`Vector` stores its length in an `Int`, and `concat` adds the two lengths with
no overflow check. Because `concat` shares structure, doubling a vector is
O(log n) — so a vector with more than 2^31 elements is cheap to build, and
`length()` then goes negative and `is_empty()` starts returning `true` for a
non-empty vector.

## Reproducer

```moonbit
test {
  let mut v = @vector.singleton(0)
  for _ in 0..<30 {
    v = v.concat(v)
  }
  println(v.length())              // 1073741824  (2^30, fine)
  let a = v.concat(v)
  println(a.length())              // -2147483648
  let b = a.concat(a)
  println("\{b.length()} \{b.is_empty()}")  // 0 true
}
```

Each doubling is a single `concat`, so this runs in milliseconds and allocates
almost nothing — no 2 GB array is ever materialised.

## Notes

Every `Int`-indexed collection shares this ceiling, so this may well be
"working as intended". It is worth a separate look here because structural
sharing removes the usual practical barrier: for `Array` you would have to
actually allocate the memory first, while for `Vector` you cannot. The internal
`Tree::size` arithmetic overflows alongside it.

Options, roughly in increasing cost: document the ceiling; `abort` on overflow
in `concat`/`push`; or widen the length. Filing so the trade-off is a decision
rather than an accident.

Found while reviewing `immut/vector` (see also #4083, #4084). Not addressed by
the PR that fixes those two, since the right answer here is a design call.

title: immut/vector: `makei`/`make`/`from_iter` return wrong elements above 32768
body:
## Summary

The bulk constructors build a malformed tree for sizes above 32768 whose
remainder is at most 1024 elements. Reads then return the **wrong element**, and
`Tree::size` reports garbage. This is silent corruption — no abort, no wrong
length.

## Reproducer

```moonbit
test {
  let v = @vector.makei(32832, i => i)
  println(v[32800])   // prints 32768, expected 32800
}
```

`@vector.makei(33792, i => i)` gets 992 of its indices wrong. The same happens
via `@vector.make`, `@vector.from_array` and `@vector.from_iter`, since they all
go through `from_leaves`.

Observed while sweeping sizes (0 = correct):

| size | wrong reads | first bad index |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32768 | 0 | — |
| 32800 | 0 (tree still malformed) | — |
| 32832 | 32 | 32800 |
| 33792 | 992 | 32800 |
| 33800 | 992 | 32800 |
| 65568 | 0 (tree still malformed) | — |

## Cause

`from_leaves` (`immut/vector/vector.mbt`) takes a shortcut whenever at most
`BRANCHING_FACTOR` leaves are left:

```moonbit
} else if leaves.length() <= BRANCHING_FACTOR {
  let arr = FixedArray::make(leaves.length(), Empty)
  for i, leaf in leaves {
    arr[i] = Leaf(leaf)
  }
  Node(arr, None)
}
```

That always builds a **height-1** node, but the height must come from `cap`
(`cap` = `BRANCHING_FACTOR` ^ (height + 1)), not from how many leaves happen to
be left. From three levels up the remainder chunk gets attached one or more
levels too high, so a `Leaf` ends up above shift 0.

For `makei(32832)`: `cap` = 32^4, so the root is at shift 15 with children at
shift 10. The remainder is 2 leaves, and the shortcut builds
`Node([Leaf, Leaf], None)` — a shift-5 node — as a shift-10 child. Radix descent
then consumes the wrong number of index bits:
`radix_indexing(32800, 10) = 0` selects the first leaf, and
`leaf[32800 & 31] = leaf[0]` yields 32768.

`Tree::size` breaks the same way, since it assumes children sit at
`shift - NUM_BITS` (`makei(32832)` reports a tree size of 33824 for 32832
elements).

## Impact

Silent wrong answers from `at`/`get`/`set` for a range of sizes reachable with
one ordinary constructor call. Worse than a crash, and easy to miss.

## Suggested fix

Drop the shortcut and always recurse, deriving the fan-out from `cap` (count in
leaves rather than elements, so the arithmetic cannot overflow).

title: immut/vector: `at`/`set` abort with "Node should not have sizes in get_radix"
body:
## Summary

`@immut/vector.Vector::at` (and `Vector::set`) can abort with

```
Unreachable: Node should not have sizes in get_radix
```

on a vector built entirely through the public API.

## Reproducer

```moonbit
test {
  let mut v = @vector.makei(1024, i => i)
    .slice(0, 1020)                     // right-most leaf is L28, tail empty
    .concat(@vector.makei(4, i => i))   // 4 elements parked in the tail
    .concat(@vector.makei(30, i => i))  // overflows the tail
  for k in 0..<1027 {
    v = v.push(k)
  }
  let p = v.pop().unwrap()
  println(p[0])                         // abort
}
```

`take(2048)` on the same vector reproduces it without the `pop`, and
`Vector::set` fails the same way.

## Cause

`compute_sizes` (`immut/vector/tree.mbt`) decides a node is radix-indexable —
and drops its `sizes` array — from the children's **sizes** alone:

```moonbit
flag = flag && sz == full_subtree_size
```

But `Tree::get`/`Tree::set` descend a `Node(_, None)` via `get_radix`/`set_radix`,
which abort on the first descendant they meet that still *has* a sizes array.
So `None` carries a second obligation that is never checked: no descendant may
need sizes.

Being exactly full does not imply that. `append_right_leaf` and `push_end` grow
a relaxed node by **patching** its sizes array (`append_sizes_last`,
`push_sizes_last`, `update_sizes_last`) and never re-derive it, so a node can
reach exactly its full size while still carrying one.

In the reproducer, the `slice` leaves a partial `L28`; the first `concat` parks
4 elements in the tail; the second overflows it, so `normalize_tree` calls
`append_right_leaf` with delta = 4, topping `L28` up to a full `L32`. The node
is now 32 full leaves / 1024 elements and still relaxed. The later `pop` empties
the root's last child, so the root is rebuilt from children that are all full,
`compute_sizes` marks it radix, and the descent walks into the relaxed child.

## Impact

Aborts (crash), not silent corruption. Needs several rebuild paths to line up —
a slice for the partial leaf, a tail-overflowing concat to top it up, pushes to
fill the level, a pop or boundary-aligned take to rebuild the root — which is
why the existing property tests never hit it.

## Suggested fix

Require each child to be full **and** radix itself in `compute_sizes`. A shallow
check suffices, because `None` is only ever assigned to a node whose whole
subtree is radix.

title: quickcheck: Arbitrary is derivable but Shrink is not
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

`check` requires both `Arbitrary` and `Shrink`, but only one of them can be derived:

```moonbit
pub struct Point { x : Int; y : Int } derive(Debug, @qc.Arbitrary)          // ok
pub struct Point { x : Int; y : Int } derive(Debug, @shrink.Shrink)         // error
// Don't know how to derive trait @shrink.Shrink for type Point
```

So the path of least resistance for a custom type is a hand-written no-op instance, which **silently disables shrinking** — the counterexample keeps irrelevant noise. Same seed, same property shape:

```
derived Arbitrary + no-op Shrink -> Falsified(counterexample={ x: 3, y: -8 }, shrinks=0, shrink_attempts=0)
Int (real Shrink instance)       -> Falsified(counterexample=3,              shrinks=0, shrink_attempts=2)
```

The `y: -8` is unrelated to the failing predicate and would be minimized away by any structural shrinker. Nothing warns that shrinking is inert.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

`derive(Shrink)` for structs and enums:
- struct: shrink one field at a time, holding the others fixed;
- enum: shrink the payload within a constructor, optionally toward earlier constructors.

**Important:** for recursive types, field-wise shrinking alone is close to useless — it only ever shrinks leaves, so the structure never gets smaller and counterexamples stay large. A derived instance should also replace a node with its same-typed subterms (what Haskell's `genericShrink` does via `subterms`); the compiler knows which fields are Self-typed, and subterms are structurally smaller so well-foundedness is preserved. I would argue the feature is only worth shipping with that included.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Hand-writing instances (what we did — 97 lines for a two-type model, most of it mechanical field/entry plumbing), or accepting the no-op and losing shrinking.

**Additional context**

I understand this is a compiler-side change rather than a core-library one: `derive` is a closed set in `moonc` (a user-defined trait cannot be derived at all), and the table is `Arbitrary, Compare, Debug, Default, FromJson, Hash, Show, ToJson`. Filing here because that is where quickcheck lives and where the pain is felt — please move it if the compiler repo is the right home. `Arbitrary` already being in that table suggests the incremental cost is a table entry plus a codegen rule shaped like Arbitrary's.

Note that #4076 (`Shrink for Map`) blocks derive from being useful on map-shaped models regardless.

Verified against the 2026-08-11 toolchain. Related: #4076, #4077, #4078.

- [x] I do think that this should be part of the core library and should be delivered to all the MoonBit developers.

title: quickcheck: no way to drive a property with an explicit Generator (forall)
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

`check`/`report` always draw inputs from the type's `Arbitrary` instance. There is no way to say "test this property over *this* generator", the equivalent of classic QuickCheck's `forAll gen prop`:

```moonbit
@qc.check((x : Int) => x > 0, generator=@qc.int_range(1, 100))
//                            ^ no such parameter
```

This makes the `Generator` combinator API (`int_range`, `char_range`, `frequency`, `zip*`, `sized`, …) unusable for the thing generators exist for — restricting the distribution of a property's input — unless you own the input type.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Both available workarounds are unsatisfying, measured on the 2026-08-11 toolchain:

1. **`filter`** — semantically wrong tool, and it fails outright on narrow predicates. A 1-in-50 condition never completes the run:
   ```moonbit
   @qc.report((x : Int) => x % 50 == 0, filter=x => x % 50 == 0)
   // => GaveUp(tests=47, discarded=1000)
   ```
2. **Newtype wrapper with its own `Arbitrary`** — works, but costs a wrapper struct, an `Arbitrary` impl, a `Shrink` impl and an extra import per distribution, and it changes the property's signature (`p.0` unwrapping everywhere). It is also simply unavailable when the natural input is a foreign type you do not own.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A `forall`-style entry point taking the generator explicitly, e.g.

```moonbit
pub fn[A : @shrink.Shrink + @debug.Debug] forall(
  Generator[A], (A) -> Bool raise?, /* same optional params as check */
) -> Unit raise
```

as a sibling of `check` (dropping the `Arbitrary` bound, keeping `Shrink`), rather than an optional parameter on `check` — the two differ in their trait bounds. A `report`-shaped variant returning `QuickCheckReport[A]` would pair with it.

Worth deciding at the same time whether shrink candidates should be constrained to the generator's range: `Shrink` is keyed on the type, so shrinking a restricted generator's output can produce values the generator would never emit (classic QuickCheck answers this with `forAllShrink`). Passing the existing `filter` alongside is a workable answer if documented.

**Additional context**

Found while migrating a TOML parser's property tests to core quickcheck (moonbit-community/toml-parser#122). We only avoided the problem because we own the model type and could point its `Arbitrary` instance at our generator — that escape hatch is not available for properties over `Int`, `String`, or any foreign type.

Related: #4076, #4077.

- [x] I do think that this should be part of the core library and should be delivered to all the MoonBit developers.

title: quickcheck: Shrink trait is not reachable from the quickcheck facade
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

`@quickcheck.check` and `@quickcheck.report` both require their input type to implement `Shrink`, but the trait is not reachable through the `quickcheck` package — `@quickcheck.Shrink` does not resolve, and users must separately discover and import `moonbitlang/core/quickcheck/shrink`:

```
import {
  "moonbitlang/core/quickcheck" @qc,
  "moonbitlang/core/quickcheck/shrink",   // required to write `impl Shrink for MyType`
}
```

Nothing in the `check` signature or the package README points at the second import, so the first custom-type property test in a project stalls on a `@qc.Shrink` that does not exist. `Arbitrary` has no such problem — it lives in the facade.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Re-export the trait from the facade, e.g. `pub using @shrink { trait Shrink }`, so `@quickcheck.Shrink` works and one import covers both bounds of `check`.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Documenting the extra import in the README — cheaper, but it leaves the facade incomplete relative to what `check` demands. Core's own package-organization guidance says a facade should own or re-export the public API users are expected to name.

**Additional context**

Verified against the 2026-08-11 toolchain. Related: #4076.

- [x] I do think that this should be part of the core library and should be delivered to all the MoonBit developers.

title: quickcheck: no Shrink instance for the builtin Map[K, V]
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

`@quickcheck/shrink` ships instances for `HashMap`, `SortedMap`, the immutable maps, `Array`, tuples and the scalars — but not for the builtin `Map[K, V]`. Any property whose input type contains a `Map` therefore cannot satisfy the `Shrink` bound that `check`/`report` require:

```moonbit
pub fn probe(m : Map[String, Int]) -> Iter[Map[String, Int]] {
  @shrink.Shrink::shrink(m)
}
// Type Map[String, Int] does not implement trait
// @moonbitlang/core/quickcheck/shrink.Shrink: no `impl` is defined
```

Since `Map` is the idiomatic map type, this is a common shape for model/document types under test. Found while migrating a TOML parser's property tests to core quickcheck (moonbit-community/toml-parser#122), whose model is `struct SimpleDocument { fields : Map[String, SimpleValue] }` — the whole shrinker had to be hand-written.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

`pub impl[K : Shrink + Eq + Hash, V : Shrink] Shrink for Map[K, V]`, mirroring the existing `HashMap` instance: drop one entry at a time, then shrink individual values.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Hand-writing the instance per project (what we did — the entry-removal logic is ~20 of our 97 shrinker lines and is entirely generic), or converting to `HashMap` in the property, which changes the type under test.

**Additional context**

Verified against the 2026-08-11 toolchain. Happy to send the PR if the approach looks right.

title: string: Regex thread set grows exponentially when a repetition body has variable length (OOM at 31 characters)
body:
## Summary

A repetition whose body can consume a *variable* number of characters makes the thread set grow exponentially with the length of the subject. `^(?:.a?)*$` — "any number of (any character, optionally followed by `a`)" — exhausts a 1.4 GB heap on a **31-character** subject.

```moonbit
///|
test "blowup" {
  let re = @string.Regex("^(?:.a?)*$")
  // Fine up to about 30 characters, then the heap goes.
  ignore(re.execute("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa")) // 31 'a's
}
```

On wasm-gc this ends the process:

```
<--- Last few GCs --->
[…] Scavenge (interleaved) 1369.4 (1397.9) -> 1363.3 (1414.4) MB […] allocation failure;
[…] Mark-Compact (reduce) 1363.3 (1414.4) -> 1363.2 (1383.6) MB […]
# Fatal JavaScript out of memory: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit
```

Nothing about the pattern is exotic — the same shape turns up as `^(?:.\s?)*$`, `(?:[[:alpha:]][[:digit:]]?)*`, `(?:\w-?)*` and so on. A 31-character subject is not an adversarial input.

## What the trigger is

The body has to be able to match more than one length. When it cannot, the engine is fine:

| pattern | body | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `^(?:.a)*$` | always 2 characters | fine at 200 characters (and beyond) |
| `^(?:.a?)*$` | 1 or 2 characters | out of memory at 31 |
| `^(?:.a?b?)*$` | 1, 2 or 3 characters | out of memory at 31 |

Greedy or lazy makes no difference — `^(?:.a?){2,}?$` dies at the same length — and neither does the quantifier: `*`, `+` and `{2,}` all reproduce it.

The `re""` literal path is affected as well, since an optional element cannot be folded into a character class the way an alternation of classes can:

```moonbit
///|
test "the literal path too" {
  let re = re"^(?:.a?)*$"
  ignore(re.execute("aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"))
}
```

## Why it looks like a defect rather than a limit

A body matching 1 or 2 characters means a subject of length n can be split into iterations in Fibonacci(n) ways, and the growth measured here matches that: each extra character costs roughly a factor of φ, and 31 characters is where ~1.4 GB runs out. So the engine appears to be carrying one thread per *partition* of the subject rather than one per reachable state.

Threads at the same state should be interchangeable — that is what `ThreadSet::remove_duplicates` in `internal/regex_engine/automata/thread_set.mbt` is for. It only merges threads sitting at the same expression id *within one set*, though, and here the equivalent threads end up wrapped in `Seq` nodes of differing shapes, so they are never compared. Deduplicating by state rather than by syntactic position — the usual Thompson-simulation invariant, at most one thread per NFA state per input position — would bound this at O(states) per character.

This is separate from #4072, which is about the same code path producing wrong answers. Both were found by the same property suite, but this one reproduces on `main` untouched.

## Notes

Found while property-testing `Regex` against the textbook definition of the language a regular expression denotes. The suite reaches this shape within a few thousand generated cases.

title: string: Regex mismatches when alternation branches accept the same character (missed matches, spans outside the language, repeat bounds exceeded)
body:
## Summary

When an alternation's branches are single-character matchers whose character sets **overlap**, and the alternation is followed by anything else, `Regex::execute` fails to match. The characters that lie in exactly one branch match fine; the ones in the intersection are the ones that break.

```moonbit
///|
test "overlapping alternation branches" {
  let re = @string.Regex("(?:[ab]|[bc])x")
  inspect(re.execute("ax") is Some(_), content="true")  // 'a' — only branch 1
  inspect(re.execute("cx") is Some(_), content="true")  // 'c' — only branch 2
  inspect(re.execute("bx") is Some(_), content="true")  // 'b' — in BOTH: fails
}
```

The third assertion fails: `execute("bx")` returns `None`.

The smallest reproducer is an alternation of a character with itself:

```moonbit
///|
test "minimal" {
  // "ac" is plainly in the language of (?:a|a)c
  inspect(@string.Regex("(?:a|a)c").execute("ac") is Some(_), content="true")
}
```

## Scope

It is not backend-specific — wasm, wasm-gc, js and native all behave identically.

**The `re""` literal is mostly not affected**, because that path normalises an alternation of character classes into a single union class before it reaches the engine, so no `Alternation` node is ever built:

```
re"(?:[ab]|[bc])x"              =>  Sequence([Char([(97, 99)]), Char([(120, 120)])])
@string.Regex("(?:[ab]|[bc])x") =>  Sequence([Alternation([Char([(97, 98)]), Char([(98, 99)])]), Char([(120, 120)])])
```

The second one is what fails. So the exposed paths are the ones that build an `Alternation` of `Char` nodes and hand it to the engine:

- `Regex::Regex` / `Regex::compile` — i.e. any pattern that is not a compile-time literal;
- the **combinator API**, even when every piece is a literal:

```moonbit
///|
test "combinators are affected too" {
  let re = (re"[ab]" | re"[bc]") + re"x"
  inspect(re.execute("ax") is Some(_), content="true")  // ok
  inspect(re.execute("bx") is Some(_), content="true")  // fails
}
```

Everything downstream of `execute` inherits it — `find` yields no matches, `split` returns the subject unsplit, `replace_by` replaces nothing.

## What does and does not trigger it

| pattern | subject | result | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `(?:a\|b)c` | `ac` | `"ac"` | disjoint branches — fine |
| `(?:[ab]\|[cd])x` | `bx` | `"bx"` | disjoint — fine |
| `(?:a\|a)c` | `ac` | **none** | identical branches |
| `(?:a\|.)x` | `ax` | **none** | one branch subsumes the other |
| `(?:[ab]\|[bc])x` | `bx` | **none** | partial overlap, on the shared character |
| `(?:[ab]\|[bc]\|[cd])x` | `bx`, `cx` | **none** | both shared characters |
| `(?:ab\|ac)d` | `abd` | `"abd"` | multi-character branches — fine |
| `(?:a\|a)` | `a` | `"a"` | no continuation — fine |
| `c(?:a\|a)` | `ca` | `"ca"` | alternation last — fine |
| `(a\|.)c` | `ac` | `"ac"` | **capturing** group — fine |
| `(?:a\|.)*c` | `ac` | `"ac"` | quantified — fine |

Two things stand out. The alternation only breaks when something follows it, and wrapping the same alternation in a **capturing** group makes it work.

## Hypothesis

`internal/regex_engine/automata/delta.mbt` documents step 4 of the derivative loop as "Removes duplicate threads to avoid redundant computation". When a character is in the intersection of two branches, both branches produce a thread at the same position, and those threads are indistinguishable — so they are candidates for that dedup. A capture group gives the two threads distinct slots, which is consistent with the capturing form being the one that works, and with the failure needing a continuation to be observable at all. So the suspicion is that dedup is collapsing the two threads in a way that also drops the continuation they were supposed to carry, rather than keeping one thread *with* its continuation.

That is a hypothesis from the outside, not a diagnosis — I have not traced the thread set.

## Notes

Found by a property-based suite that compares `Regex` against the textbook definition of the language a regular expression denotes (all reachable end positions, computed inductively with a fixpoint for unbounded repetition). Four separate properties fail on this: anchored membership, leftmost match, `find`, and capture positions. Happy to open that suite as a PR alongside whichever fix you prefer; as it stands it would go red on this, so I have kept it back.

title: lazy_list: LazyList::concat is not stack-safe under left-nesting
body:
## Summary

`LazyList::concat` forces its result by recursing once per nesting level, so a left-nested chain of `concat`s overflows the stack when the chain gets long. The trigger is the idiomatic accumulator loop:

```moonbit
let mut acc : @lazy_list.LazyList[Int] = @lazy_list.empty()
for i in 0..<10000 {
  acc = acc.concat(@lazy_list.from_iter([i].iter()))
}
let _ = acc.take(2).to_array()   // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Note that it does not take a full traversal to hit this — `acc.head()` is fine, but reaching the **second** element is already enough, because that is the first tail force that has to walk the whole nesting.

## Reproduction

```moonbit
///|
fn left_nested(depth : Int) -> @lazy_list.LazyList[Int] {
  let mut acc : @lazy_list.LazyList[Int] = @lazy_list.empty()
  for i in 0..<depth {
    acc = acc.concat(@lazy_list.from_iter([i].iter()))
  }
  acc
}

///|
test "left-nested concat" {
  inspect(left_nested(10000).take(2).to_array().length(), content="2")
}
```

| target | depth 2000 | depth 5000 | depth 10000 | depth 50000 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wasm | ok | ok | **overflow** | **overflow** |
| wasm-gc | ok | ok | **overflow** | **overflow** |
| js | ok | ok | **overflow** | **overflow** |
| native | ok | ok | ok | ok |

Stack trace (wasm-gc):

```
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at @moonbitlang/core/lazy.Lazy::force[...LazyList[Int]]
    at @moonbitlang/core/lazy_list.LazyList::concat[Int].anonymous
    at @moonbitlang/core/lazy.Lazy::force[...LazyList[Int]]
    at @moonbitlang/core/lazy_list.LazyList::concat[Int].anonymous
    ...
```

## Cause

`lazy_list/lazy_list.mbt`:

```moonbit
pub fn[A] LazyList::concat(self : LazyList[A], other : LazyList[A]) -> LazyList[A] {
  match self.cell {
    Empty => other
    Cons(x, tail~) => LazyList::lazy_cons(x, () => tail.force().concat(other))
  }
}
```

Construction is fine — `self.cell` is already materialized, so building the chain is O(1) per step. The problem is the thunk. For `((a ++ b) ++ c) ++ d`, forcing the outermost tail runs `tail.force().concat(other)`, whose `tail.force()` is the depth-(d-1) concat's thunk, whose `tail.force()` is the depth-(d-2) one, and so on: the recursion depth is the nesting depth. Because the result is re-nested to the same depth after each step, every subsequent element costs the same again, so the traversal is also quadratic in time.

`concat_lazy` (used by `flat_map`) has the same shape, though `flat_map` nests to the right and so does not hit it.

## Why this looks like a bug rather than a limitation

Stack safety is an explicit design goal elsewhere in this package — `flat_map` documents that it "Skips empty inner lists iteratively so a long run of empty mappings does not blow the stack", and `filter`, `drop`, `drop_while`, `each`, `fold` and `to_array` are all written as loops for the same reason. `concat` is the one combinator whose forcing path is recursive in a way the caller can drive without realising it, and `acc = acc.concat(...)` in a loop is a natural thing to write.

## Notes

Found while writing a property-based specification suite for the package. That PR is tests-only and deliberately does not include a case for this, so it stays green. Happy to add a regression test alongside whichever fix you prefer.

title: json: parser constructs ill-formed strings from unpaired \uXXXX escape sequences
body:
## Summary

`@json.parse` decodes every `\uXXXX` escape by writing the hex value directly into the result (`buf.write_char(c.unsafe_to_char())` in `json/lex_string.mbt`, `lex_string_slow`). For surrogate-range values this **manufactures an ill-formed, lone-surrogate MoonBit string out of perfectly valid ASCII JSON input**:

```moonbit
test {
  let s = @json.parse("\"\\uD800\"")
  // s is String containing the unpaired leading surrogate U+D800 —
  // an ill-formed UTF-16 sequence no safe API should be able to produce.
}
```

This violates the String well-formedness invariant ("we should maintain String unicode safe, so `unsafe_to_char` is indeed unsafe"): user code that never touches unsafe APIs can end up holding ill-formed strings simply by parsing attacker-controlled ASCII JSON.

## Spec position

- **RFC 8259 §8.2** explicitly flags unpaired surrogate escapes as unpredictable-behavior territory: the escape *syntax* is grammatically valid, but "the behavior of software that receives JSON texts containing such values is unpredictable".
- **RFC 7493 (I-JSON)** forbids them outright: messages MUST NOT contain `\uXXXX` escapes representing unpaired surrogates.
- Ecosystem: **JS `JSON.parse` and Python `json` accept** them (producing ill-formed strings), **Go `encoding/json` substitutes U+FFFD**, **serde_json (Rust) rejects** with a parse error. Under the Rust-style well-formedness stance, we align with **serde_json**: reject with the documented `ParseError`.

## Proposed resolution

In `lex_string_slow`'s `\u` handling: a leading-surrogate escape (`\uD800`–`\uDBFF`) must be immediately followed by a trailing-surrogate escape (`\uDC00`–`\uDFFF`) and the pair combined into one Unicode scalar value; a bare trailing-surrogate escape, an unpaired leading-surrogate escape, or a non-escape following a leading-surrogate escape raise `InvalidChar`. Valid escaped pairs (e.g. `\uD83D\uDE00` → U+1F600) keep parsing exactly as before.

This is a **behavior change**: `"\uD800"` currently parses successfully and would become a parse error.

## Affected targets

All backends — wasm-gc, js, native (shared code).

Related: #4049 covers the raw (unescaped) lone-surrogate side, including the process abort. Found during adversarial QuickCheck testing (#4045).

title: math: pow special cases pow(1, NaN) and pow(±1, ±inf) return NaN, diverging from IEEE 754/C99 pow
body:
## Behavior

On every backend (wasm-gc, wasm, js, native), the following all return `NaN`:

```moonbit
@math.pow(1.0, @double.not_a_number)   // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(1.0, @double.infinity)       // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(1.0, @double.neg_infinity)   // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(-1.0, @double.infinity)      // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
@math.pow(-1.0, @double.neg_infinity)  // NaN, IEEE 754 / C99 Annex F say 1.0
```

## Discussion

- IEEE 754-2019 (§9.2.1) and C99 Annex F (F.9.4.4) specify `pow(1, y) = 1` for **any** y, including NaN, and `pow(±1, ±∞) = 1` — the rationale being "1 to any power is 1".
- The current behavior follows the classic fdlibm ordering (NaN check first) and matches ECMAScript's `Math.pow` / `**`, so it is at least internally consistent and consistent across backends.
- However, the function's doc comment claims IEEE 754 semantics, so today either the docs or the behavior is wrong.

## Possible resolutions

1. Align behavior with IEEE 754/C99: special-case `x == 1.0` (and `|x| == 1.0` with infinite y) before the NaN check. This is what glibc/musl/Rust/Go do.
2. Keep JS-`Math.pow` behavior and fix the doc comment to say so explicitly.

Either way the divergence should stop being implicit. Found while adding QuickCheck special-value coverage in #4055 (the property suite currently pins the *actual* behavior, and can be flipped to the IEEE behavior if option 1 is chosen).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: json: parse("-0") loses the sign of negative zero
body:
## Summary

`@json.parse("-0")` returns **+0.0**, while `parse("-0.0")` and `parse("-0e0")` return **-0.0**. The same mathematical literal parses to different IEEE-754 values depending on its spelling.

## Minimal repro

```moonbit
test {
  guard @json.parse("-0") is Number(a, ..)
  inspect(a.reinterpret_as_int64() < 0L, content="false") // sign lost (should be true)
  guard @json.parse("-0.0") is Number(b, ..)
  inspect(b.reinterpret_as_int64() < 0L, content="true")  // sign kept
}
```

RFC 8259 numbers are IEEE-754 doubles and every mainstream implementation (e.g. JS `JSON.parse("-0")`) yields -0. The bug is invisible to `Json` equality because `-0.0 == 0.0` under `Double` comparison, so it silently corrupts sign-sensitive data (`1.0 / x`, `atan2`, ...).

Negative values that *underflow* to zero (`-1e-400`, `-4.9e-325`) already preserve the sign correctly — only the plain integer spelling `-0` is affected.

## Root cause

`json/lex_number.mbt`, `ParseContext::lex_number_end` — the safe-integer fast path negates the mantissa as an `Int64` before converting to `Double`:

```moonbit
let v = scan.mantissa.reinterpret_as_int64()
let signed = if scan.negative { -v } else { v }   // -0L == 0L: sign lost
return { value: signed.to_double(), repr: None }
```

Negating after the `to_double()` conversion preserves `-0.0` and is exact for the whole safe-integer range.

## Affected targets

All backends — wasm-gc, js, and native (shared code; confirmed on all three).

## Severity

Low-to-medium: silent data corruption limited to the sign of zero for the exact literal `-0`; internally inconsistent with the `-0.0` / `-0e0` paths of the same lexer. Found by adversarial QuickCheck testing (random 64-bit patterns essentially never produce exactly `-0.0`, which is why existing property tests missed it).

title: js BigInt::to_octets(0N, length=0) silently returns b"" instead of panicking on non-positive length
body:
## Summary

`BigInt::to_octets` documents that a non-positive requested `length` panics ("Throws a panic if: ... The specified length is negative or zero"). The native and wasm-gc implementations honor this for every input. The js implementation skips the validation when `self` is zero and silently returns an empty byte string.

## Minimal repro

```moonbit
test "panic" {
  let _ = 0N.to_octets(length=0)
}
```

- native/wasm-gc: panics with `negative length` (as documented) — test passes
- js: returns `b""` — no panic, test fails ("panic is expected")

## Affected targets

- js: wrong (silent `b""`)
- native, wasm-gc: correct

## Root cause

`bigint/bigint_js.mbt`, `BigInt::to_octets`: the zero shortcut runs before the length validation:

```moonbit
if self == 0 {
  return match length {
    Some(len) => Bytes::make(len, 0) // len <= 0 never checked
    None => [0]
  }
}
```

The non-zero path checks `if len <= 0 { abort("negative length") }`; the zero path should do the same before calling `Bytes::make`.

Found by deep QuickCheck property testing of the bigint package (cross-target octet round-trip sweep).

title: diff: group(context=0) emits zero-length Equal edits, violating the documented Edit invariant
body:
## Description

`Diff::group(context=0)` produces hunks whose `edits()` contain zero-length `Equal` edits whenever an interior equal run is split. The `Edit` enum documents (diff/edit.mbt): "edits never have zero length, and adjacent edits of the same kind are coalesced" — so every consumer of `Hunk::edits()` may rely on positive lengths, and this output violates that invariant.

## Minimal repro

```moonbit
test "context=0 zero-length Equal edits" {
  let old = [1, 9, 2, 2, 2, 3, 9, 4][:]
  let new = [1, 8, 2, 2, 2, 3, 7, 4][:]
  let hunks = @diff.Diff(old~, new~).group(context=0)
  for h in hunks {
    debug_inspect(h.edits(), content="")
  }
}
```

Actual output — the first hunk ends with a zero-length `Equal`, the second begins with one:

```
[
  Delete(old_index=1, old_len=1, new_index=1),
  Insert(old_index=2, new_index=1, new_len=1),
  Equal(old_index=2, new_index=2, len=0),
]
[
  Equal(old_index=6, new_index=6, len=0),
  Delete(old_index=6, old_len=1, new_index=6),
  Insert(old_index=7, new_index=6, new_len=1),
]
```

Rendered output (`header()` / `render()`) happens to be unaffected because a zero-length edit contributes no lines, so the bug is only visible through the structured `Hunk::edits()` API — e.g. custom renderers that branch on the first/last edit kind, or any consumer trusting the documented invariant.

## Root cause

In `group_edits` (diff/edit.mbt), the split branch for a large interior equal run unconditionally pushes a context-sized `Equal` trailer into the closing hunk and seeds the next hunk with a context-sized `Equal` leader:

```moonbit
if len > context * 2 {
  pending.push(Equal(old_index~, new_index~, len=context))       // len=0 when context=0
  result.push({ edits: pending, old, new })
  let offset = len.saturating_sub(context)
  pending = [Equal(old_index=old_index + offset, ..., len=len - offset)] // len=0 when context=0
}
```

With `context=0` both pushed edits have `len=0`. The fix is to skip both pushes when `context == 0` (they carry no elements).

Found by a QuickCheck property that applies grouped hunks back onto `old` as a patch while enforcing the documented `Edit` invariants.

title: BigInt::to_uint/to_uint64 (and to_int/to_int64) return wrong values for large negatives on native/wasm-gc
body:
## Summary

On the native and wasm-gc targets, `BigInt::to_uint` and `BigInt::to_uint64` (and therefore `to_int` / `to_int64`, which reinterpret their results) return wrong values for negative inputs whose magnitude exceeds one modulus, i.e. `|x| >= 2^33` for the 32-bit conversions and `|x| >= 2^65` for the 64-bit ones. The js target is correct (it uses `BigInt.asUintN` / `BigInt.asIntN`), so the same program produces different results per target.

## Minimal repro

```moonbit
test {
  inspect((-(1N << 33) - 5N).to_uint(), content="4294967291") // actual on native/wasm-gc: 5
  inspect((-(1N << 65) - 5N).to_uint64(), content="18446744073709551611") // actual: 5
}
```

Mathematically `x mod 2^32` for `x = -(2^33 + 5)` is `2^32 - 5 = 4294967291`; js agrees, native/wasm-gc return `5`.

## Affected targets

- native: wrong
- wasm-gc: wrong
- js: correct (`BigInt.asUintN(32, x)` / low-64 composition)

## Root cause

`bigint/bigint_nonjs.mbt`, `BigInt::to_uint` / `BigInt::to_uint64`:

```moonbit
let value = if self.sign == Negative { (1N << 32) + self } else { self }
value.limbs[0]
```

Adding one modulus only makes the value non-negative when `|self| < 2^32`. When the sum is still negative, `value.limbs[0]` reads the **sign-magnitude** low limb of the (still negative) sum, not the two's-complement truncation. Same pattern in `to_uint64` with `(1N << 64) + self`.

Correct truncation is the wrapping negation of the magnitude's low bits (truncation to `2^k` is a ring homomorphism): `0U - self.limbs[0]` for negative values.

Existing tests only cover negatives within one modulus (e.g. `-1234567890`), which the buggy path handles correctly.

Found by deep QuickCheck property testing of the bigint package (interop-truncation property).

title: json: parser aborts on strings containing lone surrogates combined with escapes
body:
## Summary

`@json.parse` crashes the process (an abort from a `guard!`, not a catchable `ParseError`) when a JSON string contains a **raw lone trailing surrogate** together with **any escape sequence**.

## Minimal repro

A 5-code-unit JSON text: `"` U+DC00 `\n` `"`

```moonbit
test {
  let lone_low = String::from_array([(0xDC00).unsafe_to_char()])
  // aborts in StringView::sub (builtin/stringview.mbt guard!) instead of parsing:
  ignore(@json.parse("\"" + lone_low + "\\n\""))
}
```

Escape-free strings with the same lone surrogate parse fine (the fast path accepts them), so this is an internal inconsistency as well as a totality violation: a parser should either succeed or raise its documented `ParseError`, never abort.

## Root cause

`json/lex_string.mbt`, `ParseContext::lex_string_slow` — the local `flush` helper slices the pending run with the **checked** `ctx.input[start:end]` (`StringView::sub`), which `guard!`-aborts when the code unit at a slice boundary is a trailing surrogate. The fast path in `lex_string` uses the bounds-check-only `view(start_offset~, end_offset~)` and therefore tolerates raw lone surrogates; only the slow path (taken whenever the string contains a backslash escape) crashes.

## Affected targets

All backends — wasm-gc, js, and native (the abort is in shared library code; reproduced on all three).

## Severity

High for robustness: any consumer parsing untrusted JSON text can be crashed (denial of service) by a short crafted input. Found by adversarial QuickCheck testing (the default `Arbitrary String` never generates lone surrogates, which is why existing property tests missed it).

title: Specialize UInt16 relational operators to avoid generic Compare calls
body:
## Summary

`UInt16` relational operators currently compile through the default `Compare::op_lt` / `op_le` / `op_gt` / `op_ge` implementations on Wasm, Wasm-GC, and JavaScript. `Int` comparisons compile directly to primitive comparisons.

This creates avoidable calls and comparison work in hot loops even though a `UInt16` is already represented as an `i32` (or a JavaScript number) and a zero-extending load has established its range.

Native does not show the same codegen problem: its generated C already simplifies both forms to identical direct comparisons.

## Environment

```text
moon 0.1.20260807 (4da23f8 2026-08-07)
moonc v0.10.7+bc794d341 (2026-08-11)
macOS / Apple M4 Max
```

## Reduced example

```moonbit
///|
#inline(never)
fn find_u16(s : String) -> Int {
  for i, u in s.code_units() {
    if u >= 0x41 && u <= 0x5A {
      return i
    }
  }
  -1
}

///|
#inline(never)
fn find_int(s : String) -> Int {
  for i, u in s.code_units() {
    let value = u.to_int()
    if value >= 0x41 && value <= 0x5A {
      return i
    }
  }
  -1
}
```

Build in release mode for Wasm/Wasm-GC with `--output-wat --no-strip`, or inspect the generated JavaScript.

## Current output

Both Wasm variants load the code unit as an unsigned value (`i32.load16_u` for linear Wasm, `array.get_u` for Wasm-GC). `UInt16::to_int()` in `find_int` adds no instruction.

The `Int` condition lowers directly:

```wat
(i32.ge_s (local.get $value) (i32.const 65))
...
(i32.le_s (local.get $value) (i32.const 90))
```

The `UInt16` condition instead calls the generic defaults:

```wat
(call $Compare::op_ge (local.get $u) (i32.const 65))
...
(call $Compare::op_le (local.get $u) (i32.const 90))
```

Those defaults call `compare` and test its sign. In the emitted Wasm each one performs `i32.ge_s`, `i32.le_s`, a subtraction, and another sign comparison.

Generated JavaScript has the same distinction:

```js
// UInt16
if ($default_compare_op_ge(u, 65) && $default_compare_op_le(u, 90)) { ... }

// Int
if (value >= 65 && value <= 90) { ... }
```

`#inline` on a caller/helper does not remove this difference in the Wasm or JavaScript output.

## Why

`UInt16` currently implements only the required `Compare::compare` method:

```moonbit
pub impl Compare for UInt16 with fn compare(self, that) {
  self.to_int().compare(that.to_int())
}
```

Therefore the four relational operators use the generic defaults. `Int`, `UInt`, `Char`, `Int64`, and `UInt64` provide specialized intrinsic `op_*` methods. `Byte` also provides all four explicit specializations by converting to `Int`. `Int16` appears to have the same missing specializations as `UInt16`.

## Performance observation

This was found while reviewing #3806. With its ASCII uppercase scan changed from `Int` comparisons to an inlined `UInt16` helper, a representative Wasm release run changed the short no-match case from about **24.4 ns** to **29.4 ns** (+20%). Native changed-input cases also moved by several percent, although native's final generated C comparison itself is identical and those smaller differences may include layout/noise.

A local `UInt16` fix using direct comparison intrinsics restored the Wasm case to **23.6 ns** and emitted the same primitive comparison sequence as the `Int` form.

## Suggested fix

Specialize all four `UInt16` relational operators, preferably using the same primitive `i32` intrinsics as `Char` because `UInt16` values are already zero-extended:

```moonbit
pub impl Compare for UInt16 with fn op_lt(x, y) = "%i32.lt"
pub impl Compare for UInt16 with fn op_le(x, y) = "%i32.le"
pub impl Compare for UInt16 with fn op_gt(x, y) = "%i32.gt"
pub impl Compare for UInt16 with fn op_ge(x, y) = "%i32.ge"
```

The local experiment makes the emitted Wasm `UInt16` scan structurally equivalent to the `Int` scan. It may be worth applying the corresponding signed specializations to `Int16` as well.

## Expected behavior

For operands already known to be valid `UInt16` values, relational operators should lower to direct primitive `i32` comparisons without routing through the default `Compare` implementation.

title: BigInt::from_octets produces a non-canonical zero for all-zero input on the native backend (breaks ==, <, to_string)
body:
**Title:** `BigInt::from_octets` produces a non-canonical zero for all-zero input on the native backend (breaks `==`, `<`, `to_string`)

**Environment**
- MoonBit version: `0.1.20260729`
- Affected backend: **native** (`bigint_nonjs.mbt`). The JS/wasm backend
  (`bigint_js.mbt`) parses via `parse_bigint(…, base=16)` and is unaffected.

**Summary**
On the native backend, `BigInt::from_octets` returns a **non-canonical zero**
when the input byte string is all zeros: the result keeps `len > 0` while every
limb is `0`. Because `Eq` / `Compare` compare `len` first, this value never
equals the canonical `0N` (`len == 0`), and `to_string` crashes.

This is a **security-relevant** footgun: cryptographic code that rejects zero
scalars/signatures (e.g. `r == 0`, `s == 0`, `d == 0` checks in ECDSA) silently
fails to reject, since the byte-derived zero compares unequal to the canonical
`0N`.

**Expected vs actual**

| Operation | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `from_octets(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00") == 0N` | `true` | `false` |
| `from_octets(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00").to_string()` | `"0"` | panics (`PanicError`) |
| `from_octets(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00") < 1N` | `true` | `false` (compares by `len`: 3 vs 1) |

**Steps to reproduce** (native target)

```moonbit
let z = @bigint.BigInt::from_octets(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00")
println(z.to_string()) // PanicError (SIGABRT)
println(z == 0N)       // false — should be true
```

**Root cause** (`bigint_nonjs.mbt`, `BigInt::from_octets`)
After building `limbs`, the "top limb is zero" branch sets
`len = max(1, limbs_len - 1)`. For an all-zero input this leaves
`len = limbs_len - 1 > 0` with all-zero limbs, so the value is a non-canonical
zero. `Eq` / `Compare` compare `len` before the limbs, and `to_string` indexes
`v[v_idx - 1]` assuming a non-zero top limb.

**Proposed fix**
Return the canonical `zero` when every limb is zero. The check can be folded
into the existing limb-building loop so the all-zero case is handled without an
extra pass over the built array:

```moonbit
// in BigInt::from_octets, after building `limbs`:
let mut nonzero = false
for i = 0; i < limbs_len; i = i + 1 {
  if limbs[i] != 0 { nonzero = true; break }
}
if not nonzero { return zero }
```

**Severity**
Low-to-medium. Not directly exploitable, but it silently disables zero-value
guard checks (e.g. ECDSA `r`/`s`/`d` rejection) in code that converts byte
strings to `BigInt`, which can turn a "reject invalid input" path into an
accepted one.

**Workaround (affected users)**
Normalize all-zero byte strings to the canonical `0N` around `from_octets`.
`RabitLogic/mjwt` does this in a private `bi_from_octets` helper in both the
`ecdsa/` and `rsa/` packages (see `SECURITY.md`).

title: RFC: A standard database-access interface (Driver seam) for MoonBit
body:
**Background**

MoonBit already has a dozen database packages — `oboard/morm`, `mizchi/sqlite`, `jaredzhou/moonpg`, `mattn/postgres`, `bikallem/mariadb`, and more — and no interface between them.

**And**

Each one invents its own `Value`, `Row`, error type, and execute/query surface.

**But**

So an ORM or query builder is welded to a single backend, a new backend can reuse nobody's pooling, decoding, or transaction machinery, and there is no shared type for anything to interoperate through. Go solved exactly this with the `database/sql` / `database/sql/driver` split: a small contract that backends implement, and a thick layer written once above it.

**Therefore**

This RFC proposes that split for MoonBit — adapted to no reflection and sealed enums by making the value model trait-based rather than a closed enum — and asks whether the sync, zero-dependency subset belongs in `moonbitlang/core`. A driver-backed reference implementation already exists (links at the end); this issue is the design discussion before any code is proposed for `core`.

## Proposed interface

A closed value vocabulary as the *internal* interchange type, and open `ToParam`/`FromValue` traits as the *public* surface. The `Driver` trait is the whole backend contract.

```moonbit
pub(all) enum Value {                    // interchange vocabulary; drivers match exhaustively
  Null; Bool(Bool); Int(Int); Int64(Int64); Double(Double); Text(String); Blob(Bytes)
} derive(Eq)

pub(open) trait ToParam   { to_param(Self) -> Value }                       // bind side (open)
pub(open) trait FromValue { from_value(Value) -> Self raise DbError }       // read side (open)
// blanket impls carry NULL:  impl[T:ToParam] ToParam for T?;  impl[T:FromValue] FromValue for T?

pub(open) trait QueryExecutor {          // a Conn, a Pool, or a Tx — all substitutable
  execute(Self, String, params? : Array[&ToParam]) -> ExecResult raise DbError
  query(Self, String, params? : Array[&ToParam]) -> Array[Row] raise DbError
}
pub(open) trait Driver : QueryExecutor { // the out-of-tree backend contract, ~6 methods
  begin(Self) -> Unit raise DbError
  commit(Self) -> Unit raise DbError
  rollback(Self) -> Unit raise DbError
  close(Self) -> Unit
  capabilities(Self) -> Capabilities = _
}

pub(all) struct Row { columns : Array[String]; values : Array[Value] }
pub fn Row::get[T : FromValue](Self, Int) -> T raise DbError               // typed, checked
pub(all) struct ExecResult { rows_affected : Int64; last_insert_id : Int64 }

pub(all) suberror DbError {
  ConnectError(String); QueryError(kind~ : ErrorKind, code~ : String, msg~ : String)
  TypeError(String); NoRows; Closed
}
pub(all) enum ErrorKind {                // portable classes; raw vendor code stays a String
  UniqueViolation; ForeignKeyViolation; NotNull; Check
  SerializationFailure; ConnectionLost; Timeout; Syntax; Other
}
```

Layered above the seam, written once, generic over `Driver`: `Pool[D]`; a closure-scoped `transaction(f)` that commits on `Ok` and rolls back on any `raise` (MoonBit has no `Drop`, so this is the primary transaction API); `Tx : QueryExecutor` so query code runs unchanged inside a transaction; and optional capability traits `Streamer`/`Cursor` (large result sets), `Preparer`/`Stmt` (prepared handles), and `Tx::savepoint`. `open` is not a trait method — connection setup is backend-specific; the seam begins at a live handle, which is what keeps it transport-agnostic (native TCP, native C-FFI, wasm host imports).

Params are always a positional array at the seam; the placeholder token (`?` vs `$1`) is read from `Capabilities`, not baked in. NULL is `Value::Null` and `Option[T]`, never a sentinel. IndexedDB is an explicit non-goal — it has no SQL surface — and belongs to a sibling KV trait; the browser's SQL story is a wasm-SQLite `impl Driver`.

Everything in this section is the proposed target surface. The reference implementation currently ships a smaller, concrete first cut of it, and the exact built-versus-proposed gap is spelled out under **Reference implementation** below — nothing here is claimed as already-built beyond what that section lists.

## Async

The standard seam is **sync** (`raise`), so it is zero-dependency and compiles on native, wasm, and js; native drivers run their async runtime internally behind it. A parallel native-only `AsyncDriver` trait (in a sub-package that deps `moonbitlang/async`) mirrors the six I/O methods for callers who want true async concurrency. MoonBit has no colour polymorphism, so the two trait *definitions* are unavoidable — but the entire value model (`Value`, `Row`, `ToParam`/`FromValue`, `DbError`, `Capabilities`, `TxOptions`, pool and transaction logic) is colour-neutral and shared verbatim. Only the method colours differ.

The reference implementation stressed this boundary and surfaced a limit worth stating plainly. An FFI driver (sqlite, blocking C) satisfies the sync seam completely, transactions included. A wire-protocol driver cannot: `moonbitlang/async` is async-only and exposes no re-entrant sync bridge — its one public entry, `run_async_main`, tears down its socket fds on return, so a synchronous `execute`/`query` can only work by reconnecting per call, which cannot hold a transaction across calls, and `begin`/`commit`/`rollback` on the sync adapter must therefore raise. The honest division of labour that falls out of this: the sync `Driver` is the portable, FFI-complete floor and the autocommit face of network drivers, while the native-only `AsyncDriver` is where transactional wire-protocol drivers actually live. That makes `AsyncDriver` not optional polish but a first-class half of the design — and it is exactly why it must stay a native-only sibling and never fold into an all-target `core`.

## Why a standard package

The value is interop, and interop only exists if there is one shared type. If `moonorm` decodes `moondb.Row` and `moon-postgres` produces it, they compose with no adapter. A custom `Uuid` that implements `moondb.ToParam` binds on every backend at once. A `Pool` written against `moondb.Driver` pools every backend. None of this is possible while each package owns its own `Value`/`Row`/error. This is the same reason `database/sql`, `java.sql`, and DB-API live in their respective standard libraries rather than as competing third-party crates.

## Extensibility guarantees

- **New backend**: implement `Driver` (+ optional capability traits) in a separate package. Map columns to the 7 `Value` cases, errors to `ErrorKind`, quirks to `Capabilities`. Zero edits to the standard package; `Pool`, `transaction`, and every query layer work unchanged.
- **New value type** (Decimal, Uuid, Timestamp, JSON): implement `ToParam` + `FromValue` in a separate package. Zero edits to the standard package **and zero edits to any driver** — the type rides existing `Text`/`Blob`. This is what a closed `Value` enum cannot do: adding a case there would force a release plus a match-arm in every driver and break every downstream `match`. The closed enum is the portable floor; the open traits are the unbounded ceiling.
- **Backward-compatible growth**: new capabilities are new optional traits and new defaulted `Capabilities` fields — existing drivers keep compiling (Go's additive property, without Go's invisible runtime type-asserts, because capabilities are an inspectable value).
- A zero-dependency `MockDriver` in the standard package proves the contract is implementable on every target and serves as every query layer's test double.

## Prior art

- **Go `database/sql`/`driver`** — the two-layer split (thin driver contract, thick shared layer); closed 7-type `driver.Value`; symmetric `Valuer`/`Scanner`. We keep the split, drop the reflection.
- **Rust sqlx** — `Encode`/`Decode`/`Type` as an *open* value model, no closed value enum, NULL via `Option`; the direct inspiration for `ToParam`/`FromValue`. We drop the GAT-heavy `ValueRef` (own values at the row boundary) and the async-only, drop-cancel model.
- **Python DB-API 2.0** — the portable exception category tree (our `ErrorKind`); a warning against five fragmented paramstyles (we fix one positional convention) and duck typing (we use real traits).
- **JDBC / ADO.NET** — interface-as-contract + registry-as-discovery; a warning about unsound NULL (`wasNull`/`DBNull`) and wide mandatory interfaces (we use a tiny core + optional capability traits, not `SQLFeatureNotSupportedException` stubs).
- **JS/wasm (Kysely)** — the `{sql, positional params}` → `{rows, insert_id, affected}` data boundary; placeholders as compiler output; IndexedDB kept out of the SQL driver.

## Placement: the sync value-model subset belongs in `core`

**We propose the sync, zero-dependency subset — `Value`, `Row`, `ToParam`/`FromValue`, `Driver`, `DbError`, `Capabilities`, `ExecResult` — for `moonbitlang/core`; `AsyncDriver`, `Pool`, and concrete drivers stay as separate packages.**

This subset is what `core` is for: zero dependencies, all three targets (native/wasm/js), small, and stable. It is the single shared vocabulary that lets independent drivers and query layers interoperate — the role `database/sql/driver` plays in Go's standard library. `core` membership is also the only thing that anoints *one* seam over competing third-party ones; without it, fragmentation is the status-quo failure. The parts that stay outside are exactly the parts that cannot be all-target or stable: `AsyncDriver` depends on the native-only `moonbitlang/async`, and `Pool` and the concrete drivers need to move on their own semver. That boundary is a feature — `core` holds a frozen seam while the ecosystem iterates.

The honest constraint is that a seam should be frozen only after a real driver has stressed it. A reference implementation accompanies this proposal — a query layer over the seam, an FFI `sqlite` driver, and native-wire `postgres` and `mysql` drivers, each tested against a real database in CI (SQLite, PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8) — so the seam is proposed driver-backed, not on paper. That same exercise is what surfaced the async boundary described above — the proposal reflects what a real driver ran into, not a whiteboard guess.

To be precise about the gap between this proposal and the prototype: the shipped `moondb` is a smaller first cut. Its `Driver` is six concrete methods — `execute`/`query` take `(String, Array[Value])` directly, plus `begin`/`commit`/`rollback`/`close`; its `DbError` is four cases (`ConnectError` / `QueryError(String)` / `TypeError` / `Closed`); `Value`, `Row` (with concrete typed accessors), `ExecResult`, and an in-memory `MockDriver` are as described above. The `sqlite`, `postgres`, and `mysql` drivers each implement that concrete `Driver` against a real database in CI. The open `ToParam`/`FromValue` traits, the `QueryExecutor` split, `Capabilities`, the `ErrorKind`-tagged `QueryError`, `Pool`, and the closure `transaction` shown in the proposal above are the intended evolution — not yet built, and exactly what this RFC asks maintainers to weigh before the surface is frozen. The prototype exists to prove the seam is real and driver-backed, not to present the final surface.

## Reference implementation

All packages are public, Apache-2.0, and green in CI against real databases. They live in one repository — `Lfan-ke/moonorm` — as independently-published packages (the ORM at the root, the interface and drivers as sub-packages), each with its own `moon.mod` and mooncakes version:

- `moondb` — the interface package itself, plus the in-memory `MockDriver`: https://github.com/Lfan-ke/moonorm/tree/master/db
- `moon-sqlite` — FFI driver over the SQLite amalgamation (the one C-touching package): https://github.com/Lfan-ke/moonorm/tree/master/drivers/sqlite
- `moon-postgres` — pure-MoonBit PostgreSQL v3 wire driver, tested against PostgreSQL 16 in CI: https://github.com/Lfan-ke/moonorm/tree/master/drivers/postgres
- `moon-mysql` — pure-MoonBit MySQL/MariaDB wire driver, tested against MySQL 8 and MariaDB 10.11/11 in CI: https://github.com/Lfan-ke/moonorm/tree/master/drivers/mysql
- `moonorm` — a query/ORM layer written entirely against the seam, to show a consumer composes with any driver: https://github.com/Lfan-ke/moonorm

Question for maintainers: **is the sync value-model subset acceptable for `core`, and is there anything you would change before it is frozen under `core`'s stability guarantees?**

title: Array::append reallocates even when reserved capacity is sufficient
body:
## Summary

`Array::append` delegates to `ArrayView::blit_to`. When the append grows the logical length, `blit_to` calls `unsafe_grow_to_length`, which unconditionally allocates a new buffer of exactly `new_len`.

This happens even when the destination already has enough reserved capacity, so the operation discards the reservation.

## Example

```moonbit
let dst : Array[Int] = Array::new(capacity=4096)
dst.append([1, 2, 3, 4])
```

On non-JS targets, the resulting buffer capacity becomes 4 instead of retaining the already sufficient capacity. The append should only need to update the logical length and copy the new elements.

The same behavior affects code that intentionally precomputes the final size, including `Array::repeat`, which creates `Array::new(capacity=total)` and then repeatedly calls `append`.

## Cause

`ArrayView::blit_to` correctly decides that the logical length must grow:

```moonbit
if dst_offset + len > dst.length() {
  dst.unsafe_grow_to_length(dst_offset + len)
}
```

But `unsafe_grow_to_length` does not distinguish logical growth from buffer growth and always reallocates:

```moonbit
let new_buf = UninitializedArray::make_and_blit(
  self.buf,
  allocate_len=new_len,
  len=self.len,
)
```

## Suggested direction

When `new_len <= self.capacity()`, update `self.len` without replacing `self.buf`. Reallocate only when the requested logical length exceeds capacity.

This issue is intentionally separate from whether capacity growth should be geometric when the existing buffer is insufficient.
