title: Improve `powf` accuracy and range handling for large exponents near 1.0
body:
## Motivation

Should we improve the accuracy of `@math.powf` when the base is close to `1.0` and the exponent has a very large magnitude?

Several C libraries and language runtimes produce finite binary32 results for the examples below, while MoonBit currently returns either `0.0` or `Infinity`.

## Cross-implementation comparison

The inputs are specified by their exact binary32 bit patterns:

- base: `0x3f7ffff7` ≈ `0.999999463558197`
- positive exponent: `0x4d000001` = `134217744`
- negative exponent: `0xcd000001` = `-134217744`

All results below are shown as binary32 bit patterns.

| Implementation | Evaluation model | Positive exponent | Negative exponent |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| MoonBit `@math.powf` | native binary32 implementation | `0x00000000` | `0x7f800000` |
| System libm `powf` | C `float powf(float, float)` | `0x0b8bac79` | `0x736a9a99` |
| NumPy 2.1.2 `np.power(float32, float32)` | binary32 ufunc | `0x0b8bac79` | `0x736a9a99` |

The corresponding reference values are approximately:

- `0x0b8bac79` = `5.380036e-32`
- `0x736a9a99` = `1.858724e31`

Both results are comfortably inside the finite binary32 range. Therefore, this is more than a last-bit rounding difference: the current result changes from a finite number to zero or infinity.

## MoonBit reproduction

```moonbit
test "powf large exponents near one" {
  let base = Float::reinterpret_from_uint(0x3f7ffff7U)

  let positive_exponent =
    Float::reinterpret_from_uint(0x4d000001U)
  let negative_exponent =
    Float::reinterpret_from_uint(0xcd000001U)

  inspect(
    @math.powf(base, positive_exponent).reinterpret_as_uint(),
    content="0", // 0x00000000
  )

  inspect(
    @math.powf(base, negative_exponent).reinterpret_as_uint(),
    content="2139095040", // 0x7f800000: +Infinity
  )
}

title: improve queue performance
body: Let's use Deque here because @queue.Queue currently uses a linked list and is hence slow. Should be fixed on moonbitlang/core, though

title: [BUG] `atan2` loses the sign of an underflowed negative result
body:
### Description

On non-JS targets, `@math.atan2` returns positive zero when the mathematically negative result underflows to zero.

```text
y = -minimum subnormal
x = maximum finite
atan2(y, x)
```

the result must be negative zero, but native and wasm-gc return positive zero.

### Cross-target results

Inputs:

```text
y bits: 0x8000000000000001  // negative minimum subnormal
x bits: 0x7fefffffffffffff  // maximum finite Double
```

| Target | Result |
|---|---|
| JS | `-0.0`, bits `0x8000000000000000` |
| native | `+0.0`, bits `0x0000000000000000` |
| wasm-gc | `+0.0`, bits `0x0000000000000000` |

### Minimal regression test

```moonbit
test "atan2 preserves negative zero when its result underflows" {
  let negative_min_subnormal = 0x8000000000000001UL
    .reinterpret_as_double()
  let max_finite = 0x7fefffffffffffffUL
    .reinterpret_as_double()

  assert_eq(
    @math
      .atan2(negative_min_subnormal, max_finite)
      .reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x8000000000000000UL,
  )
}
```

This test passes on JS and fails on native and wasm-gc.

### Expected behavior

Because `y < 0` and `x > 0`, the exact mathematical result is negative:

```text
atan2(y, x) ≈ y / x < 0
```

Its magnitude is too small to be represented even as a binary64 subnormal, so it rounds to zero. The sign of the negative result must be retained:

```text
expected: -0.0
bits:     0x8000000000000000
```

This agrees with JavaScript `Math.atan2` and Python/C `atan2`.

### Actual non-JS behavior

```text
actual: +0.0
bits:   0x0000000000000000
```

title: [BUG] `hypot` returns `NaN` instead of `+Infinity` for mixed `NaN`/`Infinity` inputs
body:
### Description

On non-JS targets, `@math.hypot` returns `NaN` when one argument is `NaN` and the other is infinity.

For `hypot`, infinity should take precedence over NaN: if either argument is positive or negative infinity, the result should be positive infinity, even when the other argument is NaN.

### Cross-target results

For:

```text
hypot(NaN, +Infinity)
```

| Target | Result |
|---|---|
| JS | `+Infinity`, bits `0x7ff0000000000000` |
| native | `NaN`, bits `0x7ff8000000000001` |
| wasm-gc | `NaN`, bits `0x7ff8000000000001` |

The same discrepancy occurs when:

- The arguments are reversed.
- The infinity argument is negative.
- The NaN has a different payload or sign.

### Minimal regression test

```moonbit
test "hypot gives infinity precedence over NaN" {
  let nan = 0x7ff8000000001234UL.reinterpret_as_double()
  let positive_infinity = 0x7ff0000000000000UL.reinterpret_as_double()
  let negative_infinity = 0xfff0000000000000UL.reinterpret_as_double()

  assert_eq(
    @math
      .hypot(nan, positive_infinity)
      .reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x7ff0000000000000UL,
  )

  assert_eq(
    @math
      .hypot(positive_infinity, nan)
      .reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x7ff0000000000000UL,
  )

  assert_eq(
    @math
      .hypot(nan, negative_infinity)
      .reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x7ff0000000000000UL,
  )

  assert_eq(
    @math
      .hypot(negative_infinity, nan)
      .reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x7ff0000000000000UL,
  )
}
```

This test passes on JS and fails on native and wasm-gc.

### Expected behavior

```text
hypot(NaN, +Infinity) = +Infinity
hypot(+Infinity, NaN) = +Infinity
hypot(NaN, -Infinity) = +Infinity
hypot(-Infinity, NaN) = +Infinity
```

This behavior agrees with JavaScript `Math.hypot` and the conventional IEEE/C `hypot` special-case semantics.

The result is always positive because `hypot(x, y)` represents a nonnegative magnitude.

### Actual non-JS behavior

All four combinations return NaN:

```text
bits: 0x7ff8000000000001
```

title: [BUG] `Double::round` is incorrect for signed zero, half-boundary, and large-integer inputs
[BUG] `log2` loses about 4% relative accuracy immediately above 1
body:
### Description

`@math.log2` has a large relative error for the first representable `Double` above `1.0`.

The input is:

```text
nextUp(1.0)
bits: 0x3ff0000000000001
value: 1 + 2^-52
```

Results by target:

| Target | Result bits |
|---|---|
| JS | `0x3cb71547652b82fd` |
| native | `0x3cb8000000000000` |
| wasm-gc | `0x3cb8000000000000` |

The non-JS result differs by approximately 3.97% relative error and `258078592498947` ULP at the result’s scale.

### Minimal regression test

```moonbit
test "log2 is accurate immediately above one" {
  let input = 0x3ff0000000000001UL.reinterpret_as_double()

  assert_eq(
    @math.log2(input).reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0x3cb71547652b82fdUL,
  )
}
```

This test passes on JS and fails on native and wasm-gc.

### Expected behavior

A 200-digit high-precision evaluation of

```text
log2(1 + 2^-52)
```

rounded to binary64 gives:

```text
value: 3.203426503814917e-16
bits:  0x3cb71547652b82fd
```

This result also agrees with JavaScript `Math.log2` and Python `math.log2`.

### Actual non-JS behavior

```text
value: 3.3306690738754696e-16
bits:  0x3cb8000000000000
```

Approximate relative error:

```text
abs(actual - expected) / expected ≈ 0.03972
```

### Suspected cause

The non-JS implementation computes `log2` using:

```moonbit
pub fn log2(x : Double) -> Double {
  let (f, e) = frexp(x)
  if f == 0.5 {
    return e.to_double() - 1.0
  }
  ln(f) / LN2 + e.to_double()
}
```

For `nextUp(1.0)`, `frexp` produces a fraction immediately above `0.5` and exponent `1`. Therefore:

```text
ln(f) / LN2 ≈ -1
e             = 1
```

Adding these nearly equal opposite values causes catastrophic cancellation. Almost all significant bits of the small final result are lost.

title: [BUG] `tanh` flips the sign of negative tiny inputs
body:
### Description

`@math.tanh` returns a positive result for negative, nonzero inputs with approximately `|x| < 2^-55` on non-JS targets. The magnitude is retained, but the sign is reversed.

### Minimal regression test

```moonbit
test "tanh preserves the sign of negative minimum subnormal" {
  let input_bits = 0x8000000000000001UL
  let output_bits = @math
    .tanh(input_bits.reinterpret_as_double())
    .reinterpret_as_uint64()

  assert_eq(output_bits, input_bits)
}
```

An odd-symmetry regression is:

```moonbit
test "tanh is odd for tiny finite inputs" {
  let positive_bits = 0x0000000000000001UL
  let negative_bits = 0x8000000000000001UL

  let positive_output = @math
    .tanh(positive_bits.reinterpret_as_double())
    .reinterpret_as_uint64()
  let negative_output = @math
    .tanh(negative_bits.reinterpret_as_double())
    .reinterpret_as_uint64()

  assert_eq(
    negative_output,
    positive_output | 0x8000000000000000UL,
  )
}
```

Both tests pass on JS and fail on native and wasm-gc.

### Expected behavior

```text
input bits:  0x8000000000000001
output bits: 0x8000000000000001
```

For the minimum subnormal, the correctly rounded value of `tanh(x)` is `x` itself. This also agrees with JavaScript `Math.tanh` and Python `math.tanh`.

### Actual non-JS behavior

```text
input bits:  0x8000000000000001
output bits: 0x0000000000000001
```

### Suspected cause

The tiny-input branch in `math/hyperbolic_double_nonjs.mbt` already computes a signed result:

```moonbit
let z = if ix < 0x40360000 {
  if ix < 0x3c800000 {
    x * (1.0 + x)
```

For a negative tiny input, `z` is negative. The final sign adjustment negates it again:

```moonbit
if x >= 0.0 {
  z
} else {
  -z
}
```

Other branches construct a positive magnitude before applying this final sign adjustment, but the tiny branch uses the original signed `x`. Consequently, negative nonzero inputs in this branch become positive.

title: [BUG] `cbrt` misclassifies negative normal inputs as subnormal on non-JS targets
body:
### Bug Description

`@math.cbrt` produces an inaccurate result for large negative finite values on non-JS targets.

For the exactly representable input `-2^971`:

| Target | Result bits |
|---|---|
| JS | `0xd42965fea53d6e3d` |
| native | `0xd42965fea53d5000` |
| wasm-gc | `0xd42965fea53d5000` |

The non-JS result differs by 7,741 ULP.

The JS result is independently confirmed by Python `math.cbrt` and by the odd-symmetry property `cbrt(-x) == -cbrt(x)`.

### Minimal regression test

```moonbit
test "cbrt handles a large negative normal input" {
  let input = 0xfca0000000000000UL.reinterpret_as_double() // -2^971
  assert_eq(
    @math.cbrt(input).reinterpret_as_uint64(),
    0xd42965fea53d6e3dUL,
  )
}
```

An oracle-independent version is:

```moonbit
test "cbrt preserves odd symmetry for large finite inputs" {
  let positive = 0x7ca0000000000000UL.reinterpret_as_double()
  let negative = 0xfca0000000000000UL.reinterpret_as_double()

  let positive_output = @math.cbrt(positive).reinterpret_as_uint64()
  let negative_output = @math.cbrt(negative).reinterpret_as_uint64()

  assert_eq(
    negative_output,
    positive_output | 0x8000000000000000UL,
  )
}
```

The symmetry test passes on JS and fails on native and wasm-gc.

### Expected behavior

```text
input:  -1.99584030953472e+292
result: -2.7125344542490313e+97
bits:   0xd42965fea53d6e3d
```

### Actual non-JS behavior

```text
result: -2.7125344542460942e+97
bits:   0xd42965fea53d5000
```

### Suspected cause

In `math/algebraic_double_nonjs.mbt`, the high word is converted to a signed integer before the sign is removed:

```moonbit
let hx = get_high_word(x).reinterpret_as_int()
let sign = if x < 0.0 { true } else { false }
let x = abs(x)
let t = if hx < 0x00100000 {
  // subnormal path
```

For every negative normal value, the sign bit makes `hx` negative, so `hx < 0x00100000` is true and the implementation incorrectly enters the subnormal initialization path. For sufficiently large values, its `2^54 * x` scaling also overflows.

title: [BUG] `parse_double` returns 0.1 instead of 1.0 for an 801-digit coefficient
body:
**Describe the bug**

`@string.parse_double` produces an incorrect result when the decimal coefficient contains more than 800 digits.

For the input consisting of `1`, followed by 800 zeros, followed by `e-800`, the exact mathematical value is:

```text
10^800 × 10^-800 = 1
```

However, `parse_double` returns `0.1`.

The parser appears to cap the stored digit count at 800 and also uses that capped count when determining the decimal-point position. The decimal-point position should instead reflect all 801 scanned integer digits.

**To Reproduce**

1. Add the following test to `string/parse_double_test.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
test "parse_double 801-digit integer coefficient" {
  // 10^800 * 10^-800 is exactly 1.
  let input = "1" + String::make(800, '0') + "e-800"
  inspect(@string.parse_double(input), content="1")
}
```

2. Run and the test fails with:

```diff
-1
+0.1
```

**Expected behavior**

`parse_double` should return `1.0`, because the input represents exactly `10^800 × 10^-800 = 1`.

The parser does not need to retain all 801 coefficient digits, but it must preserve the original decimal-point position when truncating its internal digit buffer.

title: [BUG] Commit 96c6e6c2 removed negative index support from `Array::view`, breaking `:-1` slice syntax used by bobzhang/toml
body:
**Describe the bug**

Commit 96c6e6c2 ("Remove negative index support from view/slice operators") removed the `if x < 0 { len + x }` normalization from `Array::view`, `ArrayView::view`, `FixedArray::view`, and their `get_view` counterparts. As a result, `arr[:-1]` now passes `end = -1` literally to `Array::view`, which fails the bounds guard (`start <= end && end <= len`) and panics with `abort("View index out of bounds")`. Previously `[:-1]` was equivalent to `[0:len-1]`.

This breaks `bobzhang/toml` (and the older `bob/toml`), which uses `path[:-1]` in its `create_array_of_tables` function. Any TOML document containing `[[array_of_tables]]` syntax crashes at runtime.

**To Reproduce**

1. Create a MoonBit project with `bobzhang/toml` as a dependency
2. Run this test:

```moonbit
test "negative index in array slice panics" {
  let path = ["lights"]
  // Previously: path[:-1] == view(start=0, end=0)  (empty, safe)
  // Now:        path[:-1] == view(start=0, end=-1)  (panics)
  let _view = path[:-1]
}
```

Or with bobzhang/toml:

```moonbit
test "TOML array of tables crashes" {
  let toml_content =
    #|[[lights]]
    #|type = "point"
    #|
  let _result = @toml.parse(toml_content)
}
```

3. Run with `moon test --target native`
4. See panic: `View index out of bounds`

**Expected behavior**

`arr[:-1]` should produce an empty view (equivalent to `[0:0]`) when the array has one element, or a view of all-but-the-last element for longer arrays, matching the previous behavior and common Python-like conventions.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: macOS (darwin)
 - moonc version: v0.10.4+2cc641edf (2026-07-15)
 - moon version: 0.1.20260713
 - Target: native

**Additional context**

The regression was introduced in commit 96c6e6c2 ("Remove negative index support from view/slice operators"). That commit removed the following normalization from `Array::view` (and analogous functions across `ArrayView`, `FixedArray`, `MutArrayView`, `StringView`, `BytesView`):

Before:
```moonbit
let end = match end {
  None => len
  Some(end) => if end < 0 { len + end } else { end }
}
let start = if start < 0 { len + start } else { start }
```

After:
```moonbit
let end = match end {
  None => len
  Some(end) => end
}
```

The `bobzhang/toml` parser is the most widely-used TOML library on mooncakes.io (92k+ downloads). It calls `for key in path[:-1]` in `create_array_of_tables` to navigate `[[array_of_tables]]` TOML paths. This means **any** TOML document using `[[...]]` syntax panics under moonc v0.10.x on native.

Full stack trace:
```
View index out of bounds
PanicError
  at @moonbitlang/core/abort.abort[...]       (abort.mbt:50)
  at @moonbitlang/core/array.Array::view.inner (arrayview.mbt:265)
  at @bobzhang/toml.create_array_of_tables     (toml_utils.mbt:103)
  at @bobzhang/toml.parse                      (parser.mbt:329)
```

title: #locals does not propagate through calls to #locals-annotated callees
body:
`#locals(f)` cannot be used on a function that forwards its callback to another function, even when the callee declares the same parameter local. Minimal repro on current main, adding the attribute to the delegating `Array::any`:

```moonbit
#locals(f)
#alias(exists)
pub fn[T] Array::any(self : Array[T], f : (T) -> Bool raise?) -> Bool raise? {
  self[:].any(f)
}
```

```
Error: [4163]
 562 │   self[:].any(f)
     │               ┬
     │               ╰── This parameter is expected to be local, but it escapes.
```

`ArrayView::any` declares `#locals(f)`, so `f` provably does not escape through that call — but the analysis treats any argument-passing as an escape rather than consulting the callee's `#locals` contract. Consequently every thin `Array → ArrayView` delegating wrapper (`Array::any`, `Array::all`, and the same shape elsewhere) silently loses closure stack-allocation at its call sites, precisely on the hottest, most-used entry points.

There is an existing in-repo acknowledgment of the same limitation from the other direction — `immut/hashmap/HAMT.mbt` (`HashMap::fold`):

```
/// TODO: can not mark `f` as `#locals(f)` because
/// it will be shadowed by the `f` in the `@list.List::fold` function
/// TO make it more useful in the future, we may need propagate
```

**Suggested fix**: when a `#locals` parameter is passed as an argument to a parameter that is itself declared `#locals` in the callee's signature, treat it as non-escaping (interprocedural propagation via the existing annotation, no new analysis needed — the callee's contract is already checked at its own definition).

**Workaround applied meanwhile**: inline the loop bodies into the delegating wrappers so the attribute applies directly (PR to follow, linked below).

title: bytes/ and string/ regex engines share ~365 lines of byte-identical files
body:
`bytes/internal/regex_engine/` and `string/internal/regex_engine/` contain byte-identical copies of: `symbolize.mbt` (42 lines), `compile.mbt` (43), `using.mbt` (49), `ast/pattern.mbt` (205), `ast/using.mbt` (13), `symbol_map/using.mbt` (13) — roughly 365 lines duplicated verbatim that must be kept in sync by hand (`translate.mbt` and the `.mbti` files legitimately differ, and drift has already crept in: the `string/` copy of `translate.mbt` used an imperative loop where the `bytes/` twin uses a comprehension — realigned in #3821).

Both packages already depend on the shared `internal/regex_engine` (`automata/` + `shared_types/`), so the identical files look liftable into a shared internal package. This is an architectural consolidation rather than a mechanical dedup — the byte/string engines are parameterized differently at the edges — so filing for design discussion rather than PRing directly.

title: bigint: to_string_radix is O(n²) for non-power-of-two radixes other than 10
body:
`bigint/bigint_nonjs.mbt:1101-1133`: radix 10 and power-of-two radixes have optimized paths, but other radixes (3, 5, 6, 7, ...) extract digits by repeatedly calling `grade_school_div(v, base)` — each O(n) — once per output digit (~O(n) digits), i.e. O(n²) overall.

Standard fix: divide by `base^k` per step, where `base^k` is the largest power fitting in a limb, extracting `k` digits per full-bigint division — cutting the number of O(n) divisions by a factor of ~k (e.g. k=20 for radix 3 with 32-bit limbs, k=12 for radix 6).

Low urgency (odd radixes are rare) but the fix is mechanical and the surrounding radix-10 code (`decimal_mask` batching at line ~1019) already demonstrates the pattern.

title: join converts every element to a string view twice
body:
`builtin/arrayview.mbt` (~1493) and `builtin/fixedarray.mbt` (~1483) — and therefore `Array::join` / `ReadOnlyArray::join`, which delegate via `self[:]` — call each element's `to_string_view()` twice: once in the size-hint pass (`s.to_string_view().length()`) and again in the write pass.

For `String` elements the conversion is identity and this costs nothing. For element types whose `ToStringView` does real formatting work (`Int`, `Double`, custom types), it doubles the conversion cost of `[...].join(",")`.

Straightforward fix: materialize the views once into a length-`n` temp array, sum lengths, then write from it. Trade-off: one extra `n`-length allocation, so it's a net win only when conversion is non-trivial — worth benchmarking with the `bench/` framework before/after (numeric joins are the common case that benefits).

title: strconv: mantissa digit parsing reads one character at a time
body:
`strconv/number.mbt:104` (and its duplicate `internal/strconv/strconv_number.mbt:104`) carries this TODO on the float-parsing hot path:

> TODO: optimization chance. In the original Rust implementation, [they] try to parse 8 digits at a time [into a u64].

`parse_digits` currently accumulates digit-by-digit. The Eisel-Lemire reference implementation reads 8 bytes into a `u64` and validates/converts them in a handful of arithmetic ops, which is a substantial constant-factor win for long mantissas.

Care needed around digit-count/overflow boundaries and the two copies of the code (`strconv/` and `internal/strconv/` must stay in sync — or better, be deduplicated as part of this work).

title: sorted_set: union defensively copies both trees and recounts the result size
body:
`sorted_set/set.mbt` `SortedSet::union` (the `TODO: optimize this. Avoid counting the size of the set` at ~line 175):

1. `copy_tree` is called on **both** operands up front. The copies are required by the current mutable design (`add_node`/`delete_node`/rotations mutate nodes in place, so subtree sharing would corrupt the source sets) — but it means union is O(n+m) allocations before any merging starts.
2. After the split/join merge, the result size is recomputed by a full `each` traversal because nodes store only `height`, not subtree size.

Possible directions:
- Store subtree `size` in `Node` (as the immutable `immut/sorted_set` does) — kills the recount and gives O(1) `length` for subtrees; costs one word per node and bookkeeping in every rotation.
- Count duplicates during `split` (a duplicate is discovered exactly when `split` hits `comp == 0`), then `size = size1 + size2 - dups` — no node layout change, but `split` needs a counting variant.
- For the copy overhead: iterate the smaller set and `add` into a copy of the larger — O(n + m log n) with one copy instead of two and no recount (`add` maintains size). Loses the asymptotic edge of split/join union for balanced sizes.

Related: `symmetric_difference` had the same shape and is addressed by #3819 with a merge-walk; `intersection` (each + contains) may also benefit from a merge-walk.

title: `find_by` returns a character index while `find`/`rev_find` return code-unit offsets
body:
Found during a systematic scan (verified against `builtin/string_methods.mbt`).

`String::find_by` / `StringView::find_by` are implemented as `for i, c in self { if pred(c) { return Some(i) } }`, where `iter2`'s first component is a **Unicode character index** (a surrogate pair counts as 1). Their siblings `find` / `rev_find` — and every slicing API (`view`, `at`, `sub`, `s[a:b]`) — use **UTF-16 code-unit offsets**. Both families are documented identically as returning "the offset of the first ...".

The in-repo test even pins the divergence: `"😀😁😂".find_by(c => c == '😂') == Some(2)` (char index), while the code-unit offset of `😂` is 4, and `"😀😀".rev_find("😀") == Some(2)` (code-unit offset).

**Hazard**: `let i = s.find_by(pred)` followed by `s[:i]` — the natural composition — splits surrogate pairs for any non-BMP text. E.g. `"😀X".find_by(c => c == 'X')` returns `Some(1)`; `s[:1]` is a broken half-surrogate rather than `"😀"`. `to_lower`/`to_upper` internally rely on this exact mix and only work by accident of buffer reassembly.

Options (maintainer call, all have costs):
1. Change `find_by` to return code-unit offsets (breaking; the pinning test would change)
2. Keep both, rename/document loudly (`find_by` → e.g. `find_char_index_by`), add a code-unit variant
3. Documentation-only: state explicitly that `find_by` results must not be used with slicing APIs

Filed from an automated repo scan; happy to implement whichever direction is chosen.

title: [BUG] BigInt XOR result depends on construction history
body:
**Describe the bug**
Two BigInt values that compare equal can produce different results when used in the same XOR expression.

A value parsed from hexadecimal behaves differently from the equivalent BigInt literal, indicating that bitwise XOR depends on internal storage capacity or construction history rather than only on numeric value.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior, add the following test:

```moonbit
test "xor depends on value, not construction history" {
  let from_hex = @bigint.BigInt::from_string("80000000", radix=16)
  let literal = 2147483648N

  assert_eq(from_hex, literal)
  assert_eq(from_hex ^ -from_hex, literal ^ -literal)
}
```

Run it on a non-JavaScript backend:

```bash
moon test --target wasm
```

1. The first assertion passes, confirming that both operands are equal.
2. The second assertion fails:

```
0 != -4294967296
```

The observed results are:

```
from_hex ^ -from_hex = 0
literal ^ -literal   = -4294967296
```

**Expected behavior**
Equal BigInt values should be substitutable in all arithmetic and bitwise operations.

For `x = 2147483648`, using arbitrary-precision two’s-complement semantics:

```
x ^ -x = -4294967296
```

Both construction paths should therefore produce `-4294967296`.

title: [BUG] `BigInt::from_octets` with leading zero limbs produces an incorrectly ordered value
body:
**Describe the bug**
`BigInt::from_octets` can construct a non-canonical BigInt when the input contains multiple leading zero limbs. The resulting value prints correctly but compares greater than the corresponding canonical BigInt.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Add the following test:

```moonbit
test "leading zero limbs do not change numeric comparison" {
  let actual = @bigint.BigInt::from_octets(
    b"\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x26",
  )
  assert_eq(actual.to_string(), "38")
  assert_eq(actual.compare(38N), 0)
}
```

Run it on a non-JavaScript backend:

```bash
moon test --target wasm
```

Observe the failure:

```
1 != 0
```

`actual.to_string()` returns `"38"`, but `actual.compare(38N)` returns `1`.

**Expected behavior**
Leading zero bytes should not affect the numeric value. The constructed BigInt should compare equal to `38N`, so `actual.compare(38N)` should return `0`.

title: Logger trait's write_view/write_substring mutual defaults allow infinite recursion at runtime
argparse: add clap-style `args_conflicts_with_subcommands` and `subcommand_negates_reqs` for a top-level default action alongside subcommands
body:
## Problem

When building a CLI whose **bare invocation is a default action** *and* which also has subcommands (e.g. `tool` opens an interactive UI; `tool run|serve|…` are headless subcommands), argparse forces two awkward tradeoffs. The natural design is: put the default action's options on the root command, keep `subcommand_required=false`, and dispatch on `matches.subcommand` (`None` ⇒ default action). But then:

### Gap 1 — a top-level option is silently accepted before a subcommand that ignores it

With a default-action option (say `--prompt`) on the root and subcommands `run`/`serve`/…:

```
tool --prompt x run TASK
```

argparse parses `--prompt x` at the root, then `run`. The dispatcher hands `run` only the `run` matches, so `--prompt` is **silently accepted and ignored** — a footgun. There is no way to say "these root options are for the default action only; reject them if a *different* subcommand is chosen."

### Gap 2 — a `required` root option is enforced for *every* subcommand

If the default action needs `--api-key` (`required=true` on the root), that requirement is enforced for **all** subcommands — so an offline subcommand like `sessions list` wrongly demands a key. There is no way to say "required for the default action, but not when a subcommand is chosen."

(`global=true` options are inherited by subcommands, which is great for genuinely-shared options, but it doesn't address either gap: a global still can't be "default-action-only," and a required global still blocks every subcommand.)

## Prior art: clap

clap solves exactly this with two `Command` settings — notably **without** a first-class "default subcommand" feature (that's the long-open clap-rs/clap#975); these two toggles are what make the top-level-default-action pattern clean:

- **`args_conflicts_with_subcommands(true)`** — the top-level args and a chosen subcommand become mutually exclusive. So `tool --prompt x` → default action; `tool run …` → subcommand; `tool --prompt x run` → **clean error** (closes Gap 1).
- **`subcommand_negates_reqs(true)`** — when a subcommand is present, the parent command's `required` args are not enforced (closes Gap 2: `--api-key` can be required for the default action / `run` / `serve` yet not block `sessions list`).

## Request

Add equivalent `Command` settings to `argparse` — alongside the existing `subcommand_required` / `arg_required_else_help`:

- `args_conflicts_with_subcommands : Bool = false`
- `subcommand_negates_reqs : Bool = false`

With both, argparse would fully support the "bare command = default action + subcommands" shape that clap/yargs/cobra allow, with no workarounds.

## Concrete motivation (what we do today without them)

In a single-binary CLI (`openseek`, whose default action is an interactive UI, with `run`/`serve`/`review`/`sessions` subcommands) we had to:

1. Move all default-action-only options onto an explicit `tui` subcommand so they can't be silently accepted before an engine subcommand (Gap 1) — which loses the natural `openseek --prompt "…"` form.
2. Re-parse a bare invocation *as* the `tui` subcommand (prepend the subcommand token and parse again) so the default UI still honors those options' env bindings — a hack purely because of the above.
3. Drop `--api-key` from argparse `required` and validate it by hand, because a required root/global option blocks the key-free `sessions list` (Gap 2).

`args_conflicts_with_subcommands` + `subcommand_negates_reqs` would let us delete all three.

Related but separate: subcommand typo suggestions (#3768).

Environment: `moon 0.1.20260624`, `moonc v0.10.1+1f52b86e1-nightly`.

title: argparse: suggest a near-miss subcommand on "unknown subcommand" (the Levenshtein suggester is options-only)
body:
## Summary

`argparse` already has a Levenshtein "did you mean" suggester, but it is wired only to unknown **options/flags** — not to unknown **subcommands**. A mistyped subcommand gets a bare rejection with no suggestion, which is a worse experience than the option case and worse than most subcommand CLIs (git/cargo/clap all suggest).

## Where

- The suggester exists and is used for options: `suggest_long` / `suggest_short` → `suggest_name` → `levenshtein` in `argparse/parser_suggest.mbt`, invoked from `parser.mbt` for unknown `--long` / `-x`.
- The unknown-subcommand path does **not** call it — `argparse/parser_lookup.mbt` (around the subcommand lookup):

  ```
  guard subs.iter().find_first(sub => sub.name == name) is Some(sub) else {
    raise InvalidArgument("unknown subcommand: \{name}")
  }
  ```

  So `mytool serv` (meant `serve`) yields `unknown subcommand: serv` with no hint, even though `mytool --serv` (an option typo) would suggest `--serve`.

## Request

Apply the existing suggester to the unknown-subcommand error, e.g. build the candidate list from `subs` (`subcommand` names, and probably the built-in `help` subcommand when enabled) and, when `suggest_name` returns a match within `suggestion_threshold`, append `(did you mean '<name>'?)` to the message — mirroring the option/flag behavior. The helper is already there; this is just reusing it on the subcommand branch.

Alternatively (or additionally), exposing `suggest_name` / a small public "closest match" helper would let downstreams produce consistent suggestions, but wiring it into the built-in subcommand error is the higher-value fix.

## Motivation / context

Building a single-binary subcommand CLI, we wanted mistyped subcommands to say "did you mean 'serve'?". Because argparse doesn't offer this for subcommands, we either hand-roll a duplicate Levenshtein (undesirable — the library already has one) or accept the plain `unexpected value '…'` / `unknown subcommand: …`. We chose the latter and are tracking this issue so we can drop to the library's suggestion once it lands.

Environment: `moon 0.1.20260624`, `moonc v0.10.1+1f52b86e1-nightly`.

title: immut/vector: concat can build a radix node with a partial leaf, breaking get/at/set
body:
## Summary

`@immut/vector.Vector::concat` can produce a tree whose `iter()`/`to_array()` view is correct but whose **random access** (`get`/`at`/`set`) is broken. The tail-normalization path of `concat` builds a `Node(_, None)` — which the getter treats as a full, radix-indexable node — that actually contains a **partial (non-full) leaf**, violating the tree invariant in `types.mbt`:

> For `Node`, the sizes array is `None` if the tree is full, i.e., we can use radix indexing.

## Minimal reproduction

```moonbit
test "concat breaks random access" {
  let mut v = @vector.new()
  let mut total = 0
  for _ in 0..<8 {
    v = v.concat(@vector.from_iter((total).until(total + 17)))
    total += 17
  }
  // iter()/to_array() are correct (all 136 elements, 0..135):
  assert_eq(v.iter().to_array(), Array::makei(136, i => i))
  // but random access throws "array element access out of bounds":
  for j in 0..<total {
    assert_eq(v.get(j), Some(j)) // RuntimeError: array element access out of bounds
  }
}
```

- `iter()` / `to_array()` / `each` / `fold`: **correct** (they traverse children directly).
- `get(j)` / `at(j)` / `set(j, _)`: **throw** `array element access out of bounds` inside `Tree::get`'s radix fast path (`tree.mbt:76`, `leaf[index & BITMASK]`), for an interior index.

A single `concat` does not trigger it; it takes a few normalizations to accumulate a partial leaf in a non-final position under a `None` node. Eight 17-element chunks (136 elements) is the smallest case I found.

## Root cause

The bug is on the small-right-operand path of `concat` (`other.tree is Empty`), which folds the left tail into the tree via `Vector::normalize_tree` → `Tree::push_end` / `Tree::append_right_leaf`. When a **partial** branch is appended to a node that is currently `None` (radix/full), these helpers keep `sizes = None`:

- `tree.mbt` `push_end`: the "create a new node" arms produce `Node([self, new_branch], None)` (e.g. `tree.mbt:233`, `tree.mbt:239`) and `push_sizes_last(None) => None` (`tree.mbt:177`), even though `new_branch` wraps a partial leaf.
- `tree_append.mbt` `append_right_leaf`: same pattern — `Node([self, new_branch], None)` (`tree_append.mbt:98`, `:103`) and `push_sizes_last(None) => None` (`:34`) when the appended leaf is shorter than `BRANCHING_FACTOR`.

Because the resulting node is marked `None`, `Tree::get`/`set` use `radix_indexing`, which assumes every leaf has exactly `BRANCHING_FACTOR` elements. The partial leaf then gets indexed out of range.

These code paths were previously uncovered by the test suite, which is how the bug went unnoticed.

## Expected

After any sequence of `concat`s, `get(j) == Some(v.to_array()[j])` for all valid `j` (random access must agree with iteration).

## Environment

- Found on `main` (`immut/vector`), all backends.

title: ICE: `Key_not_found` during codegen for or-pattern binding `.. rest` across bits sub-patterns
body:
## Summary

`moonc` raises an internal compiler error (`Moonc.Basic_core_ident.Hash.Key_not_found(_)`) during **code generation** when an or-pattern combines two `BytesView`/array patterns that each contain a bits sub-pattern (`u64be` / `u64le`) **and** bind a `.. rest` tail variable used in the shared branch body.

`moon check` (type checking) succeeds — the crash happens only in `moonc build-package` (codegen). It reproduces on **wasm-gc, js, and native**.

## Minimal reproduction

`moon.mod.json`:
```json
{ "name": "ice/repro" }
```

`repro.mbt`:
```mbt
fn read_bits(big : Bool, v : BytesView) -> Int {
  match (big, v) {
    (true, [u64be(_), .. rest]) | (false, [u64le(_), .. rest]) => rest.length()
    _ => 0
  }
}

test {
  assert_eq(read_bits(true, (b"\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\x09")[:]), 1)
}
```

```
$ moon build
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
Error: Moonc.Basic_core_ident.Hash.Key_not_found(_)
```

## Observations / workarounds

- `moon check` passes; only codegen (`build-package`) crashes.
- Dropping the tail binding (`..` instead of `.. rest`) compiles fine:
  ```mbt
  (true, [u64be(x), ..]) | (false, [u64le(x), ..]) => x   // OK
  ```
- Splitting the or-pattern into separate `match` arms / an `if` also avoids it.
- A single (non-or) pattern binding `.. rest`, e.g. `[u64be(v), .. rest]`, is fine.

## Versions

- moon 0.1.20260618 (afb4494 2026-06-18)
- moonc v0.10.1+a46be2066
- Targets affected: wasm-gc, js, native

title: Type-alias re-export does not export the same-named constructor: `@facade.T(...)` fails while `@facade.T::T(...)` works
body:
## Summary

When a package re-exports a type via a type alias (`pub type T = @owner.T`), the alias does **not** bring the type's same-named associated constructor (`T::T`) into the re-exporting package's *value* namespace. So the natural constructor-call form `@facade.T(...)` fails to resolve — even though:

- `@owner.T(...)` works (the owner package has the constructor value), and
- `@facade.T::T(...)` works (associated-function lookup resolves through the aliased type to the owner).

This asymmetry is surprising for the common "facade package re-exports core types" pattern: callers reasonably expect `@facade.T(...)` to construct a `T`.

## Minimal reproduction

Three packages — `owner` defines the type + constructor, `facade` re-exports via a type alias, `consumer` uses it.

`owner/point.mbt`:
```moonbit
pub struct Point {
  x : Double
  y : Double
} derive(Eq)

pub fn Point::Point(x : Double, y : Double) -> Point {
  { x, y }
}
```

`facade/facade.mbt`:
```moonbit
pub type Point = @owner.Point
```

`consumer/consumer.mbt`:
```moonbit
pub fn demo() -> Unit {
  let _a : @owner.Point = @owner.Point(1.0, 2.0)         // ok
  let _b : @owner.Point = @facade.Point::Point(1.0, 2.0) // ok (method form via alias)
  let _c : @owner.Point = @facade.Point(1.0, 2.0)        // error
}
```

## Actual

```
Error: [4021]
 5 │   let _c : @owner.Point = @facade.Point(1.0, 2.0)
   │                           ──────┬──────
   │                                 ╰──────── Value Point not found in package `facade`.
```

`@owner.Point(...)` and `@facade.Point::Point(...)` both compile; only the `@facade.Point(...)` form errors.

## Expected

`@facade.Point(1.0, 2.0)` should resolve to the re-exported constructor, the same way `@facade.Point::Point(...)` and `@owner.Point(...)` do. (Alternatively, if this is intentional, a clearer diagnostic and documented guidance would help.)

## Why it matters

This is exactly the facade pattern that the package-organization guidance encourages: a root/facade package re-exports concrete types from sub-packages. Today, callers who write the natural `@facade.Type(...)` hit an error and must instead use `@facade.Type::Type(...)`, `@owner.Type(...)`, or bare `Type(...)` (which only works when the expected type is inferable from context).

Real-world occurrence — in `bobzhang/vg` the root package has `pub type Point = @geometry.Point`, so `@vg.Point(...)` fails while `@vg.Point::Point(...)` works.

## Proposal

Re-exporting a type (via `pub type Alias = @owner.T`, and arguably `pub using`) should also re-export the type's same-named associated constructor into the re-exporting package's value namespace, so that `@facade.Alias(...)` resolves consistently with `@facade.Alias::Alias(...)`.

## Environment

```
moon    0.1.20260618 (afb4494 2026-06-18)
moonc   v0.10.1+d1acd7ec2-nightly (2026-06-18)
```

title: Compiler desugars char-array literals to StringBuilder::new (blocks deprecating ::new)
body:
The MoonBit compiler desugars array literals like `[char_a, char_b]` into a `StringBuilder::new` + `to_string()` call when the expected type is `String`. Affected sites in core today (visible after renaming `StringBuilder::new` → `StringBuilder::StringBuilder` and tagging the old name `#alias(new, deprecated)`):

- `builtin/char.mbt:443` — `fn char_to_string(char) -> String { [char] }`
- `builtin/show.mbt:83` — `[to_hex_digit(b / 16), to_hex_digit(b % 16)]` in `Byte::to_hex`
- `builtin/traits.mbt:136` — `self.write_string([value])` in `impl Logger with write_char`

Each of these emits `Warning (deprecated): \`new\` is deprecated, use \`StringBuilder\` instead` even though the source code never names `StringBuilder::new`. With `--deny-warn` (used by `bleeding-check`, `pre-release-check`, `stable-check`) the build fails.

Because the compiler hard-codes the symbol name, the same warning would be emitted in every downstream user file that uses a char-array string literal — not just core.

### Workarounds

PR #(this PR) lands the rename as a non-deprecated alias (`#alias(new)` instead of `#alias(new, deprecated)`) so both names are valid and neither warns. Fully deprecating `StringBuilder::new` is blocked on the compiler emitting `StringBuilder::StringBuilder` (or just `StringBuilder`) in the desugar instead.

### Ask

Update the compiler to desugar char-array string literals to the new constructor name. Once that ships, this issue can be closed by changing the alias attribute back to `#alias(new, deprecated)` here in core.

title: Warning [0025] suggests wrong alias when module name's last segment differs from package directory name
body:
## Summary

Warning `[0025] test_unqualified_package` suggests an alias derived from the **module name's last segment** (from `moon.mod.json`'s `name` field) rather than from the **package directory name**. When those two don't match — and especially when the module-name segment contains a dash — the suggestion is misleading or outright unparseable.

## Repro

```bash
mkdir repro && cd repro

cat > moon.mod.json <<'JSON'
{ "name": "demo/animals", "source": "." }
JSON

mkdir cats
: > cats/moon.pkg

cat > cats/lib.mbt <<'MBT'
///|
pub fn meow() -> String { "meow" }
MBT

cat > cats/lib_test.mbt <<'MBT'
///|
test { ignore(meow()) }
MBT

moon check --warn-list +a
```

### Observed

```
Warning: [0025]
   ╭─[ cats/lib_test.mbt:2:14 ]
   │
 2 │ test { ignore(meow()) }
   │              ──┬─
   │                ╰── Warning (test_unqualified_package): \`meow\` is implicitly imported in test. Use \`@animals.meow\` instead.
```

Following the suggestion fails:

```
Error: [4020] Package \"animals\" not found in the loaded packages.
```

### Expected

The auto-derived alias should match MoonBit's documented convention — **the package directory name** (\`cats\` here), giving `@cats.meow`. The compiler's own implicit-import for blackbox tests should be aligned with that convention so the suggestion is also actionable.

## Worse failure mode: dashes

When the module-name segment contains a dash (e.g. `bobzhang/toml-e2e`), the suggested `@toml-e2e.foo` doesn't even parse since `-` is invalid in MoonBit identifiers, producing `[3002]` parse error in addition to the wrong alias:

```
Error: [3002] Parse error, unexpected token \`-\`, you may expect \`.\` id (lowercase start).
```

## Root cause hypothesis

The blackbox-test implicit import passes the package's mbi via `-i ...:<modname-segment>` rather than `-i ...:<dirname>`. Aligning the implicit alias with `<dirname>` (and threading the same alias into the [0025] suggestion) would fix both this case and the dash case in one go.

## Workaround

Add an explicit alias in the test imports so the package is bound under a parseable name:

```
import {
  \"demo/animals\" @cats,
} for \"test\"
```

then write `@cats.meow`.

## Environment

- \`moon 0.1.20260509 (8d0f1a5 2026-05-09)\`
- \`moonc v0.9.2+0687dbb64 (2026-05-09)\`
- macOS Darwin 25.0.0, target wasm-gc

title: Parser: newline before guard in comprehension/match gives confusing parse errors
body:
### Summary
A newline before `if` guard in array comprehensions and `match` arms causes parse errors like `Unexpected line break here, missing =>`, which can be surprising when formatting multiline code.

### Reproduction

#### 1) Comprehension
```moonbit
fn main {
  let xs = [1, 2, 3]
  let _ = [
    for x in xs
    if x > 1 => x
  ]
}
```

#### 2) Match guard
```moonbit
fn main {
  let x = Some(2)
  let y = match x {
    Some(v)
    if v > 1 => 1
    _ => 0
  }
  println(y.to_string())
}
```

### Actual
- `E3002 Unexpected line break here, missing => at the end of this line`
- Follow-up parse errors (e.g. unexpected `if`)

### Expected
Either:
1. Allow guard on the next line after pattern/iterable, or
2. Keep current grammar but emit a targeted diagnostic like: "guard `if` must be on the same line as `for ... in ...` or pattern".

### Notes
Same-line forms compile:
- `for x in xs if x > 1 => x`
- `Some(v) if v > 1 => 1`

title: wasm-gc backend: ReadOnlyArray::at fails to compile with packed-i8 array.get error
body:
Running `moon test` on a clean checkout of `main` (or any branch — reproduces independently of source changes) fails on the wasm-gc backend during execution of the `bool` blackbox test driver:

```
CompileError: WebAssembly.Module(): Compiling function #248:"_M0MPC15array13ReadOnlyArray2atGjE" failed: array.get: Immediate array type 71 has packed type i8. Use array.get_s or array.get_u instead. @+38042
Error: Failed to run the test: /Users/dii/git/core/_build/wasm-gc/debug/test/bool/bool.blackbox_test.wasm
The test executable exited with exit status: 1
```

The mangled symbol `_M0MPC15array13ReadOnlyArray2atGjE` resolves to `ReadOnlyArray::at` (`builtin/readonlyarray.mbt:25-41`), which delegates to `FixedArray::at`. The emitted wasm uses the unsigned `array.get` opcode against an array type whose element is declared as packed `i8`, which the wasm-gc spec only allows via `array.get_s` / `array.get_u`. Node's V8 engine therefore rejects the module at instantiation.

The compile-time output is fine; the failure happens when V8 validates the module, so the problem is in moonc's wasm-gc codegen for `ReadOnlyArray[T]` instantiated at a type whose backing FixedArray uses a packed representation.

## Reproduction

```sh
git clone git@github.com:moonbitlang/core.git
cd core
moon test                        # fails
moon test -p moonbitlang/core/bool   # smaller repro
moon test --target js            # passes (6367 tests)
moon test --target native        # passes (6321 tests)
```

## Environment

- macOS (Darwin 25.4.0, arm64)
- `moon 0.1.20260429 (26f35db 2026-04-29)`
- `moonc v0.9.1+dd1e997c9-nightly (2026-04-30)`
- `moonrun 0.1.20260429`
- Node.js v25.8.2 (Homebrew)

## Notes

- JS and native backends are unaffected.
- CI presumably uses an older Node.js (or a moonrun that bundles its own runtime), since the wasm-gc job passes there. This may be a regression triggered by stricter validation in newer V8 versions, or by recent codegen changes for `ReadOnlyArray` / packed `FixedArray`.

Originally surfaced while validating an unrelated PR (#3505); filing here so it can be tracked independently.

title: [Perf] JS target: abort() in moonbitlang/core (StringView, Array) silently pulls ~5KB into release builds
body:
## Summary

When MoonBit code is compiled to JS with `--release`, `abort()` calls pull in SourceLoc formatting code (SourceLocRepr, StringBuilder, StringView, Int.to_string — about 5KB minified) that bundlers like esbuild cannot tree-shake.

The problem is that **`moonbitlang/core` uses `abort()` internally** for bounds checking in `StringView`, `Array`, and `ArrayView`. Library authors who never write `abort()` themselves unknowingly inherit this overhead just by using standard string/array operations. There is no way to discover this from the MoonBit source — it only becomes visible by inspecting the compiled JS output.

## How we discovered this

In [mizchi/luna](https://github.com/mizchi/luna.mbt) (UI library), I track JS bundle sizes with esbuild tree-shaking. After a compiler upgrade, `signals-only` went from 5,915 to 11,175 bytes (+89%). Investigation showed the entire increase was SourceLoc/StringBuilder code pulled in by a single `abort()` in our dependency (`mizchi/signals`).

I replaced that `abort()` with `panic()` to fix our own code. However, if any code path in the package can reach an `abort()` — even indirectly through `moonbitlang/core`'s `StringView` bounds check or `Array` indexing — the entire SourceLoc/StringBuilder chain is included in the compiled output and cannot be tree-shaken away. This means that any package using standard string or array operations may silently carry this overhead without the author being aware of it.

## Dependency chain

```
User code
  → String.sub() / String.view()
    → StringView constructor (stringview.mbt:399)
      → abort("Invalid index for View")
        → SourceLocRepr.parse()     -- parses "file.mbt:42:5" string
        → StringBuilder             -- Logger trait impls (write_string, write_char, write_view, write_substring)
        → Int.to_string             -- formats line/column numbers
        → Compare impls             -- op_ge, op_le for Int
```

The same applies to:
- `Array` indexing → `abort("index out of bounds: ...")` (arraycore_js.mbt:251)
- `ArrayView` indexing → `abort("index out of bounds: ...")` (arrayview.mbt:135)

## Reproduction

https://github.com/mizchi/repro_abort_size

```bash
bash compare.sh
```

Two packages with identical logic, differing only in error handling:

```moonbit
// src/with_abort/lib.mbt — uses abort()
None => abort("unreachable")

// src/with_panic/lib.mbt — uses panic()
None => panic()
```

```
=== Minified (esbuild --bundle --minify) ===
  with_abort: 4,897 bytes (26 functions)
  with_panic:   136 bytes ( 2 functions)
  overhead:  +4,761 bytes
```

## Suggestion

For JS `--release` builds, consider compiling `abort(msg)` without the SourceLoc formatting machinery — for example, as `throw new Error(msg)` directly. The formatted source location (file:line:column) is valuable during development but adds significant dead weight to production bundles.

This would also benefit `moonbitlang/core` itself, since its bounds checks would no longer pull in StringBuilder/StringView/Int.to_string in release builds.

## Environment

- moon 0.1.20260309 (f21b520 2026-03-09)
- esbuild 0.25.x for tree-shaking measurement

title: Missing min, max, clamp, signum for Float/Double/Int64/UInt
Add clamp and lerp methods to Float/Double
body:
## Summary

`Float` and `Double` are missing common numeric utility methods that many projects end up reimplementing. Currently `Float` has `abs`, `ceil`, `floor`, `round`, `trunc`, `sqrt`, but lacks `clamp` and `lerp`.

## Missing methods

### `Float::clamp(self: Float, min: Float, max: Float) -> Float`
Clamps a value into the inclusive range `[min, max]`. This is extremely common in graphics, animation, and game code. Rust, C# (`Math.Clamp`), GLSL, HLSL, and Swift all provide this as a standard numeric operation.

### `Float::lerp(self: Float, target: Float, t: Float) -> Float`
Linear interpolation: `self + (target - self) * t`. Widely used in animation, easing, color blending, and physics. Available in C# (`MathF.Lerp`), GLSL/HLSL (`mix`/`lerp`), Rust (`f32::lerp` unstable), and Swift.

The same methods should also be added to `Double`.

## Motivation

While writing a 2048 game in MoonBit with raylib, I needed both `clampf` and `lerpf` for tile animation (slide interpolation and scale pop effects). I had to write custom free functions for these in a utility file. `abs` was also custom but I was able to replace it with the built-in `Float::abs()` -- `clamp` and `lerp` had no such equivalent.

These are fundamental numeric operations that belong in the standard library alongside `abs`, `ceil`, `floor`, etc.

title: Make `builtin.abort` virtual
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
I want to optimize for _binary size_.

The `builtin.abort()` uses formatted string and `SourceLoc`, which brings in ~5kB when compiled to WASM. As `builtin.abort()` is used a lot throughout the core library then it's really hard to avoid it.

https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/d3224da03524d09e0cd568e896bf904bd619327a/builtin/intrinsics.mbt#L69-L78

**Describe the solution you'd like**
MoonBit has virtual packages. Could `builtin.abort()` be moved into a virtual package? Or could the formatting and `SourceLoc` be moved to the `abort` package as it's already a virtual package?

https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/d3224da03524d09e0cd568e896bf904bd619327a/abort/abort.mbt#L26-L30

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I've tried overriding `abort` package as suggested in https://github.com/moonbitlang/moon/issues/1369, but that doesn't remove the string formatting and `SourceLoc` code as that code lives in `builtin.abort()`


**Additional context**
When using MoonBit on embedded devices (e.g [Firefly Zero](https://fireflyzero.com/)) then binary size is very important, where +5kB is a lot. For the Firefly Zero use case we also use `Bytes` a lot instead of `String` as the FFI requires UTF-8, and so we don't want to include the string-related code in the final build.

- [x] I do think that this should be part of the core library and should be delivered to all the MoonBit developers.

title: Request: wasm SIMD (v128) support in Dwarfsm inline WAT parser
body:
## Motivation

I'm building a SIMD abstraction module for MoonBit ([mizchi/simd](https://github.com/mizchi/simd)) that provides optimized array operations (sum, dot product, adler32, etc.). The native target achieves 13–33x speedup via C FFI, but the wasm target is stuck on scalar fallback because Dwarfsm doesn't fully support v128 SIMD instructions.

Related: #2844

## Current Dwarfsm v128 Support Status

I investigated the Dwarfsm source (`dwarfsm_parse.ml` in moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler) and tested inline WAT with various v128 instructions:

| Feature | Status | Notes |
|---------|--------|-------|
| `v128` as valtype (`param`/`result`) | ✅ Works | |
| `v128.load` / `v128.store` | ✅ Works | Memory access |
| `f32x4.add`, `f32x4.mul`, `f64x2.add`, `f64x2.mul` | ✅ Works | Float SIMD ops |
| `v128.const` | ❌ Parse error | Constant initialization |
| `i32x4.add`, `i32x4.mul`, etc. | ❌ Parse error | Integer SIMD ops |
| `i32x4.extract_lane`, `i8x16.shuffle` | ❌ Parse error | Lane manipulation |

## Two Remaining Blockers

### 1. Missing instruction table entries in Dwarfsm

`i32x4.*`, `i8x16.*`, `v128.const`, and other integer SIMD instructions are not registered in `dwarfsm_parse.ml`. The float SIMD ops (`f32x4.*`, `f64x2.*`) already work, so adding the missing patterns to the instruction table should be straightforward.

### 2. `#external type` maps to `externref` in wasm

When defining `#external type V128` in MoonBit, it compiles to `externref` in the wasm output. This causes a type mismatch with inline WAT that uses `v128`:

```
CompileError: type mismatch (externref vs v128)
```

A language-level `v128` type or a way to control the wasm representation of `#external type` would be needed.

## Context

- Repository with benchmarks and investigation: https://github.com/mizchi/simd
- The `wasm_memory_ptr` pattern (`FixedArray` ptr + 8 byte offset) for linear memory access has been verified and is ready for use once SIMD support lands.

## Requested Changes

1. Add missing v128 instruction patterns to `dwarfsm_parse.ml` (integer SIMD ops + `v128.const`)
2. Provide a way to use `v128` as a proper wasm value type (not `externref`) from MoonBit code

title: [BUG]`inspect` should reject invisible character / control character
body:
Consider the following code:

```moonbit
///|
test {
  let multi_str = "a\r\nb\r\nc"
  inspect(multi_str)
}
```

The expected output is `a\r\nb\r\nc`. Currently on the `moon` side, when executing `moon test --update`, it will split by `\n`, and transform the rest of the code as is into something like `"#|\{rest}"`. This is problematic with `\r`, because now the generated snapshot will be `#|a\r\n` `#|b\r\n` `#|c\r\n` (here the `\r\n` are the corresponding ascii char. But the compiler will consider `\r\n` as line separator, so the final string generated will be considered as `a\nb\nc\n`, which does not correspond to the actual code. Thus, `moon test --update` will never succeed.

The other issue happens when we have `\0`. Following the same principle, the updated file will have the character `\0` inside the file. But tools like `rg` will consider it as binary file and refuse to work correctly.

Therefore, I propose that `inspect` rejects the strings that contains ascii control sequences, except `\n`, and strings that contain zero-width characters.

title: [BUG] BigInt parses “-0” as negative zero in non‑JS backend
body:
In the non‑JS implementation, BigInt::from_string("-0") and BigInt::from_hex("-0") produce a "negative zero".to_string() returns "0", but the internal sign remains negative, so equality and comparison against 0N are inconsistent.

### Impact
- @bigint.BigInt::from_string("-0") == 0N is false
- @bigint.BigInt::from_hex("-0") == 0N is false
- compare(0N) returns -1
- to_string() returns "0"
- JS backend doesn’t have this issue (`-0n == 0n` is true)

```mbt
test "from_string negative zero" {
  let z = @bigint.BigInt::from_string("-0")
  inspect(z.to_string(), content="0")
  assert_true(z == 0N)
  assert_eq(z.compare(0N), 0)
}
test "from_hex negative zero" {
  let z = @bigint.BigInt::from_hex("-0")
  inspect(z.to_string(), content="0")
  assert_true(z == 0N)
  assert_eq(z.compare(0N), 0)
}
```

title: [BUG] Deque::retain / Deque::retain_map do not clear when full and wrapped
body:
When a deque is full and wrapped (head != 0), calling retain(_ => false) or retain_map(_ => None) does not clear it. The length stays non‑zero and views still contain the original elements.

```moonbit
test "retain full wrapped" {
  let dq = @deque.new(capacity=4)
  dq..push_back(1)..push_back(2)..push_back(3)..push_back(4)
  ignore(dq.pop_front())
  dq.push_back(5) // full + wrapped
  dq.retain(_ => false)
  inspect(dq.as_views(), content="([], [])")
}

test "retain_map full wrapped" {
  let dq = @deque.new(capacity=4)
  dq..push_back(1)..push_back(2)..push_back(3)..push_back(4)
  ignore(dq.pop_front())
  dq.push_back(5) // full + wrapped
  dq.retain_map(_ => None)
  inspect(dq.as_views(), content="([], [])")
}
```

Expected

  - retain(false) / retain_map(None) clears the deque
  - dq.is_empty() is true
  - dq.as_views() returns ([], [])

  Actual

  - dq.as_views() stays ([2, 3, 4], [5])
  - dq.is_empty() is false

title: Basic operator overloading capability extension
body:
In vector operations, we typically need to overload multiplication and division operators to implement vector scaling operations.

For example: 
```c++
Eigen::Vector3 v;
auto r = v * 3.0; // Expand the vector by 3 times
```
Therefore, we need to overload the multiplication operator, one of which is `self`, and the other is a scalar.

Currently, the `Mul` trait only supports two `Self` operators, which is insufficient for this operation. We can only achieve this by implementing a `scale` function, but this approach doesn't align with mathematical intuition.

```
pub(open) trait Mul {
  mul(Self, Self) -> Self = _
  #deprecated("use `mul` instead", skip_current_package=true)
  op_mul(Self, Self) -> Self = _
}
```

We hope to extend the `Mul`, `Div`, and other traits.

We also hope to extend the `AssignAdd`, `AssignSub`, `AssignMul`, and `AssignDiv` traits.

title: Add two functions Map::merge and Map::merge_in_place
body:
Introduce two complementary APIs for merging maps:
	1.	Map::merge — pure, returns a new map
	2.	Map::merge_in_place — mutating, updates the receiver

This provides an explicit and predictable way to combine maps without ambiguity about whether the operation mutates.

⸻

Motivation

Map merging is a very common operation across parsing, configuration loading, environment propagation, JSON/TOML merging, and AI-generated code.

Currently, users need to manually iterate and insert entries, or clone + extend, which is verbose and error-prone.

We want to provide:
	•	a pure API for functional-style usage
	•	a mutating API for performance-sensitive paths
	•	clear naming that avoids ambiguity

The pair merge + merge_in_place is explicit, IDE-discoverable, and consistent with MoonBit’s principle:

non-mutating operations are short; mutating operations are explicit.

title: Forbid to create ill-formatted String
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Yes.

The current `String::from_array()` API allows creating ill-formatted strings while panicking at `char_length_eq` or returning `None` from `get_char(0)`, for example:

https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/pull/1642/files#diff-2bcc32825564e7b03c6f324bbca9ac41660e7bfb8e0dd868cfe18e3661d63f24R414-R433

In my opinion, if you have a `String` object already, it should always be valid. I'm working on an alternative MoonBit runtime, where `String` is physically stored as UTF-8 characters, offering a UTF-16-like emulation layer on top to be compliant to MoonBit. This particular ill-formatted `String` assumption is basically impossible to emulate in my implementation.

### Describe the solution you'd like

`String::from_array()` should simply panic if the given array is an illegal UTF-16 string.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I don't see any alternative in MoonBit API design, because it doesn't make sense when you have a `String` object, but you cannot do anything about it. I can possibly use invalid UTF-8 characters to emulate invalid UTF-16 characters in my runtime, but that just doesn't make sense either.

**Additional context**

title: [performance] Improve performance of `Int::to_string`
body:
**Background** `Int::to_string` is a commonly used API and it's implemented by calling `Int::output`

**But** `Int::output` is not implemented very efficiently for two reasons: 1. the inner function `write_digits` is not a tail-recursive function; 2. it calls `logger.write_char`, which is a dynamic object method call, repeatedly.

**Therefore** I would like it to be improved in several ways: 1. using a tail-recursive helper function or a loop to write each digit; 2. write to a buffer of type `FixedArray[Byte]` or `StringBuilder` first and then dump it to the logger. This should improve the performance.

title: [Consistency Review] Unify `::from_array` and `::of` to `::from_array`
Proposal: Change Array::`chunks` and `chunk_by` to Return Views
body:
The current implementations of `Array::chunks` and `Array::chunk_by` create a new `Array[T]` for each chunk. This has two main drawbacks:

1.  **Performance Overhead**: For each chunk, new memory must be allocated, and elements from the original array must be copied into the new array. This can be very inefficient, especially when dealing with large arrays or a large number of chunks.

2.  **Increased Memory Usage**: Creating copies of data for each chunk leads to a significantly higher memory footprint, as the data is duplicated in memory.

By returning an `Array[ArrayView[T]]`, we can adopt a **zero-copy** approach. `ArrayView` is a lightweight structure that simply points to a slice of the original array's data without taking ownership or creating a copy.

## Impact

This is a **breaking change**. Code that relies on the return type being `Array[Array[T]]` will no longer compile. For example, code that attempts to modify the returned chunks will fail, as `ArrayView` is immutable.

Migration is straightforward:
- If the user only needs to read from the chunks, no change is needed other than updating type annotations.
- If the user needs a mutable `Array[T]` for a chunk, they must now explicitly call `.to_array()` on the `ArrayView`.

body:
It is more than often that AI and me mistakenly think calling `write_string` from `Logger` implementation on `@buffer.Buffer` will write a `String` into the buffer with UTF-8 encoding.

Therefore, I'd like to suggest the removal of `Logger` implementation from `@buffer.Buffer` as its semantics is not obvious by purely reading the function signature. Informally,

1. `@buffer.Buffer` is encoding-agnostic;
2. `Logger` are built around `String`/`Char`, which internally use UTF-16.

This mismatch can sometimes lead to misuse and mix-encoded content.

However, the migration needs MoonBit compiler to support deprecating an implementation of a trait.

```moonbit
#deprecated("Use write_string_utf8/write_string_utf16 instead")
pub impl Logger for Buffer ...
```

Alternatively, we may also:

1. Change the behavior of `write_string` to write UTF-8 string instead. IMO, this is dangerous because it silently changes the behavior significantly without warning.
2. Change the definition of `Logger` trait to something like:

   ```moonbit
   trait Logger {
     write_string_utf16(...) // LE, BE?
     ...
   }
   ```

   So that its semantics are more obvious from plain sight. This methods does not need any extra support from compiler, and is probably simpler to implement.

title: performance(`$moonbit.unsafe_bytes_sub_string`)
Change the internal behavior of expect/snapshot tests
body:
## Background

I am currently doing a major rewrite of `moon` at moonbitlang/moon#802. During rewrite, a behavior that consistently annoyed me is how expect tests (`inspect` and friends) work under the hood when updating snapshots. 

This might be blocker to achieving feature-parity with legacy code for `moon test` -- I am against implementing the legacy behavior again in the new code, which is supposed to be actually maintainable.

(And no, I'm not talking about all those heuristics needed to find the patch point. That's #2601.)

## The issue

When an expect test fails, it aborts the current control flow by throwing an `InspectError`. The error bubbles up the call stack, ultimately reaching the `test` block containing it, and gets captured.

https://github.com/moonbitlang/core/blob/3c615179f2ee3a60773d674cee7df4ebf56d857b/builtin/console.mbt#L40-L53

This is a very valid control flow when doing regular tests. However, the `inspect` function does not know whether we're updating snapshot results or not. This means that, upon an expect test failure when we're updating results, the function also unconditionally **aborts the control flow** to send the "expect failed" message, preventing the tests after it (if any) to execute.

The main consequence of it is that **all failed expect tests need at least 2 execution rounds in order to be updated** to the expected value and ensure that no other checks fails within it, which costs significant time, compilation effort, and degrades user experiences.

Moreover, since when updating expect tests, an inspection failure is not an error, the test error representing the failure must not be displayed. Instead, the displayed result should be the test result **after all expect tests are updated**. This means either:

- You give up batch updates, but you need to do the expect updates midway during test result processing, or
- You want batch updates, but you need to hold the result reporting back. until all your updates has finished.

Either way, you severely degrade the user experience because the issue lies in how expect tests are updated.

## The solution

> This part is inspired by expect test implementations in other languages.

I propose that we add an internal global flag, which we will call it `update_expect` from here. The flag is `true` if we're updating expect tests, `false` otherwise.

When `update_expect` is `false`, the behavior is exactly the same as the current one -- bail out on the first expect failure.

When `update_expect` is `true`, `inspect` and similar functions **should never throw an error**. If the expected value require updating, it reports the to-be-updated value to the test driver (the actual method TBD), and returns normally as if the check has passed.

In this way, **all expect tests can be updated at once**, and the test result is the same as that if the expected values are already updated (either case the expect tests will pass). All test cases will need to be executed once and only once, and all updates can be applied in a single batch. It would greatly simplify how the relevant test handlers are implemented, and provide a much better and consistent experience to the user.

## Remaining questions

- How should we set the flag? Env var, special flags in the test driver, or what else?
- How should we accept the update requests? If needing to be cross-platform and matching existing tools, it should be within delimiters in `stdout`.

title: [Consistency Review] `Option` and `Result` API
body:
**Current behaviors**

MoonBit `Option` has the following three helper functions, while `Result` does not. These APIs need to be aligned.

```moonbit 
fn[T] Option::unwrap_or(T?, T) -> T
fn[T : Default] Option::unwrap_or_default(T?) -> T

```

**Expected behaviors**

```moonbit
fn[T,E] Result::unwrap_or(Result[T,E], T) -> T
fn[T : Default,E] Result::unwrap_or_default(Result[T,E]) -> T
fn[T,E] Result::unwrap_or_else(Result[T,E], () -> T raise?) -> T raise?
```

**Justification**

`Option[T]` and `Result[T, Unit]` are equivalent.

title: [BUG] Hash for immut hashmap
HashMap / HashSet use fixed seed (0) in xxHash32 — vulnerable to HashDoS attacks
body:
Hello Moonbit team,

I noticed that the current implementation of HashMap / HashSet in the core library uses xxHash32 with a fixed seed = 0 as the default hashing strategy.

This design choice has some serious security implications:

### Problem

1. xxHash32 is not collision-resistant. It was designed for speed, not for adversarial scenarios.
2. With a fixed seed 0, the hash function becomes deterministic and predictable.
3. An attacker can precompute a large set of colliding keys that all map to the same hash value.
4. By sending these crafted keys to any Moonbit program that stores untrusted input in a HashMap/HashSet, the hash table operations degrade from O(1) average time to O(n) or worse, leading to CPU exhaustion DoS attack.

This is exactly the kind of vulnerability that affected PHP, Python, Java, Ruby, and many other languages in the past (see [HashDoS 2011 advisory](https://ocert.org/advisories/ocert-2011-003.html)).

### Benchmark Evidence

I wrote a small benchmark to demonstrate:
1. SequentialKey1 – a set of sequential keys, no collisions.
2. SequentialKey2 – another set of sequential keys, aslo no collisions.
3. CollidingKey – 64 keys that all collide under xxHash32.

```moonbit
test (b : @bench.T) {
  let key1 = [
    "key0", "key01", "key02", "key03", "key004", "key005", "key006", "key007", "key008",
    "key009", "key010", "key011", "key012", "key013", "key014", "key015", "key016",
    "key017", "key018", "key0019", "key0020", "key0021", "key0022", "key0023", "key0024",
    "key0025", "key0026", "key0027", "key0028", "key0029", "key0030", "key0031",
    "key0032", "key0033", "key0034", "key0035", "key0036", "key0037", "key0038",
    "key0039", "key0040", "key0041", "key0042", "key0043", "key0044", "key0045",
    "key0046", "key0047", "key0048", "key0049", "key0050", "key0051", "key0052",
    "key0053", "key0054", "key0055", "key0056", "key0057", "key0058", "key0059",
    "key0060", "key0061", "key0062", "key0063",
  ]
  b.bench(name="SequentialKey1", fn() {
    let map = @hashmap.new()
    for i in 0..<key1.length() {
      map.set(key1[i], i)
    }
  })
  let key2 = [
    "cat0", "cat01", "cat02", "cat03", "cat004", "cat005", "cat006", "cat007", "cat008",
    "cat009", "cat010", "cat011", "cat012", "cat013", "cat014", "cat015", "cat016",
    "cat017", "cat018", "cat0019", "cat0020", "cat0021", "cat0022", "cat0023", "cat0024",
    "cat0025", "cat0026", "cat0027", "cat0028", "cat0029", "cat0030", "cat0031",
    "cat0032", "cat0033", "cat0034", "cat0035", "cat0036", "cat0037", "cat0038",
    "cat0039", "cat0040", "cat0041", "cat0042", "cat0043", "cat0044", "cat0045",
    "cat0046", "cat0047", "cat0048", "cat0049", "cat0050", "cat0051", "cat0052",
    "cat0053", "cat0054", "cat0055", "cat0056", "cat0057", "cat0058", "cat0059",
    "cat0060", "cat0061", "cat0062", "cat0063",
  ]
  b.bench(name="SequentialKey2", fn() {
    let map = @hashmap.new()
    for i in 0..<key2.length() {
      map.set(key2[i], i)
    }
  })
  let key3 = [
    "key0", "key15", "key72", "key94", "key337", "key349", "key387", "key407", "key451",
    "key456", "key474", "key572", "key706", "key720", "key724", "key828", "key929",
    "key932", "key999", "key1097", "key1115", "key1186", "key1246", "key1271", "key1304",
    "key1350", "key1353", "key1385", "key1409", "key1445", "key1456", "key1568",
    "key1703", "key1746", "key1768", "key1805", "key1903", "key1916", "key2073",
    "key2088", "key2149", "key2233", "key2277", "key2358", "key2370", "key2395",
    "key2429", "key2457", "key2529", "key2555", "key2558", "key2663", "key2665",
    "key2725", "key2738", "key2755", "key2831", "key2846", "key2889", "key2892",
    "key3109", "key3152", "key3181", "key3183",
  ]
  b.bench(name="CollidingKey", fn() {
    let map = @hashmap.new()
    for i in 0..<key3.length() {
      map.set(key3[i], i)
    }
  })
}
```

Benchmark results on my machine:
```
name           time (mean ± σ)         range (min … max) 
SequentialKey1    4.64 µs ±   0.06 µs     4.57 µs …   4.75 µs  in 10 ×  20681 runs
SequentialKey2    4.36 µs ±   0.02 µs     4.33 µs …   4.39 µs  in 10 ×  22589 runs
CollidingKey     10.54 µs ±   0.03 µs    10.49 µs …  10.58 µs  in 10 ×   9458 runs
```
Even with only 64 colliding keys, the runtime already doubles compared to non-colliding cases. With larger numbers of colliding keys, the cost grows roughly O(n²), which makes DoS attacks very feasible. 

Benchmark results with 256 keys on my machine:
```
name           time (mean ± σ)         range (min … max) 
SequentialKey1   20.56 µs ±   0.20 µs    20.39 µs …  21.03 µs  in 10 ×   4697 runs
SequentialKey2   21.34 µs ±   0.11 µs    21.13 µs …  21.45 µs  in 10 ×   4668 runs
CollidingKey    116.14 µs ±   0.22 µs   115.80 µs … 116.47 µs  in 10 ×    857 runs
```

If you want to reproduce this issue yourself, I have created [a small script](https://gist.github.com/quake/24553468f0da10ece737bdd641f0022a) that generates colliding keys for xxHash32(seed=0). You can use these generated keys with the current HashMap / HashSet implementation to easily observe the performance degradation caused by collisions.

### Suggested Fix

1. Do not use a fixed seed (0) by default.
2. Instead, initialize the seed with a random value at program startup (similar to Rust’s RandomState or Go’s runtime hash seeding).
3. This makes it impractical for an attacker to precompute collisions, since the seed changes on every run.
4. Consider using a stronger keyed hash function (e.g., SipHash or AHash) for default hashing in security-sensitive contexts. (If performance is the main concern, xxHash32 is fine with random seeding)

### Why this matters
Most developers will rely on HashMap/HashSet without thinking about hash function details. The current implementation exposes every Moonbit application that accepts untrusted keys (e.g. from HTTP requests, JSON parsing, etc.) to potential DoS attacks.

Making random seeding the default behavior provides a safe baseline without affecting existing APIs.

Importantly, in the recent years, all mainstream production-ready languages and runtimes (including Rust, Go, Java, Python, JavaScript/Node.js, Ruby, PHP, etc.) have already adopted randomized hash seeding to mitigate HashDoS attacks. Using a fixed seed is no longer considered a safe or modern default.

title: [BUG] `ToJson` regression in `moonc v0.6.23+906028000`
body:
**Describe the bug**
The `derive(ToJson)` of a `Newtype` containing a `Map` used to render as a JSON Object correctly, but as of `moonc v0.6.23` it now renders as a JSON Array containing a JSON Object as if it were a tuple, which is incorrect.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a MoonBit `NewType`, like this:

```mbt
pub(all) struct Header(Map[String, String]) derive(Show, Eq, ToJson)
pub(all) struct Request {
  header : Header
  url : String
} derive(ToJson)
```

2. Render it with `to_json`:

```mbt
test "Request::to_json works as expected" {
  let request = {
    header: { "key1": "one", "key2": "two" },
    url: "https://example.com",
  }
  let got = request.to_json().stringify(escape_slash=false)
  let want =
    #|{"header":{"key1":"one","key2":"two"},"url":"https://example.com"}
  assert_eq(got, want)
}
```

The above fails with:

```
test gmlewis/moonbit-pdk/pdk/http/http.mbt::Request::to_json works as expected failed: FAILED: /Users/glenn/src/github.com/gmlewis/moonbit-03-pdk/pdk/http/http.mbt:71:3-71:23 `"{\"header\":[\"Header\",{\"key1\":\"one\",\"key2\":\"two\"}],\"url\":\"https://example.com\"}" != "{\"header\":{\"key1\":\"one\",\"key2\":\"two\"},\"url\":\"https://example.com\"}"`
Total tests: 1, passed: 0, failed: 1.
```

**Expected behavior**
Previously, the `Header` would be rendered as a JSON Object, but now is rendering as a JSON Array with a JSON Object as if it were a tuple.
The full example can be found here:
https://github.com/gmlewis/moonbit-pdk/blob/1e70a1fff315af4374c9a820c5f5f285f6f1e78a/pdk/http/http.mbt#L62-L72

**Version**

```
$ moon version --all
moon 0.1.20250801 (edae1ae 2025-08-01) ~/.moon/bin/moon
moonc v0.6.23+906028000 ~/.moon/bin/moonc

title: [BUG] Incorrect String comparison implementation
